The affordable housing crisis — which critics say is exacerbated by Airbnb — means less housing is available for people displaced by disasters.

Should a for-profit enterprise use its philanthropy to offset less desirable business impacts? Leading artificial intelligence companies, currently sketching out plans to share some of their wealth, say yes.

For Chesky, the answer is emphatically “no.” He denied Airbnb is “the contributor of the reason cities are expensive” but acknowledged that some hosts take a small fraction of their area's housing off the market. This week's commitment is about doing the “right thing” with the company's “natural superpower,” he said.

“I don’t like this idea that somehow you create a nonprofit to make up for or apologize for your core business," Chesky told The Associated Press. "Our core business, independently, is gonna affect a lot more lives than this organization. And our core business needs to be responsible. And if we’re doing something that’s not responsible, we need to correct it.”

Many governments, including the country of Spain and the city of New York, have recently moved to curb short-term rentals. The company could use its growing philanthropic footprint to further ingrain its product into communities and legitimize the presence of short-term rentals as its model is contested, according to Ka­ro­lina Mikoła­jew­ska-Za­jąc, a postdoctoral fellow at Copenhagen Business School who researches the societal impacts of digital platforms. She cautioned the humanitarian sector against growing too dependent on commercial platforms.
Murray Cox, the founder of the data activist project Inside Airbnb, noted one “crisis” missing from the nonprofit's list of emergency housing interventions.

“There’s also the housing crisis that’s occurring around the world,” Cox said. “And, although they’re not causing the housing crisis, they’re contributing to it by taking millions of housing units -- residential houses -- off the housing market.”
Airbnb.org is squarely focused on short-term emergency housing.

Launched formally in 2020 as the San Francisco-based company went public, the nonprofit uses company-donated credits to book stays on its platform for those experiencing crises. Since then, the nonprofit reports having provided 1.6 million nights of free, temporary housing in nearly 140 countries. Fees are dropped and hosts are compensated. The nonprofit also provides credits for other relief organizations to book stays.

Beneficiaries include people recovering from natural disasters, families traveling for medical care and survivors escaping domestic violence. When Washington state wildfires forced tens of thousands of evacuations in August, Airbnb.org said it provided more than 1,400 nights of free housing in the disaster's early days.

Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org, compares the nonprofit to “the ambulance that'll get you to the hospital.” Short-term housing is a “great product-market fit," he said, because they're able to “house a lot of people very quickly with an enormous amount of flexibility to meet their particular needs.”
He emphasized that the new funding mechanism will provide a “lot more money” that the nonprofit can depend on each year. “It’s not just shuffling the deck chairs around,” he said.

The $500 million five-year injection would more than double the total contributions reported by Airbnb.org between 2021 and 2025. The company would have to register 5 billion bookings over the next five years to reach that figure through the sliver of each booking donated to the nonprofit.
Chesky emphasized that the commitment will be completed regardless of business outcomes.
“We felt like this is a responsible number where it’s sufficiently big to make a difference in the world," Chesky said. “But it’s also a number shareholders can be comfortable with.”

Short-term assistance from nonprofits such as Airbnb.org and government entities such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency are “key for preventing that initial displacement,” according to Noah Patton, the director of disaster recovery at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. That's especially so as an AP analysis showed President Donald Trump takes longer to approve disaster aid and denies a greater percentage of requests than his predecessors.
But Patton said there's a need for more lasting solutions so “folks have homes to return back to."
“It's a Band-Aid if you don't also focus on the long-term aspect of this,” he said.
Airbnb.org will also expand its medical stays program to 20 countries by the end of the year.

The nonprofit partners with medical relief organizations to provide housing for families traveling to get treatment. Airbnbs, according to Gorder, allow families to bring additional relatives and pets that some alternatives don't allow. Amenities such as kitchens, sometimes not available in hotels or hospital lodgings, give the option to cook patients' favorite foods.
“And then they just have a quiet place at the end of the day,” Gorder said. “So, it's a lot more than four walls and a roof.”

In Mexico, where the program was piloted last fall, Airbnb.org says it has housed medical travelers for nearly 1,500 nights. Its first partner, Vuela Fundación, supports children diagnosed with cancer. Many of the Mexico City-based organization's clients travel from poor rural towns and lack access to the country's social security system.

Diego Parada Herrera, the co-founder and CEO, said it's not uncommon to see families camping in tents or sleeping in parked cars outside of hospitals because they couldn't afford to stay anywhere else.
“The need was there. And we were conscious of it,” he said. “But we didn't know how to address it.”

Airbnb.org now provides his organization with credits that case managers use to complete bookings for families in need. Some hosts offer discounted rates, he said. Vuela Fundación stocks fridges with ready-to-cook food packages.

The challenge, he's found, is that many families aren't technologically savvy. Some aren't familiar with Airbnb's business model and struggle to grasp that they'll be staying in someone else's home. His nonprofit created instructional videos and shows them how to use the platform.
Chesky said the company will likely “keep going” based on how this expansion goes.
“Whatever people think of us, we’re doing this for decades,” he said. “It’s up to them to judge us and our motivations. And it’s up to us to have a commitment that’s a decade-long commitment.”

title: Average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
WASHINGTON -- The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month.
The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell to 7.24% from 7.32% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.17%.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also fell this week. That average rate dipped to 6.60% from 6.68% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.41%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.
The yield was at 4.98% at midday on the bond market Thursday. It surged to more than 5.30% earlier this month and remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

title: Starbucks reports lower than expected revenue on softer international demand
summary: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
story: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened.

The Seattle coffee giant said global same-store sales rose 7.2% for the July-September period, which was higher than the 6% increase Wall Street was expecting, according to analysts polled by FactSet.

That was largely due to strong demand in the U.S., where same-store sales jumped 7.7%. International same-store sales rose less than 1%, and Starbucks noted a 2.8% decline in international store traffic.
Net revenue fell 4% for the quarter to $9.14 billion. That was lower than the $9.2 billion analysts were forecasting.

title: Netanyahu’s party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his party have amplified claims that the country's election was “stolen” by Arab-led parties
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his party have amplified claims that the country's election was “stolen” by Arab-led parties

JERUSALEM -- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.

The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.

Results released by election officials early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.

Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.

Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!” it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was “aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government.”
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”

As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. “They are doing this because they lost,” he said.

Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: “I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel.”
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.

By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.

The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”

The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.

On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of “attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular.”
“Netanyahu is working to steal the election,” the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.

The head of the Arab-led Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.

President Isaac Herzog called it a “sensitive moment” and called for a full investigation. He warned that “we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”

The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.

If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.

Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate.

There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.

If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.

New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
Saeed reported from Abu Snan, Israel. Associated Press reporters across Israel contributed to this report.
This version has corrected that the final results were released early Friday, not Thursday, local time.

title: Frances Tiafoe supports young tennis players' careers while still building his own
summary: Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone
story: Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone
Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the up-and-coming American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone.

His Frances Tiafoe Fund, which supports tennis programs for young people in underresourced communities, recently passed $1 million in funds raised, only three years after its launch. It’s unusual for athletes to start nonprofits early in their careers, but the 28-year-old says he didn’t want to wait to start giving back because his impact would be greater now.

“I think young players will know me more now,” Tiafoe told The Associated Press. “While I’m at my ‘peak’ and doing things on a high level, I wanted to inspire, to give back. I wanted to be a man of the people because I was given so much.”

Tiafoe, who made his third trip in the past five years to the U.S. Open semifinals this summer, first started playing tennis when he was 4 years old at the Junior Tennis Champions Center in College Park, Maryland. His father was the center’s head of maintenance after immigrating from Sierra Leone in 1996.
“I’m just a kid who got a chance,” said Tiafoe, adding that the support he received from his team at an early age was critical to his success.

“It helped me believe it before I actually did it,” he said. “You’ve got to have a big support system. You’ve got to have people who believe in the vision before you do, who see you in a bigger place than you do so that they continue to push you. They hold you to a certain standard so you’re able to go to work every day with an approach in hand.”

Ginny Ehrlich, CEO of the USTA Foundation, the United States Tennis Association’s charitable arm which administers Tiafoe's fund, said Tiafoe is not just “one of the few players” who started a fund while still an active player, but is also hands-on in where and how its donations are made.
“He is so passionate about wanting to give back,” she said, adding he wants young people who are growing up in situations similar to his to “have that same access and opportunity.”

The Tiafoe Fund provides college scholarships, as well as smaller grants to help individual players get ready for playing collegiate tennis, Ehrlich said. The fund also supports young players so they can pay for travel, equipment and training they would otherwise not be able to afford. And Tiafoe also supports programs at some tennis centers, including the Maryland center where he got his start.

“It’s so electric to have someone who walks the talk, right?” Ehrlich said. “It’s priceless, really, in terms of his impact. I don’t mean impact in dollars, I mean impact on inspiring the next generation to achieve whatever their dreams are.”

Tiafoe said he is proud to be able to help in these ways, especially in a time where scholarships for tennis players are harder to come by as athletic departments prioritize money-generating sports like football and basketball.
“College is becoming the Wild, Wild West for sure,” he said. “But I think they’re still stages for guys to give back and help.”
Jade Flores, a freshman at Allegheny College, received a scholarship from the Tiafoe Fund and also got the chance to practice with Tiafoe during this year’s U.S. Open.
“I was a bit nervous to meet him at first – it’s Frances Tiafoe,” Flores said after the session. “But he makes you feel like he’s known you forever.”
Tiafoe said he wants to keep expanding the Tiafoe Fund as much as he can.

“Let’s just keep pushing and see where it goes,” he said. “There’s always gonna be another kid to help. There’s always going to be another club to bless. There’s gonna be a kid to take to college. So I don’t want to put the caps on it.”

title: Europe's economy brushes off energy shock from Iran war, shows moderate growth in Q3
summary: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before
story: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before

FRANKFURT, Germany -- Europe's economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the U.S.-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before.

The figure released Friday for the 21 European Union member countries that use the euro currency was better than the 0.2% expected by market analysts. Compared to the same quarter a year ago, the economy of the 21 countries using the euro grew by 1.3% in the July-September period, according to EU statistics agency Eurostat.
The continued growth shows that “households and businesses have not pared back their spending due to the Iran war,” said Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics.
“All in all, the eurozone economy remains resilient amid geopolitical turmoil and a worsening inflationary environment,” wrote Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics.

That is despite “worrying signs” that higher oil prices are spreading to other sectors. Those so-called second-round effects — where high oil prices start to influence wages and prices throughout the economy — would support higher interest rates from the European Central Bank.

Inflation of 3.8% remains above the 2% target set out by the ECB, which left rates unchanged at its policy meeting Thursday. That means the ECB may raise rates at its next meeting in December to cool inflation, imposing higher borrowing costs on the economy even as growth remains modest and unevenly distributed among member countries.

Germany, the largest of the euro economies, saw growth of 0.2% despite headwinds from high energy prices and low river levels that disrupted commerce. France, however, shrank by 0.1% as a political deadlock over how to address an outsized budget deficit continues to weigh on business confidence. Stronger performers were Spain, the Netherlands and Estonia with 0.6%

The eurozone growth figure was distorted by an increase of 5.5% in Ireland, where figures are volatile because it is host to multinational tech and pharmaceutical companies whose global activities can influence the figures. Excluding Ireland, growth was 0.2%.

title: Samsung keeps shattering profit records as AI boom lifts chip demand
summary: Samsung Electronics has reported a record operating profit of $80.5 billion, driven by high demand for computer memory chips used in AI systems
story: Samsung Electronics has reported a record operating profit of $80.5 billion, driven by high demand for computer memory chips used in AI systems

SEOUL, South Korea -- SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — Samsung Electronics said Thursday that its operating profit for the last quarter reached a record 107.4 trillion won ($80.5 billion), fueled by surging demands for its computer memory chips used in artificial intelligence systems.
Revenue for the July-September period rose to an all-time high at 195.3 trillion won ($146 billion), marking the company’s fourth straight quarter of record profit and revenue.

Samsung’s regulatory filing came a day after domestic rival SK Hynix also reported record third-quarter profit, as the two South Korean semiconductor giants, which together control about two-thirds of the global memory market, face seemingly insatiable demand for their chips amid the global AI boom.

Samsung said in a statement that it expects the demand for its AI-related chips to accelerate through 2027, outpacing supply as clients race to expand AI infrastructure. The company said it will focus on supplying advanced memory chips and storage products used in AI servers, including high-bandwidth memory chips, server DRAMs and solid-state drives.

South Korean tech companies are making major investments in semiconductor manufacturing facilities and data centers as the country expands its AI ambitions. Samsung and SK Hynix in June announced plans to invest a combined 800 trillion won ($599 billion) in a new chipmaking hub in the country’s southwest to capitalize on AI-driven demand.

But some analysts question whether the spending will ultimately pay off, and South Korea’s central bank has warned that the country’s trade-dependent economy is becoming too reliant on chips, which it said could deepen the damage of any AI-related downturn.

title: Putin woos African leaders at a Moscow summit aimed at expanding Russia-Africa ties
summary: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit, part of his efforts to bolster Moscow’s clout across the continent
story: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit, part of his efforts to bolster Moscow’s clout across the continent
MOSCOW -- Russian President Vladimir Putin courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit that wraps up Thursday as he seeks to bolster Moscow's clout across the continent.
Speaking during a meeting in the Kremlin on the second day of the summit, Putin said that “Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership.”

“We are natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order, free from diktat and double standards and based on respect for the norms of international law and the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter,” Putin said.
He mentioned Moscow's support for the African nations' anti-colonial fight during Soviet times.

“Russia has always been and remains committed to seeing African nations defend their sovereignty, achieve steady growth, and strengthen their economies and social sectors,” the Russian leader said. “We stand ready to continue working together with you across all these areas to achieve these goals."

The summit marks a persistent effort by the Kremlin to expand ties with a continent of nearly 1.6 billion people that is increasingly assertive on the global stage. Africa’s 54 nations make up the largest voting bloc at the United Nations.
Moscow first hosted the Russia-Africa summit in 2019, and then again in 2023. This week’s summit drew nearly 50 African nations, about 20 of which were represented by their leaders.

Putin noted that Russia's trade with African countries topped $27 billion last year and vowed to expand it. He noted that Russian companies have pursued major investment projects in Africa in such spheres as energy, mining, industrial cooperation and logistics.
“Our business community approaches cooperation with African partners with honesty, respect, and integrity, conducting business on an equal footing,” Putin said.

“Rather than siphoning off profits in the manner of the colonial practices by former imperial powers, they reinvest their earnings into the development of your national economies, they readily share advanced technologies and expertise, broadly engage local subcontractors, and help create new production facilities and jobs," he said.

Putin emphasized Russia's role as a major supplier of grain and other agricultural products to African markets, casting it as a “concrete and tangible contribution to ensuring food security across the entire African continent.”

He said that Russia delivered over 18 million metric tons of grain to Africa last year, and another 13 million metric tons in the first nine months of this year. Russian exports of mineral fertilizers reached approximately 1.5 million metric tons last year, and have already exceeded 2.2 million metric tons so far this year.
Putin also mentioned Russia's assistance in the spheres of healthcare and education, noting that nearly 40,000 students from African nations are currently studying at Russian universities.

He specifically underlined Moscow's efforts to help African states in “maintaining internal stability and security, and in strengthening their defense and law enforcement capabilities,” adding that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African countries.

As Russia competes with the United States, Europe and China for greater influence across Africa, it also has relied on its military contractors to strengthen its sway on many fronts, from the economy to security and politics.

title: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
summary: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
story: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
BARCELONA, Spain -- Was Spain's second major train collision this year caused by human error or failures in its once touted high-speed rail network?
It depends on whom you ask.
Spain’s transport minister was quick to lay most of the blame a traffic controller’s poor judgment for Wednesday's collision in Toledo province, which killed 69 people.

But railway unions are pushing back. They point instead to what they describe as deteriorated working conditions — fewer traffic controllers with more work than ever — that have made it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of 45 million passengers annually.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly crash, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged to get to the bottom of it.

“This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened,” Spain’s King Felipe VI said on Thursday after visiting injured passengers in a Toledo hospital. “We will have to take measures so this never happens again.”

The chain of events that ended in disaster started at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, when the communication system key to the functioning of the line’s security system went down. The system, called LZB, monitors the position of trains and can even trigger the automatic braking of a train to prevent a collision.

That malfunction meant that human controllers based at a control post in Madrid took over full responsibility for monitoring the positions and safety of the trains on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) between Madrid and Seville. At that time authorities believe there were six trains on the affected stretch of track.

At 8:36, a controller told one train, belonging to the state-owned RENFE company, that it could start running again at normal speed. The other train, operated by privately owned IRYO, located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) down the line, also tried to restart, but the engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and informed the controller.
At 8:53 the collision occurred, derailing carriages and shredding parts of the trains to bits.

It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, over two hours further south, one train jumped the track and hit another train going the other direction, killing 46 people.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente, who is under pressure to resign, called the controller's decision to let one train restart at full speed while the other remained still “inexplicable” and “erroneous.”
Puente said that the RENFE train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a stop signal active on that line.

“An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision,” Puente told reporters. The decision “was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Unions, however, argue that the context matters.

Raquel Ayllón, spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that the workload is regularly too much for the current staff to safely handle. She said that traffic controllers have been asking for more personnel for years, while the safety systems keep failing.

“We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” she said. “Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”

Spain's union for train engineers, SEMAF, said that this was not the first time the three-decade-old LZB security system, which is still in use on the Madrid-Seville line while being phased out, has gone offline and left human operators to fend for themselves.

“The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago,” said Diego Martín, spokesperson of the SEMAF union of Spain’s train engineers. “It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past.”
Train workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand the government fulfill its commitments to improve safety conditions after the January crash.
Representatives from several unions also criticized what they called the “irresponsible” leak of audio clips of conversations between the control room and the train engineers to Spanish media.
Spain’s railways only serviced state-owned trains until it opened its high-speed rail to private operators in 2021.
Both of this year’s collisions involved a train operated by RENFE and one operated by IRYO.

Rail traffic increased after the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for instance, the average number of daily trips increased from 56 to 89 between 2019 and 2024, according to the SCF union.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on railways.

“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

title: The sell-off for tech stocks drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
summary: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
story: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
NEW YORK -- A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 dropped 2.3% and was heading toward its worst day since June and a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 3.5%, as of 3:05 p.m. Eastern time, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 723 points, or 1.4%.

The U.S. stock market remains only 3.4% below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers' 401(k) accounts, but it's become increasingly shaky just days before Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States. Worries about AI in general have already become a bipartisan concern for voters, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market's performance as a measure of his own success.

Intel's stock led the way lower and is flirting with the worst day in its history, which goes back to 1972, after tumbling 30.7%. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon  sank 1.9% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.

A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12% to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.
A drop of 4.9% for the stock price of Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.

Coinbase Global fell 13.6% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 8.3%. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.
Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.
ExxonMobil climbed 1.8%, and Chevron added 1.7% after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.
Mondelez International rose 4% after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.
Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.9% after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 4.98% late Thursday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month.

Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4% to $113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.
South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5% as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5%.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1% after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Amazon's 3Q results miss analysts' estimates, but posts solid sales gains in cloud computing unit
summary: Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations
story: Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations

NEW YORK -- Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts' expectations.

The Seattle-based company, however, posted strong growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its cloud computing unit called AWS rose 39.3% during the latest quarter ended Sept. 30, higher than the 37% clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said.
Still, shares were down more than 6% in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.

Analysts will be looking for any comments from Amazon executives on the earnings call Thursday about the holiday shopping season. The tech giant said earlier this month that it would hire 300,000 U.S. seasonal workers for the shopping period. That’s up from 250,000 last year.
Investors also have been closely watching Amazon’s quarterly earnings to see if the company’s big spending on artificial intelligence is starting to pay off.

CEO and President Andy Jassy disclosed to investors in July that it now expects capital spending, mostly in artificial intelligence, to total $220 billion. That number includes outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That’s up from the $200 billion investment plan that was announced in February and well above the $128 billion in capital spending for all of last year. Jassy had cited the higher cost of memory chips as the main reason for the increase.
Jassy told investors this past summer that even at the $220 billion level, Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all of the demand it has this year.

The latest earnings report from Alphabet late Wednesday raised alarm bells when it reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The company behind Google and YouTube also said it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion. Its stock plummeted Thursday.
Such worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a big push to build data centers and fill them with AI chips.
Amazon reported net income of $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, in the three-month period. That compares with $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, in the year-ago period.
Sales rose to $201.94 billion, compared with the same year-ago period's $180.17 billion.
Analysts were expecting $1.97 per share on sales of $202.2 billion, according to FactSet.

For the fourth quarter, Amazon said it expects net sales to be between $240 billion and $247 billion, which translates to a 12% to 16% increase compared with the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $244.16 billion.

title: US unemployment claims slide to 194,000, the lowest since mid-July
summary: The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security
story: The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security
WASHINGTON -- The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — the lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security.

The Labor Department reported Thursday that initial jobless claims were down last week from a revised 195,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which strips out week-to-week volatility, fell to 196,750.

Applications for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have remained at historically low levels, never topping 230,000 in a single week. They've come in at or below 200,000 for seven straight weeks.

So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have been adding an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. That is an improvement on a lackluster 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Consumer spending has remained resilient and a surge in investment in artificial intelligence has lifted economic growth.

The Labor Department will release hiring numbers for October next Friday Nov. 6. They are expected to show that the economy added 55,000 jobs this month, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet.

title: DEA approvals could bring big tax benefits for medical marijuana businesses
summary: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses
story: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana dispensaries, a bureaucratic maneuver under President Donald Trump's historic rescheduling of the drug that could pave the way for the businesses to receive tax benefits long denied the industry.

The agency issued the registrations Friday to more than 900 state-licensed dispensaries in Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia, the Justice Department said in a news release. The department did not immediately identify the approved businesses.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement that the regulated distribution of cannabis for medical use from those shops “will help ensure broader access to chronic pain treatment and the safety of the American people.”

In April, Blanche signed an order shifting the classification of state-licensed medical marijuana from Schedule I — reserved for drugs without medical use and with high potential for abuse, like heroin — to the less strictly regulated Schedule III.

The decision largely legitimized medical marijuana programs in the 40 states that have adopted them, and it set up an expedited system for state-licensed medical marijuana producers, manufacturers and distributors to register with the DEA. Businesses must undergo a pre-registration investigation and have security, recordkeeping, inventory controls and other safeguards governing the handling of controlled substances.

Registering with the agency is also expected to ensure immense tax benefits. Historically, state-licensed cannabis businesses haven't been able to deduct normal business expenses — like advertising, rent or labor costs associated with sales — on their federal taxes because they were dealing with a federally illegal, Schedule I drug. Many in the industry have found that financially crippling.
Nearly 7,000 other cannabis dispensaries, manufacturers and distributors across the country have similarly applied for registration, according to a list published by the DEA on Friday.

Steph Sherer, the founder of the medical cannabis organization Americans for Safe Access, noted that the registrations were issued just days before the 30th anniversary of California becoming the first state to legalize the medical use of marijuana.

“For the first time, the federal government is recognizing and registering the medical cannabis dispensaries that patients fought to establish," Sherer said in a written statement. "This is a tremendous victory for patient access and an opportunity to build on 30 years of progress.”

But questions abound. The way state-licensed medical marijuana businesses are regulated is vastly different from how most companies dealing with Schedule III drugs are overseen, and it remains unclear exactly what requirements the DEA may seek to impose on medical cannabis.

For example, some cannabis industry attorneys have noted, state regulators have often sought to mitigate the effects of the drug war by allowing people with some criminal history to run licensed marijuana businesses. It isn't certain whether the DEA will adopt that approach with the businesses it registers.

Furthermore, many states have merged their recreational and medical marijuana industries. While the Trump administration has sought to reschedule marijuana more broadly, it remains unclear how the DEA will treat businesses that handle both adult-use and medical cannabis.

Two dozen states plus Washington, D.C., have authorized adult recreational use of marijuana, 40 have medical marijuana systems, and eight others allow low-THC cannabis or CBD oil for medical use. Only Idaho and Kansas ban marijuana outright.

“It's obviously a positive step to see the program taking shape,” said Chris Lindsey, vice president of policy and state advocacy at the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp. “What everybody's watching for is, what can we expect to see now that we have companies that are going to be operating in this class? What are they going to have to start to do?”
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz in New York contributed.

title: A potentially historic drop for Alphabet's stock drags the US market lower
summary: A potentially historic drop for Alphabet's stock is dragging the U.S. stock market lower
story: A potentially historic drop for Alphabet's stock is dragging the U.S. stock market lower

NEW YORK -- A potentially historic drop for Alphabet’s stock is dragging the U.S. market lower Thursday after the company behind Google and YouTube reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether all its huge investments in artificial-intelligence technology will pay off.

The S&P 500 fell 0.3% and was on track for its first loss in four days, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.2%. Most of the rest of the stocks on Wall Street were rising, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 0.2%, or 104 points, as of 11:15 a.m. Eastern time.

Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and its loss of 11.8% had it heading toward its worst day since it began trading more than 20 years ago. It was under pressure to at least meet analysts’ expectations for growth amid concerns about how much it’s spending to invest in AI.

Alphabet said late Wednesday that it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion.

Worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a frenzy to build data centers and fill them with AI chips. Not only are concerns high that the AI revolution may not produce as much profit and productivity as hoped, future spending on data centers is also under pressure because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to buy more chips.
If not for Alphabet’s drop, the S&P 500 would have been higher for the day.
Several companies rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected, including KLA Corp. The company, whose equipment helps make semiconductors, rose 6.7%.
Eli Lilly climbed 6.4%, Mastercard rose 4.7% and Merck added 5.1%.
DoorDash rose 6.6% after saying it agreed to buy Instacart in a deal valuing it at $17 billion. DoorDash also reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 14.1% higher after likewise topping expectations for summertime profit and revenue. It benefited from cruisers spending more money once aboard ships than the company expected, among other things.

Expectations are high for profit growth broadly among U.S. companies. That's what allowed the S&P 500 to set its record earlier this month despite high interest rates and other worries weighing on the stock market.
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased following several mixed reports on the U.S. economy.

The overall economy’s growth may have accelerated by more during the summer than economists expected thanks to spending by U.S. consumers and businesses investing in AI, according to a preliminary report. But Americans’ growth in incomes was weaker in September than economists expected, while a measure of inflation worsened.
Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, meanwhile, which could indicate few layoffs across the country.

Following the jumble of reports, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98% from 5.05% late Wednesday. It's been generally pulling back since topping 5.30% earlier this month and touching its highest level since 2002.
Helping to pull yields lower on Thursday was a drop in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil sank 2% to $109.42.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on the continent. The bank's president, Christine Lagarde, also said she will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term.
In Asia, indexes were mixed. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2% due to a drop for market heavyweight Samsung Electronics, which sank 4.1% even though it reported a jump in profit.
AP Business Writer Chan Ho-him contributed to this report.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly said that DoorDash's profit and revenue for the latest quarter missed analysts' expectations. They both topped forecasts.

title: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign Feb. 7
summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before her term ends
story: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before her term ends

FRANKFURT, Germany -- European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before the end of her term, a move that opens the way for European leaders to choose a successor ahead of France's presidential election next year.
Lagarde, 70, will leave Feb. 7, the ECB said Thursday. Her eight-year term was to end Oct. 31, 2027.

The resignation opens the way for complex political horse trading over her successor and replacements for two other top officials who are leaving next year. The ECB president leads the bank's governing council, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro currency, affecting borrowing costs for everything from house purchases to new factories and serving as the European Union's chief crisis fighter in times of economic and financial turbulence.

“It has been a great pride and a huge privilege to serve this institution,” Lagarde said in a video message posted on X. “I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future.”

Asked about her reasons at a news conference following the bank's decision to leave rates unchanged, she said that she wanted to be freed from the obligation of political neutrality that comes with being ECB head.

“I want to, have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” she said. “I don’t think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality at the present time." She didn't elaborate.

The announcement was expected following speculation that Lagarde would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose a successor while pro-EU French President Emmanuel Macron is still in office. That would guard against the possibility that right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen might win the election and influence the choice.
“That she leaves early is no surprise and does not change the outlook for ECB policies,” said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Berenberg bank.
European Council President Antonio Costa said that the selection process “will be initiated today and will proceed without delay.”

The term of another top ECB official — chief economist Philip Lane — is to end May 31, while another member of the ECB's executive board, Isabel Schnabel, is resigning Jan. 3 to move to the International Monetary Fund. European leaders are expected to work out a package deal to apportion the three vacancies among member countries in a complex round of political bargaining.
EU leaders would likely seek to reach agreement on all three posts before a summit meeting on Dec. 17-18, Schmieding said.

He said that leading candidates for Lagarde's job appeared to be former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. The BIS is an international organization of central banks.

“The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April-May 2027,” Schmieding wrote in an email. “Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Elysee Palace.”

Lagarde, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, was appointed in 2019 to succeed Mario Draghi. A key decision during her tenure came in 2020, when the bank deployed 1.35 trillion euros ($1.5 trillion) in emergency stimulus in the form of bond purchases to keep the COVID-19 pandemic from drying up credit for the economy.

The bank's ability to act swiftly — in contrast to the often drawn-out negotiations among the 27 European Union national governments — has given it a leading role in combating Europe-wide crises such as the pandemic and the peak period of the eurozone's debt crisis in 2010-2012. Most notably, Draghi's promise in 2012 to “do whatever it takes to preserve the euro” calmed bond market turmoil that raised fears the eurozone would break up.

Lagarde’s announcement overshadowed the bank’s decision Thursday to leave its interest rate benchmark unchanged at 2.5% despite annual inflation of 3.8% fed by high oil prices caused by the US-Iran war. High rates restrain inflation, which is above the bank’s target of 2%. However, rising bond market rates are already tightening credit independent of the ECB, in effect doing the central bank’s job for it, analysts say.
This story has been corrected to show Christine Lagarde succeeded Mario Draghi in 2019, not 2011.

title: ExxonMobil and Chevron top Q3 estimates on higher prices and strong output
summary: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
story: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production.

Besides the disruption caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine that have driven up the cost of fuel, Exxon is also seeing strong production in its fields in Guyana and the Permian Basin in the Southwest. Chevron said its results include one month of production in Venezuela where it’s making a big investment.
Utilization at Exxon's U.S. Gulf Coast refineries was at 100%, and U.S. Gulf Coast diesel production was at the second-highest on record.
The price of diesel, currently about $6.32 per gallon, is up 71% since last year, according to AAA. Regular gasoline is up about 38% in the past year as well.

Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chairman and CEO, noted that investments such as the expansion of its Beaumont refinery in Texas have contributed to an increase in its distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019.
For the third quarter, net income more than doubled to $3.72 per share. On an adjusted basis, profit totaled $4.23 per share, easily topping the average analyst estimate of $4.12 per share.
Revenue during the three months ended in September rose 33% to $113.16 billion, also beating estimates.
The Spring, Texas-based company also raised its quarterly dividend to $1.07 and set a $20 billion stock buyback plan.
Houston-based Chevron said Friday it earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, during the third quarter, as revenue surged 36% to $67.8 billion. Its results handily topped estimates.
Crude utilization at Chevron's U.S. refineries totaled 98%. The company said it set production records at its Eastern Mediterranean and Australian assets.

Chevron, the second-largest U.S. oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. Last month it announced it will invest $7 billion over the next five years in Venezuela. It said Friday that following an accounting-related change during the quarter, it’s now including those results.
Overall capital expenditures during the quarter were lower compared with a year ago because it spent less in the Permian Basin.

Mike Wirth, Chevron’s chairman and CEO, said that the company signed agreements to reduce Bakken midstream costs by about 50%, strengthening the asset’s competitiveness. Chevron increased its holdings in the Bakken fields in North Dakota and Montana following its $53 billion acquisition of Hess Corp. last year.
In premarket trading, Exxon shares rose 1.9%. The stock is up 64% in the past 12 months. Chevron shares rose 1.1%.

title: Allan Saint-Maximin scores the first of Orlando's 3 second-half goals as the Crown beat Orlando 4-0
summary: Allan Saint-Maximin scored the first of Orlando’s three second-half goals, Kristijan Kahlina made seven saves for his seventh clean sheet of the season, and the Crown beat Orlando 4-0
story: Allan Saint-Maximin scored the first of Orlando’s three second-half goals, Kristijan Kahlina made seven saves for his seventh clean sheet of the season, and the Crown beat Orlando 4-0

CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- Allan Saint-Maximin scored the first of Orlando's three second-half goals, Kristijan Kahlina made seven saves for his seventh clean sheet of the season, and the Crown beat Orlando 4-0 on Saturday.
Charlotte (15-10-8), which clinch a playoff spot on Wednesday with a 4-0 victory over Montreal, improved its record at Bank of America Stadium to 10-3-4 this season for 34 points.

Orlando (12-14-7), which had a five-match unbeaten streak come to an end, was hoping to clinch a playoff spot with a victory. The Lions entered with a club-record scoring streak of 25 consecutive matches across all competitions.
Charlotte took a 1-0 lead in the sixth minute when Henry Kessler was left wide open to head home Ashley Westwood’s free kick.
Saint-Maximin made it 2-0 in the 49th by dribbling from midfield to the top of the 18-yard box for a shot past goalkeeper Maxime Crépeau.

Saint-Maximin had a penalty shot blocked by Crépeau in the 84th but Abdoulaye Doucouré was first to the rebound for his first MLS goal. Then, Saint-Maximin was issued a straight red card five minutes later for an obscene gesture toward an opponent.
Rodolfo Aloko capped the scoring in stoppage time with a one-time finish of Tyger Smalls' cross.
Orlando: Hosts New England next Saturday.
Charlotte: Plays at Miami next Saturday.

title: No. 6 Utah improves to 8-0 with 49-25 win over Cincinnati
summary: Devon Dampier threw for 260 yards and two touchdowns and No. 6 Utah extended the nation’s longest active winning streak with a 49-25 victory over Cincinnati
story: Devon Dampier threw for 260 yards and two touchdowns and No. 6 Utah extended the nation’s longest active winning streak with a 49-25 victory over Cincinnati
CINCINNATI -- Devon Dampier threw for 260 yards and two touchdowns and No. 6 Utah extended the nation’s longest active winning streak with a 49-25 victory over Cincinnati on Saturday.
The Utes (8-0, 5-0, Big 12) have won 14 straight games, the longest active streak in the FBS and their longest since winning 16 straight from Dec. 20, 2007, to Sept. 12, 2009.
The Utes are 8-0 for the first time since 2010 and have won 10 consecutive Big 12 games.

“Really proud of our guys to come on the road after a big win against Houston and stay focused,” Utah coach Morgan Scalley said. “This is a very good Cincinnati team. Really proud of the coaches and the players for focusing on not letting the last game take over what we needed to do today.”
The Bearcats (5-3, 2-3) were coming off an upset of previously unbeaten Texas Tech, but no unranked team has beaten top-10 opponents in back-to-back weeks since South Carolina in 2022.
Utah possessed the ball for more than 10 minutes in the first quarter to take control.
The Utes drove 78 yards in 12 plays on their first possession and Dampier's 4-yard TD pass to Hunter Andrews put them ahead 7-0.
Wayshawn Parker scored on a 13-yard TD run, capping a 75-yard drive to make it 14-3. Parker rushed for 82 yards.

“(Offensive coordinator) Kevin (McGiven) and his staff did such a nice job dissecting how to attack their defense,” Scalley said. “They did a really nice job of spreading the ball around and running the ball efficiently.”
Early in the second quarter, Utah's Rabbit Evans returned a fumble 51 yards for a touchdown to make the score 21-3. It was the first fumble return TD for the Utes since 2022.

The Bearcats had a chance to get back into the game after a 63-yard completion to Malachi Henry gave them first-and-goal. But a holding penalty and a sack forced a 35-yard field-goal attempt which was missed.

“We knew Utah was a good team coming in and they certainly played like that in the first half,” Bearcats coach Scott Satterfield said. "When you get close to the end zone, you have to punch it in and get touchdowns.”
Utah put the game out of reach after that.
Daniel Bray's 30-yard TD run made the score 28-3. Bray also had a TD catch in the first half.
Elijah Davis' 39-yard interception return for a touchdown made the score 42-6 with 34 seconds remaining before halftime. It was the 23rd straight season that Utah had a pick six.
It was the most points scored in a half by the Utes since scoring 43 in the first half of a 53-7 win over Colorado on Oct. 25, 2025.
Andrews tied a career-high with five catches and set career highs with 112 receiving yards and two touchdowns. His previous best for yards was 44 last season at Wyoming.

“We got to find a way to get Hunter the ball,” Dampier said. “Hunter is such a dynamic player. It's crazy how big and how fast he is. I was glad he was able to get those touches and he made the most of them.”
Dampier had 45 rushing yards on Saturday, giving him 1,228 for his Utah career, most for a quarterback in program history. Travis Wilson had 1,225 rushing yards from 2012 to 2015.
“He was fantastic today," Scalley said. "That kid's ultra competitive. He wasn't pleased with how he played against Houston in terms of throwing the ball, but man did he step up big (today).”
Utah: There was no letdown for the Utes after last week's big win over Houston. Cincinnati's upset of Texas Tech assured the Utes wouldn't take the Bearcats lightly.
Cincinnati: Cole Tabb continues to be a pleasant surprise for the Bearcats since transferring from Stanford. Tabb rushed for 131 yards and had a 48-yard TD run in the third quarter.
Utah: Hosts No. 8 BYU on Saturday.
Cincinnati: Visits No. 18 Houston on Saturday.

title: Arizona freshman R.J. Mosley taken off on cart with left leg injury against Texas Tech
summary: Arizona freshman receiver R
story: Arizona freshman receiver R

LUBBOCK, Texas -- Arizona freshman receiver R.J. Mosley was taken off on a cart with an apparently serious injury to his left leg late in the third quarter of the No. 22 Wildcats' 34-26 loss at No. 13 Texas Tech on Saturday.

Mosley caught a pass underneath on third-and-18 and went down short of the first down after a hit from Texas Tech cornerback Amier Boyd. Mosley reached toward his left knee as he was sitting before lying down.
Arizona officials said after the game that Mosley was taken to an area hospital for further evaluation of a lower leg injury. They provided no further details.
ESPN chose not to show a replay of the hit that led to the injury. Mosley's leg was in a cast when he was put onto the cart.
Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita prayed as Mosley received medical attention, and his teammates surrounded him while the crowd cheered as he was driven off the field.

The Wildcats were already without top receiver Tré Spivey, whose season was cut short by a broken foot. Giovanni Richardson and Chris Hunter also have missed time but were playing against the Red Raiders.

title: Baker throws 3 TD passes to lead Louisiana Tech over South Alabama 35-20
summary: Blake Baker throws three touchdown passes as Louisiana Tech defeats South Alabama 35-20
story: Blake Baker throws three touchdown passes as Louisiana Tech defeats South Alabama 35-20
MOBILE, Ala. -- Blake Baker threw three touchdown passes and Louisiana Tech shut out South Alabama in the second half for a 35-20 victory on Saturday.
Baker completed 10 of 16 passes for 167 yards without throwing an interception. Backup Trey Kukuk threw a 27-yard touchdown to Jalen Mickens on his only pass of the game.

Marcus Calwise Jr. and Mickens led all Bulldogs' receivers with three receptions and a touchdown apiece. Luke Watkins also had a touchdown catch for Louisiana Tech (6-2, 4-0), which has a two-game lead atop the West Division in the Sun Belt Conference.
Baker’s 4-yard touchdown pass to Watkins was the only scoring in the second half.
Jared Hollins was 14-of-31 passing for 192 yards with an interception and two touchdown passes to Anthony Eager for South Alabama (4-4, 2-2). Eager finished with seven catches for 102 yards.
PJ Martin added 82 yards rushing on 12 carries for the Jaguars. Keenan Phillips added 62 yards on the ground that included an 11-yard touchdown run.

title: Stokes accounts for 5 TDs, leads Memphis over Army 49-22
summary: Marcus Stokes throws four touchdown passes and runs for another score, leading Memphis over Army 49-22 on Saturday night
story: Marcus Stokes throws four touchdown passes and runs for another score, leading Memphis over Army 49-22 on Saturday night
MEMPHIS, Tenn. -- Marcus Stokes threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score to lead Memphis over Army 49-22 on Saturday night.
Stokes completed 29 of 35 passes for 371 yards and scored on a 1-yard run late in the game.
Jermane Hayes had nine receptions for 86 yards and Jemyri Davis had four for 75. They each had two touchdown catches.
Jaylin Carter added 96 yards rushing with two touchdown runs for Memphis (7-2, 4-1 American Conference).
Godspower Nwawuihe had a short-yardage touchdown run and finished with 100 yards on 19 carries for Army (5-3, 4-2). Cale Hellums was 4-of-7 passing for 40 yards with a touchdown and interception.
Hellums' 2-yard touchdown run pulled the Black Knights to 35-22 with 4:46 remaining in the third quarter.
The Tigers finished with 554 total yards and were 11 of 15 on third-down conversions.

title: New Zealand wins the 5th T20 by 7 wickets but India wins the series 3-2
summary: Tim Seifert has made 93 from 50 balls and Glenn Phillips passed 50 for the fourth time in the series as New Zealand beat India by seven wickets in the fifth and final T20 international
story: Tim Seifert has made 93 from 50 balls and Glenn Phillips passed 50 for the fourth time in the series as New Zealand beat India by seven wickets in the fifth and final T20 international

HAMILTON, New Zealand -- Tim Seifert made 93 from 50 balls and Glenn Phillips passed 50 for the fourth time in the series Sunday as New Zealand beat India by seven wickets in the fifth and final T20 international.
India won the series 3-2.
Seifert and Phillips put on 86 for the third wicket as New Zealand ran down India's total of 191-8 with two overs in hand.
Ishan Kishan made 61 from 32 balls and captain Shreyas Iyer 50 from 23 to put India in a strong position at the midpoint of its innings, but later batters added only 80 runs in the last 10 overs.
Seifert seemed bound for his maiden T20 international century when he chopped a ball from Nitish Kumar Reddy onto his stumps with 24 runs needed for victory.
Phillips had been happy to play in Seifert's shadow but when his partner was out, he stepped up and finished unbeaten on 65 from 38 balls as New Zealand won convincingly.
Phillips' 341 runs in the series included a century and three half-centuries and was a record for a five-match bilateral series.

“The calmness and composure I've had is a nice feeling,” Phillips said. “I tried to go out there with a clear mind and play every ball on its merits and try to go out there and be a little more of the hunter and a little less of the prey.”

India failed to fully capitalize on the superb partnership between Kishan and Iyer that repaired the India innings after the loss of openers Abishek Sharma (1) and Sanju Samson (4), who both fell to Adam Milne inside the first four overs.
Kishan and Iyer added 93 from 43 balls for the third wicket, putting India in a powerful position at 111-2 after 10 overs.
The pair preyed particularly on spinners Mitchell Santner and Michael Bracewell, taking 27 runs from Bracewell in the 10th over. Santner was making his 143rd T20 appearance, a record for New Zealand.
Kishan reached his half-century from 28 balls with four fours and four sixes, while Iyer's first half-century of the series came from only 22 deliveries with four sixes and three fours.
Both players were aided by New Zealand's poor catching and fielding.
Kishan fell in the 11th over, hoisting a ball from pacer Blair Tickner directly to mid-wicket and Iyer followed in the next over, top-edging a pull shot to wicketkeeper Tim Seifert.
India's scoring rate slowed as it slipped to 133-5 but Naman Dhir and Nitish Kumar Reddy enlivened proceedings again, sharing 46 runs from 30 balls for the sixth wicket.
Milne was superb, taking 4-19 from his four overs while Bracewell conceded 38 runs for just two overs.
The teams meet in the first match of a five-match one-day series at Auckland on Wednesday.

title: Denny Hamlin is the oldest to win pole at Martinsville Speedway, Kyle Larson qualifies third
summary: With his career-best sixth pole position this season, Denny Hamlin made history while trying to put the brakes on Kyle Larson’s potentially historic run in the Chase
story: With his career-best sixth pole position this season, Denny Hamlin made history while trying to put the brakes on Kyle Larson’s potentially historic run in the Chase
MARTINSVILLE, Va. -- With his career-best sixth pole position this season, Denny Hamlin made NASCAR history while trying to put the brakes on Kyle Larson’s potentially historic run in the Chase.

Hamlin, who will turn 46 on Nov. 18, became the oldest pole sitter in 156 Cup Series races at Martinsville Speedway, turning a 98.492-mph lap on the 0.526-mile oval to beat Joe Gibbs Racing teammate Ty Gibbs (98.241).

“That’s awesome,” said Hamlin, who is 5 months older than Morgan Shepherd was when he won the April 1987 pole. “There’s times I feel like Father Time’s catching up. If that’s true, then you wouldn’t have been able to sit on six poles. It’s what drives me that I’ve got a shot and still am decent enough. So I’d love to keep setting those old man records.”

Larson qualified third at 98.114 mph and reiterated that he isn’t expecting to become the first Chase driver to clinch the championship ahead of the season finale. He has a 73-point lead on Hamlin with Martinsville and the Nov. 8 race at Homestead-Miami Speedway remaining.

“I think everybody else is convinced that we’re going to lock it up here this weekend,” said Larson, who noted that Hamlin would have gained a maximum 76 points at Martinsville if he had finished one spot better in the March 29 race that was won by Chase Elliott. “Denny’s really good here. I’m more just kind of looking at it like how to keep it up front to leave myself a buffer for next week. We’ll see how the race plays out, but that’s kind of my mindset. Denny’s definitely a much better short track racer than me.”
Five of Hamlin’s series-high six wins at Martinsville have been from the pole position.

“Our job is to stay out in front of (Larson) and then just make them think and just maybe this trickles down to a reasonable number,” he said. “You need to gain 25, 30 points probably to even have a remote feeling of optimism, and even that is probably a stretch."
Teammates Christopher Bell (qualified 14th) and Chase Briscoe (11th) will start behind Larson as the next two drivers after Hamlin in the Chase standings.
Austin Cindric qualified fourth ahead of Penske teammate Joey Logano, who is seeking to become the first driver since Rusty Wallace in 1993 to win three consecutive Cup races on short tracks.
