title: With NASCAR championship in sight, Kyle Larson isn’t expecting an early clinch at Martinsville
summary: With NASCAR history waiting to be made at Martinsville Speedway, Kyle Larson acknowledges he is tempted by the tantalizing possibility of wrapping up the Cup Series title Sunday
story: With NASCAR history waiting to be made at Martinsville Speedway, Kyle Larson acknowledges he is tempted by the tantalizing possibility of wrapping up the Cup Series title Sunday
MARTINSVILLE, Va. -- With NASCAR history waiting to be made Sunday at Martinsville Speedway, Kyle Larson acknowledges being tempted by the tantalizing possibility of wrapping up the Cup Series title.
But he isn’t counting on becoming the first driver in 23 years to clinch the championship before the season finale.

“There are some really good drivers here, so I don’t anticipate clinching anything,” Larson said Saturday before practice and qualifying at Martinsville. “I just want to have a good day and not give up too much before next week.

“It’s tough not to look at that and see what could be done this weekend, but what our team does really well is staying focused. Not being too relaxed but also trying not to put too much pressure on yourself. That is what has pushed us through the Chase.”
Larson has pushed his championship rivals to the brink with two races remaining.
The Hendrick Motorsports star opened a 73-point lead over Denny Hamlin with a last-lap rally for his first victory at Talladega Superspeedway, his third win through eight of 10 races in the Chase.

If Larson leaves Martinsville with a 77-point margin, he will be assured of a second consecutive Cup title and his third overall. According to NASCAR analytics firm Racing Insights, Larson is a 92.3% favorite to win the championship this season, which will conclude Nov. 8 at Homestead-Miami Speedway.
Only seven of 16 drivers in the Chase remain eligible for the title, and only three are within 100 points of Larson — Joe Gibbs Racing teammates Hamlin, Christopher Bell and Chase Briscoe.

Hamlin leads active drivers at Martinsville in wins (six), top-five finishes (22) and laps led (3,014). It’s been a stressful Chase for Hamlin, who began as the top seed and favorite to win his first Cup championship but has managed only two top fives, with a best of third.
He was in a relaxed mood Saturday while conceding the likelihood that his No. 11 Toyota will again come up short after losing the title to Larson in a heartbreaker at Phoenix Raceway last year.

“It’s the first weekend where there’s truthfully little pressure because the expectations are just so low,” said Hamlin, who finished second in the March 29 race at Martinsville while leading 292 laps. “Everyone believes that it’s kind of a foregone conclusion, and I’m not saying they’re wrong by any means. It’s just what have we got to lose at this point? It doesn’t matter to me at this point in my career if I finish second or fifth in the points, so it’s low pressure, high opportunity for the 11 team.”
Bell, a 2022 Martinsville winner who is 74 points behind Larson, described it as “throwing Hail Marys” to win the season’s final two races.
“We know that’s the only way forward,” Bell said. “In reality, we have nothing to lose, so now the pressure is off.”

Briscoe, who trails Larson by 79 points as the only other driver with multiple wins in the Chase, said he will be more aggressive with bumping his way through the field at Martinsville, a 0.526-mile oval that is the shortest track on the circuit. But moving the competition aside could be trickier after NASCAR removed energy-absorbing foam and softened bumper structures to discourage slam tactics with the highly durable Next Gen car.

"I’m going to have my spotter remind me of that all day,” Bell said. “That is a super critical thing that has the potential to be a really big change for Martinsville, especially the way that the restarts and stackups happen. It’s going to be a talking point for sure.”

Larson has learned to avoid trouble at Martinsville since joining Hendrick Motorsports, which has a record 31 wins at the track. He has been ninth or better with six top fives over the past eight races at Martinsville.

A strong result Sunday could make him the first Cup champion to clinch early since Matt Kenseth in 2003, the last season before NASCAR switched to determining the champion over the final 10 races. Larson also could become the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson won five in a row for Hendrick in 2006-10.
“It would definitely be an amazing accomplishment for sure,” Larson said.

Riley Herbst is wearing a carbon fiber brace on his left wrist, which was injured in a crash at Talladega, but the 23XI Racing driver plans to complete 500 laps Sunday. Hamlin, who co-owns 23XI with NBA great Michael Jordan, said Harrison Burton is on standby as a relief driver.
“It’s really a pain tolerance thing for (Herbst), and I suspect he’ll try to get it done,” Hamlin said.

Hamlin (+400) is the favorite Sunday, followed by the Team Penske duo of Ryan Blaney (+450) and Joey Logano (+700). … Martinsville is one of four tracks that has played host to a Chase or playoff race since 2004, along with Talladega Superspeedway, Kansas Speedway and Phoenix Raceway. … Chris Buescher will make his 400th Cup start Sunday. The last driver to win in his 400th start was Jimmie Johnson at the 2013 Daytona 500.

title: Lindholm's overtime goal lifts the Bruins past the Blackhawks as Pastrnak moves past Bergeron
summary: Elias Lindholm scored in overtime as the Bruins rallied from a two-goal deficit in the third period to top the Chicago Blackhawks 5-4 and extend Boston’s home winning streak to five games
story: Elias Lindholm scored in overtime as the Bruins rallied from a two-goal deficit in the third period to top the Chicago Blackhawks 5-4 and extend Boston’s home winning streak to five games
BOSTON -- Elias Lindholm scored in overtime as the Bruins rallied from a two-goal deficit in the third period to top the Chicago Blackhawks 5-4 and extend Boston’s home winning streak to five games.
Mason Lohrei scored to pull Boston within a goal and Morgan Geekie's second goal of the season with 12 seconds left in the third period sent the game into overtime.
Ryan Greene and Connor Bedard scored in the third period as the Chicago Blackhawks took a 4-2 lead. Anton Frondell had his second career two-goal game for Chicago.

The Blackhawks came into the game with the worst power play in the NHL, converting on 4 of 40 opportunities and were 0 for 11 on the power play on the road. However, it took Frondell just 11 seconds to give Chicago the lead after Will Borgen was whistled for a delay-of-game penalty.

Goaltender Michael DiPietro kept Boston in the game with key saves as the Bruins were outshot 28-13 in the first two periods. He stopped a Bedard shot from the slot with 2:09 left in the first period. Geekie, who hasn't scored in his previous nine games, hit a shot off the post late in the first period.

David Pastrnak scored on a breakaway in the first period for his 428th career goal, passing Patrice Bergeron and moving into sole possession of third place on the Bruins’ career goal-scoring list. Casey Mittelstadt and Mason Lohrei also scored for the Bruins.

Frondell redirected Tyler Bertuzzi's wrist shot from the point past a surprised DiPietro early in the second period for his second career two-goal game. DiPietro, coming off his first career NHL shutout, kept it a one-goal game with a point-blank save of 500-goal scorer Patrick Kane midway through the second period. The Bruins tied the game when Mittelstadt took a feed from James Hagen and snapped a shot past Arvid Soderblom.

title: Raiola throws for 3 TDs to help Oregon beat No. 20 Northwestern 34-26
summary: Dylan Raiola completed 22 of 31 passes for 336 yards and three touchdowns to help Oregon rally to beat No. 20 Northwestern 34-26 on Saturday
story: Dylan Raiola completed 22 of 31 passes for 336 yards and three touchdowns to help Oregon rally to beat No. 20 Northwestern 34-26 on Saturday
EUGENE, Ore. -- Dylan Raiola completed 22 of 31 passes for 336 yards and three touchdowns to help Oregon rally to beat No. 20 Northwestern 34-26 on Saturday.
Raiola made his second straight start for the Ducks (5-3, 3-2 Big Ten) with Dante Moore ruled out for the season.
“I feel like that’s the closest we’ve been to a complete performance,” Oregon coach Dan Lanning said. “That being said, there’s a lot of things we can still do better.”

After running back Jordon Davison left the game with what Lanning said was a leg injury in the first half, freshman Brandon Smith led the comeback with 82 yards rushing and scored the go-ahead touchdown in the fourth quarter.

“That’s all you want as a coach, is a guy that is not necessarily begging for their opportunity, but ready when their opportunity comes, and I think Brandon’s been that for us throughout this year,” Lanning said. “His role will continue to grow with this team. He’s obviously very capable.”
Aidan Chiles was 22 of 38 for 281 yards and a touchdown for Northwestern (6-2, 3-2). He ran for 93 yards and another TD late in the second quarter, his 10th of the season.

Northwestern had a 10-0 first-quarter lead and was up 20-13 at the half after Raiola’s 10-yard touchdown pass to Dakorien Moore with 49 seconds remaining. Raiola hit Moore again in the fourth quarter on a 75-yard strike, with Moore finishing with 128 yards and two TDs in his first collegiate 100-yard game.

Raiola found Jamari Johnson for a 17-yard touchdown pass, and Smith rushed for a 2-yard touchdown on fourth-and-goal to put Oregon ahead for the first time, 27-23, in the fourth quarter before Moore’s second touchdown sealed the game.
“We weren’t gonna go down without swinging, and I think that kind of got lost a little bit,” Raiola said. “I don’t think we completely lost it, but we got back to our DNA.”

Oregon fired offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer Oct. 25 following the loss to Illinois and elevated assistant quarterbacks coach Jay Johnson to lead play-calling role. He paired with Raiola’s clean game and Oregon-career-high passing total to spark the Ducks’ offense, which averaged 3.8 yards per rush and 15.3 yards per pass.
Northwestern kicker Jackson Kleather was 4 of 5, missing late in the fourth quarter. Oregon held the Wildcats to six second-half points.

“I thought our defense did a great job of not folding down in the red area and making sure we were able to keep them out of touchdown situations and force field goals,” Lanning said. “And then it’s all about one more play.”

title: Saddiq Bey and Jeremiah Fears lead the Pelicans past the Hawks, 121-99

story: Saddiq Bey scored 25 points in a reserve role, Jeremiah Fears added 20 points, and the New Orleans Pelicans beat the Atlanta Hawks 121-99
NEW ORLEANS -- Saddiq Bey scored 25 points in a reserve role, Jeremiah Fears added 20 points, and the New Orleans Pelicans beat the Atlanta Hawks 121-99 on Saturday night.
Zion Williamson and Trey Murphy III each scored 15 for the Pelicans, who lead by 28 en route to their second straight victory after losing their first four games.

CJ McCollum, playing in New Orleans for the first time since the Pelicans traded him to Washington in June 2025, scored 14 points for Atlanta. Fans applauded while a tribute video that the Pelicans produced for McCollum played on the videoboards above the court.
But the Hawks, who’ve lost four of five, missed 38 of 46 3-point shots (17.4%) they attempted and never trailed by fewer than 10 points after falling behind by that amount late in the first quarter.

Making matters worse for Atlanta, reserve guard Kingston Flemmings, who scored 12 points, received a technical foul and was ejected for elbowing Pelicans reserve guard Bryce McGowens in the face during the final minutes.
The incident caused a brief scrum in which most players and coaches served as peace makers. Officials reviewed video before ejecting Flemmings.

Both of New Orleans' victories have come since first-year coach Jamahl Mosley tinkered with the starting lineup, inserting versatile Croation Karlo Matkovic at and defensive standout Herb Jones at shooting guard. They joined incumbent starters Williamson, Murphy and Fears.
Matkovic grabbed 10 rebounds and hit a pair of corner 3s on his way to eight points. Jones scored 11 points. Fears, meanwhile, hit the 20-point mark for a second straight game.
The Pelicans raced to a 35-18 lead in the first quarter, when they shot 56% and turned eight Hawks turnovers into 16 points. New Orleans still led by double digits at halftime, 63-48.
New Orleans led by as many as 20 in the third quarter before taking a 92-74 lead into the fourth quarter.

title: Mobley scores 27, Allen adds 25 as Cavaliers ride 48-point second quarter to get past Bucks 136-111

Chance Gamble intercepted a pass in the end zone with 3:02 left in the game to seal it.

summary: Josh Anderson had two goals and an assist and the Montreal Canadiens beat the Pittsburgh Penguins 5-4 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory
story: Josh Anderson had two goals and an assist and the Montreal Canadiens beat the Pittsburgh Penguins 5-4 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory
MONTREAL -- Josh Anderson had two goals and an assist and the Montreal Canadiens beat the Pittsburgh Penguins 5-4 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory.

Chris Kreider added a one goal and an assist, and Oliver Kapanen and Alexandre Texier also scored as Montreal (9-3-2) returned home from an undefeated four-game Western trip. Lane Hutson had two assists.
Jacob Fowler made 25 saves and became the third Canadiens rookie goalie in the past 40 years to win seven consecutive games.
Sidney Crosby and Erik Karlsson each had a goal and two assists for Pittsburgh, and Tommy Novak and Rickard Rakell each had a goal and an assist. Sergei Murashov stopped 22 shots.
Anderson gave Montreal a two-goal lead with 6:54 left on a deflection. Crosby pulled one back with 3:11 remaining with Murashov off for an extra attacker.

Earlier, with his 1,112th career assist, Crosby passed Boston Bruins great Ray Bourque for the most with one franchise in NHL history. The 39-year-old center also tied Marcel Dionne for sixth on the scoring list with 1,771.
Penguins: Host Vegas on Tuesday night.
Canadiens: Host Winnipeg on Tuesday night.

title: Kemper Hodges' 4 TDs lead Air Force ground attack in 35-26 win over UConn
summary: Kemper Hodges rushed for 200 yards and four touchdowns as Air Force, once again, leaned on its ground game to hold off UConn 35-26 on Saturday
story: Kemper Hodges rushed for 200 yards and four touchdowns as Air Force, once again, leaned on its ground game to hold off UConn 35-26 on Saturday
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo. -- Kemper Hodges rushed for 200 yards and four touchdowns as Air Force, once again, leaned on its ground game to hold off UConn 35-26 on Saturday.
The Falcons (6-2) did not complete a pass but rushed for 366 yards and five touchdowns on 74 carries.
UConn (4-4) pulled within 28-26 early in the fourth quarter after Kalieb Osborne connected with Alex Godavitarne for a 55-yard touchdown and Kenji Christian broke a 46-yard scoring run.
Air Force responded by taking nearly the rest of the game off the clock. The Falcons drove 75 yards in 19 plays, using 11:37 before Hodges scored from 1 yard out with 3:09 remaining.
Hodges also scored on runs of 3, 7 and 62 yards in the first half as Air Force built a 21-14 lead by the break.
Gage LaDue added a 4-yard touchdown run in the third quarter for the first score of his career.
Osborne threw for 263 yards and two touchdowns for UConn. Christian led the Huskies with 68 yards rushing, while Godavitarne had a 55-yard touchdown reception.
UConn: Hosts North Carolina next Saturday.
Air Force: At Army next Saturday.

title: So long, slipper: Why Cinderella will be harder to find at March Madness this season
summary: March Madness is famous for its underdog stories, but Cinderella teams are struggling in the world of bigger conferences spending more money
story: March Madness is famous for its underdog stories, but Cinderella teams are struggling in the world of bigger conferences spending more money

Much of the magic March Madness churns out every year comes from pitting small schools with names and players few people have heard of against the Dukes and North Carolinas of the world at a time when everyone seems to be watching.
What makes it even better is that, sometimes, those teams win.
But the NCAA Tournament's most darling participant, Cinderella, is finding it harder to survive and advance in the world of expanding conferences, payrolls and transfer portals.

The 2026-27 season ushers in the era of the 76-team tournament — an eight-team expansion to a bracket in which the biggest of the big not only control the contours of the tournament, but, more than ever, can simply elbow Cinderella out of the way using the power of their checkbooks.

“Unfortunately, you may see an upset, but it may be harder for the smaller schools to make those longer runs in the tournament," said Niko Medved, who was one excruciating buzzer-beater away from taking underdog Colorado State to the Sweet 16 in 2025 before he left to coach Minnesota a few weeks later. “We’ll see what the data shows here in the next 3-4 years, but I could see that scenario.”

Teams that once wore glass slippers, like Gonzaga or Butler, long ago shed the plucky underdog label and have either turned into behemoths or hopped into conferences with them. Others that made a splash, like St. Peter's or Loyola-Chicago, often see their best players and coaches siphoned away by the big boys.

The only two No. 16 seeds to beat a No. 1 — UMBC and Fairleigh Dickinson — along with 2022 Elite Eight team St. Peter's are among the three dozen or so teams that start with a disadvantage because they don't participate in the revenue-sharing structure that now rules talent acquisition (read: winning) in big-time college sports.

Meanwhile, the unspoken secret about tournament expansion is that it was done to afford more big-conference teams a chance of making the field and earn the millions that come with it. Their thought: The lion's share of the 32 automatic-qualifier spots in the tournament go to smaller leagues, and the seventh- or eighth-best team in their power conferences are at least as deserving as those teams.
Not everyone agrees with that notion.

“I mean, there’s eight new spots,” said Jim Phillips, the commissioner of the ACC. “Now, if they don’t get any of them, they don’t get any of them, but it’s not any less than what they’ve had before.”

The numbers: Three of the first four teams left out of the last two tournaments came from power conferences. Last year, Boise State would have made an expanded field, but so would Ohio State, Indiana and West Virginia.

Meanwhile, conference expansion has plucked some of the best mid-major teams out of their leagues and into bigger ones, and they've been replaced by lesser programs. One example: The Mountain West used to feature BYU, Utah and TCU, but all have left for the Big 12. Some newer programs in the MWC include UTEP, UC-Davis and San Jose State.

All of which means that these days, there's a better chance of the next Cinderella looking a lot like the 2024 N.C. State team that had to win the ACC simply to make the tournament, and ended up in the Final Four; and less like that 2006 George Mason squad that came out of the Colonial Athletic Conference and shocked the world en route to college basketball's biggest stage.

The N.C. State analogy is apt. It is the program that, in 1983 with coach Jim Valvano, essentially coined the term “Cinderella” with a run to the title that took on mythical proportions over the decades. Rollie Massimino and Villanova and “Danny and the Miracles” at Kansas followed shortly after, proving that massive upsets don't all have to belong to the so-called little guys.

Then, there's the largely unspoken question of just how beneficial a run by the so-called little guy is for the tournament as a whole. Yes, America loves to see a UMBC beat Virginia in the first round or Florida Gulf Coast knock off big boys on the way to the Sweet 16.

But the only two national finals to average more than 20 million viewers over the last dozen years involved Duke (2015) and North Carolina (2017). The least-watched final involved underdog San Diego State in a defensive snoozer of a game shown on CBS.
The most telling byproduct of the name, image and likeness era might be what happens to small teams that pull off big upsets or make unexpected runs through March Madness.
After its trip to the Final Four in 2024, Florida Atlantic lost seven players and its coach, Dusty May.

Two years earlier, St. Peter's made its captivating run to the Elite Eight only to see its roster and coaching staff eviscerated, led by coach Shaheen Holloway's departure to his alma mater, Seton Hall. It came as the impact of NIL and less restrictive transfer rules were hitting full gear.

“I’d say if we fell short, we’d probably be there (at St. Peter's) another year,” Daryl Banks III told The Wall Street Journal after leaving for St. Bonaventure. “We all talked to each other and we knew what we had to do going forward for our careers.”

Not that all is lost. Even with the three dozen teams that don't participate in revenue sharing and dozens more that don't spend all the way to the cap, there are tons of talented players out there and plenty of schools have the resources to lure them — at least for a while.

But, as Washington third-year coach Danny Sprinkle said recently, there is a reason the Huskies joined the Big Ten; quite simply, the conference distributes more money to schools, which makes it easier for it to put a stranglehold on the tournament and deprive Cinderella of oxygen.

“Once we get a full share (in 2030), that’ll help our program immensely,” Sprinkle said. "The disparity is just becoming wider by the day. It is hard. It’ll be interesting to see in the next five, seven, eight years, what that disparity is.”

title: Colón throws for 2 TDs and Albany defense scores twice in 45-35 win over Campbell
summary: Kai Colón threw two touchdown passes, Albany’s defense scored twice, and the Great Danes defeated Campbell 45-35
story: Kai Colón threw two touchdown passes, Albany’s defense scored twice, and the Great Danes defeated Campbell 45-35
ALBANY, N.Y. -- Kai Colón threw two touchdown passes, Albany's defense scored twice, and the Great Danes defeated Campbell 45-35 on Saturday.
The Great Danes took an early lead on Dillon Dunathan's 77-yard fumble return for a touchdown. They led 38-21 midway in the third quarter and their defense dominated the final minutes.

After Dunathan's touchdown got the scoring started for the Great Danes, a second fumble recovery led to a 14-yard touchdown run by Colón and Albany led 14-7. Later in the first quarter, Rahshan La Mons bolted 63 yards for a touchdown, giving Albany a 21-7 lead after one.
Campbell rallied with a couple of touchdowns in the second quarter and it was 31-21 in favor of Albany at halftime.
Albany made it 38-21 in the third quarter when Jamari Young intercepted a Kamden Sixkiller pass and returned it 25 yards for a touchdown.
Sixkiller connected with Chinua Ezeigbo for a 27-yard touchdown pass in the third quarter and JJ Cowan's 41-yard touchdown run made it 38-35 early in the fourth.
From there, the Albany defense regrouped, holding Campbell to a punt and two turnovers on downs.
Colón's 16-yard touchdown pass to BJ Norman wrapped up the scoring.

Colón threw for 214 yards and Norman had 99 yards on eight receptions for the Great Danes (6-3, 4-1 Coastal Athletic Association). La Mons had 119 yards rushing and defensive lineman Shawan Lewis had 3 1/2 sacks, raising his season total to 9 1/2.
Sixkiller threw for 271 yards, Ezeigbo added 110 receiving yards and Cowan ran for 97 yards, including three touchdowns.
The Fighting Camels (7-2, 4-1) are ranked No. 12 in the Stats Perform FCS Top 25. Their 7-1 start marked their first 7-win season since the program was restarted 19 years ago.
Campbell: vs. Stony Brook next Saturday.
Albany: at Bryant next Saturday. ___

title: Ayoub Jabbari, Roman Celentano help Cincinnati clinch postseason spot with 1-0 victory over Union
summary: Ayoub Jabbari scored in the second half and Roman Celentano made it stand up as FC Cincinnati clinched a postseason berth with a 1-0 victory over the Philadelphia Union
story: Ayoub Jabbari scored in the second half and Roman Celentano made it stand up as FC Cincinnati clinched a postseason berth with a 1-0 victory over the Philadelphia Union
CINCINNATI -- Ayoub Jabbari scored in the second half and Roman Celentano made it stand up as FC Cincinnati clinched a postseason berth with a 1-0 victory over the Philadelphia Union on Saturday.
Neither team scored until Jabbari was in the right place in the 70th minute after Andre Blake saved but couldn't reel in a shot by Evander Da Silva Ferreira.
Celantano had five of his six saves in the first half for Cincinnati (12-11-10). It was his third clean sheet in 29 starts this season, helping the club improve to 10-4-3 at home.
Blake finished with two saves — both in the second half — for Philadelphia (13-12-8), which had already earned a playoff spot before falling to 6-8-3 on the road.

The Union beat Cincinnati 5-0 at home on Sept. 9 behind a hat trick from Bruno Damiani. Cincinnati was forced to play a man down after the 16th minute when midfielder Obinna Nwobodo was tagged with a red card.
It's all over but the seeding for both clubs heading to Decision Day.
Philadelphia: Hosts Toronto FC to close out the regular season on Saturday.
Cincinnati: Hosts Nashville SC on Saturday to finish the regular season.

title: Pellant tosses 2 TD passes, Dawson rushes for 2 TDs in Illinois State's 35-14 win over Murray State
summary: Beckham Pellant threw for two touchdowns, Victor Dawson rushed for two and Illinois State defeated Murray State 35-14 on Saturday for the Redbirds’ third consecutive win
story: Beckham Pellant threw for two touchdowns, Victor Dawson rushed for two and Illinois State defeated Murray State 35-14 on Saturday for the Redbirds’ third consecutive win
NORMAL, Ill. -- Beckham Pellant threw for two touchdowns, Victor Dawson rushed for two and Illinois State defeated Murray State 35-14 on Saturday for the Redbirds' third consecutive win.

Pellant threw a 50-yard TD to Ethan Loss off a flea flicker for a 21-7 lead early in the third quarter then a 5-yarder to Dylan Lord early in the fourth. Rico Clay's interception led to Dawson's 14-yard score and a 21-point lead midway through the final period.
Dawson's 11-yard TD run and Seth Glatz's 1-yard score had the Redbirds (7-2, 3-2 Missouri Valley Football Conference) up 14-7 at halftime.

Pellant threw for 248 yards with the two TDs plus an interception for Illinois State, ranked No. 10 in the Stats Perform poll. Dawson rushed for 99 yards on 22 carries and his two scores. Loss had 117 yards on just two catches with a TD.

Collin Shannon was 14 of 27 for 169 yards passing and was picked off twice for the Racers (1-8, 0-5), who have lost six straight. Baxter Wright threw a 5-yard TD to Trey Firestone in the second half. Jaxon Potter had 131 yards on seven catches and Jawaun Northington 74 yards rushing including 42-yard score.
Murray State: Home against Youngstown State next Saturday.
Illinois State: At North Dakota next Saturday.

title: NASA telescope on the verge of plunging to Earth after failed rescue mission
summary: It is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering.
story: It is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering.
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday.

Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission’s chief scientist.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope’s dwindling path.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning yet full of gratitude for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma ray bursts and supernovas.

“We’ve known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic,” said Pennsylvania State University’s John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company’s three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 7 miles to 9 miles (12 kilometers to 15 kilometers) to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope’s superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
“Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe,” Nousek said in an email.

title: Graphika finds China-linked Spamouflage accounts posing as US voters on X
summary: Analysts at Graphika report that the influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections
story: Analysts at Graphika report that the influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- The long-running influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections, with accounts likely linked to China posing as U.S. voters and posting divisive content about U.S. politics, social issues and the elections, analysts say.

In a blog posted on Friday, Graphika, a New York-based firm that tracks online networks, said it had identified Spamouflage-linked activity on X that closely resembles tactics documented in 2024 ahead of the U.S. presidential election.
“The accounts post content questioning election integrity and the legitimacy of U.S. democracy,” the Graphika blog said.

Intelligence and national security officials have long warned that Russia, China and Iran have run online influence operations targeting U.S. voters ahead of elections. China, rather than supporting one presidential candidate over the other, has focused its efforts on undermining confidence in elections, voting and the U.S. in general, observers have said.
Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said in a statement that China “has never and will never interfere in the U.S. elections."

Darren Linvill, who co-directs Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub and has tracked Spamouflage activity, said there is “no chance it tips the balance in any real political conversation.”
“Spamouflage is famously bad at mimicking real Americans," Linvill said. “It's outside their wheelhouse.”

Rather, the network has been more effective in suppressing information, Linvill said, as the accounts linked to the influence operation “very frequently attack and harass members of the Chinese diaspora community” and are part of a wider effort by Beijing to silence views it dislikes.

In its blog, Graphika said it identified an account that appears to have replaced a removed account that was linked to Spamouflage and has posted divisive U.S. political content, including attacks on Democratic Party leadership during the U.S. government shutdown in October 2025 and criticism of immigration policy.

Graphika flagged four accounts with a history of Spamouflage activity that now amplify MAGA-styled personas and another account with more than 200,000 followers that presents itself as a Philippine culture blog but now posts pro-China and divisive U.S.-focused content.
Graphika said it could not determine whether the account was hijacked or whether the original operator sold or otherwise lost control of it.

title: Generations of anglers have made the pilgrimage to Montauk to catch striped bass
summary: Generations of fishermen have come to Montauk, New York, to fish for striped bass, but the fish are in the midst of a decline
story: Generations of fishermen have come to Montauk, New York, to fish for striped bass, but the fish are in the midst of a decline

MONTAUK, N.Y. -- On most October nights, fishing guide Bill Wetzel can be found navigating the shores of Montauk, New York, in a modified 4x4 pickup truck, rumbling over boulders and thick sand as he scans the surface of the Atlantic for signs of life.

He notes, and meticulously logs, where he spots seams in the water's currents, cuts in sandbars, points and coves, troughs along the shoreline or birds working over bait that was pushed to the surface by one of Montauk’s many predators. Any sign that a striped bass might be feeding beneath the waves, Wetzel will likely see it.
So, as he prepares for a mid-afternoon nap between nocturnal surfcasting customers, he tunes in his VHF radio to get the latest marine forecast. The squawking voice tells him something new.
“Northwest ...” he mutters aloud, pondering what the wind change might mean for his next outing.
He already knows the tides, the moon phase, and the best spots to fish under whatever conditions the ocean has to offer.
What he doesn’t know is if there will be any fish left to catch.

Some years, fishermen will make more than 17 million fishing trips seeking striped bass. But for countless anglers on the East Coast, that future is in danger. Scientists say the species is in decline because of a host of human-caused, environmental and ecological changes, putting the $8 billion industry in jeopardy, and threatening a generations-old tradition of standing on the ocean's edge and trying to catch a potentially humongous fish.
Here’s a look at Montauk’s anglers and what they’ve experienced amid a dramatic decline in striped bass.

Wetzel is obsessed with understanding and finding these fish, which can grow larger than 50 pounds (23 kilograms). Contrary to what one might expect, he doesn’t want to kill them. Instead, he wants to save them so future generations get the opportunity to enjoy the sport he loves.

He has led fishermen to Montauk in search of stripers for more than 25 years, and is one of the best known guides on Long Island. He also actively uses his platforms on social media to discuss conservation, and remembers the collapse of the stock decades ago that led to a fishing shutdown in the mid-1980s.
He doesn't want to relive those days. But he fears it's coming.
“I haven't seen a blitz in four years,” Wetzel said, referring to the chaotic feeding frenzies that were once a hallmark of Montauk's shores. “There's no small fish left. They're gone.”
More and more, he says, the only fish left are big ones. That's because the population isn't replenishing itself.

Jason Markowitz, an IT professional who lives outside New York City, is the former president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association. He is one of the intrepid anglers who still swim out to Montauk's offshore rocks, proven fishing grounds where strong waves can push you around and predators swim at your feet.
He said the chilly swim is worth it “if the fish are there.” Increasingly, he said, they aren't.
“You’ve got a lot of folks that are finding fish but it really is a case of ‘last of the buffalo,’” Markowitz said.

John Skinner is 65 and has been fishing for stripers on Long Island since he was a boy of 10 or younger. In the ensuing years, he has become one of the most respected and sought-after authorities on striped bass fishing.
Looking at the current state of the striped bass industry and the decline in population, two words come to his mind: “It sucks.”

Blunt, but the situation is devastating for Skinner, who runs a popular YouTube channel about striper fishing and authored a book on the subject. These days, he hits up his prime spots on Long Island's North Fork and sometimes leaves empty-handed.

Skinner is inclined to let the scientists come up with reasons for the decline, but he said he can't help but notice a lack of small fish like menhaden for the stripers to feed on. And he sees a lack of other large, predatory fish beyond just stripers.
It's about more than just fish. Sitting in his office, surrounded by decades-old fishing lures, he thinks back to his days on the family boat in the early 1970s, when the itch to fish first set in.
“What do you do with a little kid to keep him out of your hair,” Skinner said. “Give him a rod and some worms.”
With 40 years of fishing under his belt, Mahan says he’s nostalgic for a time when the fish were more abundant.
“What it was like, back in the later ‘80s and ’90s, was spectacular,” Mahan said.

Mahan, who sports a drooping white mustache and fishes from the rocks in a black hoodie and waders, fears the way to save the stripers might be to leave them alone entirely for a while. It would be hard, because striper fishing is in his blood, but sometimes it feels like the only way.
Read more about the science and regulatory issues facing striped bass here.
At “The End,” as it's known, of Long Island, Montauk’s waters are historically renowned for producing some of the best striper fishing in the world.

Part of the draw of Montauk has always been the danger and dynamic environment — there are sand beaches, boulder-strewn points and swift currents that pull bait into coves where fishermen can intercept the big predators chasing their forage.
“The lighthouse kind of draws you in,” said fisherman John Mahan on an October trip. “Beautiful conditions. There should be fish here right now.”
For a long time, Montauk's unofficial motto was “a small drinking village with a big fishing problem.”
“Not anymore,” says Wetzel, lamenting a change in culture.
But he's quick to say he still loves Montauk, and fishing.
“It's in me. If it's not in you, a lot of guys come and go. It's not in you. Plus, I mean, look at this. Look at this — that's why,” he said, motioning to the surf and the ocean beyond it.

Once a blue-collar fishing town, the community has become increasingly hard to distinguish from the nearby ultrawealthy enclaves of the Hamptons. It was a slow transformation that took place over decades and accelerated in the 2000s. But fishermen who have journeyed there for generations say it still maintains an identity all its own.
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine.

title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
summary: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish
story: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish

MONTAUK, N.Y. -- Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.
Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.

“I’m part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon,” said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.
Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren't showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.

Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.

Factors like years of warming waters — a prime concern cited by many scientists — poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.
See a visual essay featuring anglers who were fishing the shores of Long Island earlier this month here.

“Stripers” are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine's coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.

Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they're measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action — including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s — is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.

“They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned,” said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. “People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass.”
Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms — it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U.S. alone.
And it relies on a fish whose future looks grim.

“Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse,” said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.
“Sometime around 2029, 2030 it’s going to go off a cliff,” he said, “and it’s going to be ugly.”

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them — specifically, cool, wet springs.

Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.
Conditions have been poor in recent years, and fewer fish have entered the population going back to 2019, said Chris Batsavage, chair of the commission's striped bass management board.
“Low precipitation and waters that warm quickly result in weak year classes,” Batsavage said. “It seems like it's environmentally driven.”
The conditions have led to a “slump of bad years” that have made it especially difficult for the fish to maintain their population in the Chesapeake, Versak said.

John Skinner, who wrote a book about striped bass fishing and runs a YouTube channel on the subject that has more than 100,000 followers, has been fishing off Long Island for more than 50 years and says once-reliable spots have completely dried up.
“I'm not saying the fishing is bad. I’m saying when you go there in perfect conditions, you catch nothing,” Skinner said. “Absolutely nothing.”

Many other striped bass fishermen across the Northeast shared a recurring story this summer and fall — the fish's once-plentiful schools are dried up, and the individuals that remain are clearly older, meaning years of reproduction failure are starting to take their toll.

Some fishermen said stricter rules or a fishing moratorium could be the only ways to prevent the fish’s population from becoming dangerously low. And they lament what they’re seeing on the waters — smaller schools of fish, many of them older and larger, with few young fish entering the population to provide a future.

They also see more factors than just the warming environment at play. Some see years of heavy fishing on striped bass becoming apparent today in the form of a lower population. Others blame the resurgence of sharks buoyed by years of conservation efforts, as a reintroduction of competition for the fish.

The Atlantic States commission considers the stock to be overfished, although it says overfishing is not occurring at the moment. The fish are caught commercially as well as recreationally, but recreational fishing is much larger.

Most of the recreational catch is tossed back into the ocean alive. Still, some fish don't survive the encounter. Regulators have historically expected 9% to die after release, while newer data shows the number could be less than 5%.

Limits on how large a striped bass can be caught and kept are typically in the range of 28 to 31 inches (71 to 79 centimeters), with rules varying by state and location. Striped bass are popular with catch-and-release fishermen, and these days, it’s more common to catch larger bass, many well over 31 inches.
Paquette, the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association coordinator and a longtime angler himself, said that without drastic action he fears the end of striped bass fishing.
“If you’re a guy who thought he was going to retire and striped bass fish, and you’re planning on retiring soon, get a different plan,” Paquette said.
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine. Associated Press video journalist Mingson Lau contributed.

title: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
summary: The provost of Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found that he used artificial intelligence in his writing, including in a Washington Post guest column on AI cheating
story: The provost of Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found that he used artificial intelligence in his writing, including in a Washington Post guest column on AI cheating

A top administrator at Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, including in a guest column in The Washington Post on AI cheating.

The announcement Wednesday of Provost Santiago Schnell’s departure from the Ivy League university comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools.

Dartmouth touts itself as the birthplace of AI, saying the field got its start at the school in Hanover, New Hampshire, in 1956 when a small group of scientists gathered for a summer research project on the topic. A conference commemorating the 70th anniversary — titled “What Must Remain Human?” — began Thursday.
University President Sian Leah Beilock said in a written statement that keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI means “leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing.”

“That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars,” the president wrote, adding that Schnell’s departure was "his decision” and that the school wishes him well.
Schnell referred questions to his attorneys, who didn’t immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Issues arose after the news outlet Semafor ran guest columns in major newspapers through an AI filter. Schnell’s August column in the Post, titled “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem," was found to be entirely written by AI.
Schnell defended himself, saying at the time he used ChatGPT to "refine a few arguments” but that the column was based on his “own thinking.”

The college paper, The Dartmouth, then ran other publications from Schnell through an AI detector. Writing that predated ChatGPT’s 2022 public release was found to be human-written, but high rates of AI use were detected in his recent writing.

Schnell told the paper in an email last month that he uses AI for “language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organization and making writing processes more efficient.” The paper ran the statement through an AI-detector and found it was AI-written.
In a follow-up statement, Schnell told the paper that he “developed the substance and wrote a draft” of the email, then “used an AI tool to assist with language and clarity.”
An investigation ensued, and the faculty committee found that Schnell used AI to “meaningfully alter his writing” and “was not forthcoming about his AI use.”

Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously taught and held leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan and Indiana University, according to his LinkedIn profile.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
summary: DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery
story: DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery
DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery.

DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

title: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions
summary: The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
story: The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing

ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.

Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.

The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.

In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.

Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.

Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.

All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.

Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.

The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.

Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.

Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

title: Fire briefly triggers emergency at South Carolina lab on former nuclear weapons site
summary: A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is on a site that once made key parts for nuclear bombs has triggered an emergency response that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area
story: A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is on a site that once made key parts for nuclear bombs has triggered an emergency response that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area

A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is in a complex where key parts for nuclear bombs were once made triggered an emergency declaration Wednesday that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area.

The fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory on the U.S. Department of Energy’s Savannah River Site was extinguished by Wednesday night and the site returned to normal operations. No detectable levels of contamination were found, according to a Savannah River Site statement.

The Savannah River Site is a massive complex where the federal government once produced materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily tritium and plutonium-239. The lab is in its northwest corner, near the edge of the site.

The site was opened in the early 1950s as the Cold War was heating up. Today it is used for environmental stewardship and cleanup, along with nuclear waste management and disposition of nuclear materials, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

The lab currently does experiments with nuclear materials and also does processing work with radioactive material, including operating a facility for radioisotope recovery from used nuclear fuel, said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
Lyman said it is reassuring that officials said there has been no off-site contamination, noting that there is a buffer zone between most of the facilities and the public areas.

But if you have a fire where there is radioactive material, “you need to take extreme precautions because of the potential dispersal of that material and the potential for contamination, potential for the public to be exposed,” he said.

The emergency declaration put out Wednesday is the second-highest of three categories of emergencies at the site and indicates “something more serious has occurred,” according to the site’s community preparedness information. The emergency declaration ended Wednesday night after the fire was extinguished.

title: New York enacts ban on 'unsafe' chatbot behavior with kids
summary: New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions ban on certain chatbot behaviors to protect children using artificial intelligence
story: New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions ban on certain chatbot behaviors to protect children using artificial intelligence

HARRISBURG, Pa. -- New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions on companion chatbot behavior, as states increasingly move to protect children who use artificial intelligence, regulate how employers deploy AI systems and push developers to prevent an AI-caused catastrophe.
Legislation signed Wednesday by Gov. Kathy Hochul outlines a dozen definitions of “unsafe AI companion features” that will be prohibited when a companion chatbot interacts with a child under 18.

A violation could expose a chatbot developer to a lawsuit by the state attorney general's office. Penalties could include monetary damages, shutting down the chatbot and destroying data. The law takes effect Jan. 1.

Hochul, in the thick of her reelection campaign, signed the bill amid growing warnings about the existential risks posed by the rapid development of AI technology and calls for bold action by a reluctant Washington.

With Congress doing little to regulate AI, state legislatures are packed with efforts to wield state consumer protection laws to make AI use more transparent and rein in chatbots and rogue AI frontier models.
New York and California are at the vanguard of such laws that also are targeting social media platforms.

In September, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring chatbot developers to assess a model's risk to children, show how they tried to eliminate those risks and submit to an independent audit to determine whether they are complying with the law.
He also signed legislation to prohibit social media platforms from deploying addictive features for users under 16.

Meanwhile, eight states sued AI giant OpenAI earlier this month, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what one activist called “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”

However, governors acknowledge that Congress and the federal government have farther-reaching abilities to clamp down on AI-posed threats, even as President Donald Trump has brushed off concerns and warned states not to regulate AI.

Under New York's law, outlawed chatbot behavior with children under 18 includes suggestions that the chatbot is a real person that has emotions, opinions or an actual relationship with the child. It also outlaws chatbot messages that use flattery, involve sexually explicit material or encourage secrecy or unhealthy behavior.
Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of watchdog group Common Sense Media, called New York's law "the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country."

Justine Gluck, policy analyst at the Future of Privacy Forum, a nonprofit focused on data protection and AI governance, said the different regulatory approaches by California and New York could be models other states adopt after legislatures reconvene next year.

New York's law, she said, underscores how quickly chatbot regulation is evolving, as states move beyond basic disclosures and crisis-response protocols to regulating the underlying design and operation of chatbots.
Still, several categories in New York's law are broadly worded or undefined, Gluck said.
That raises questions, she said, about “where ordinary conversational responsiveness ends and prohibited behavior begins,” and could complicate how it is enforced.
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Google misses revenue expectations, Alphabet stock sinks in early after-hours trading
summary: Alphabet Inc., Google's parent company, reported strong revenue growth in its third quarter, but it fell short of Wall Street expectations
story: Alphabet Inc., Google's parent company, reported strong revenue growth in its third quarter, but it fell short of Wall Street expectations

Google parent company Alphabet Inc. came up short of Wall Street expectations despite strong revenue growth in its third-quarter results, which sent its stock falling in after-hours trading Wednesday.
The Mountain View, California-based company said its net income was $26.17 billion in the July-September period. That’s down from $34.98 billion in the same period a year earlier.

Revenue grew 25% from the same period last year to $127.58 billion, but that was shy of analysts' expectations. Analysts, on average, were expecting revenue of $127.97 billion, according to a poll by FactSet.

The company earned $2.12 per share. Results were impacted by an $8.7 billion loss on equity investments in the quarter. It was not immediately clear if the reported earnings per share are comparable to the analyst estimates, which were around $3.01 per share.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, said in a statement that the quarter was strong and that the company is “now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate. Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business,” he said, pointing to the 25% revenue growth year-over-year.
Pichai also said the Gemini app, its artificial intelligence assistant, has reached one billion users, which makes it the fastest-growing product in Google’s history.
Alphabet’s shares fell about 9% to $295.20 within an hour after the market closed.

title: FDA scientists opposed the Trump administration's effort to ease peptides access
summary: Food and Drug Administration scientists did not support an effort by President Donald Trump's administration to loosen rules on unproven peptide drugs
story: Food and Drug Administration scientists did not support an effort by President Donald Trump's administration to loosen rules on unproven peptide drugs

WASHINGTON -- A plan to give Americans easier access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was opposed by most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff members, who had limited input in drafting the policy, according to six people familiar with the policy's development.
The document, which covers certain injectable peptides popular within the wellness industry, recently underwent regulatory review at the White House, typically the final step before publication.

The effort on peptides, driven by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s longstanding mission of keeping unproven health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development.

The policy would direct the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell certain widely used peptides — substances that would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they haven’t gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness, according to three of the people.
The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. An HHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.

The chemicals subject to the new policy haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. They include BPC-157 and TB-500, which are promoted to help heal injuries and build muscle. Both are considered doping substances by international sports authorities.
Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and recently described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.
The guidance document reviewed by the White House represents a step back from HHS' original plans, according to two of the people who discussed its development.

Initially, HHS officials wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.

But FDA officials warned that the agency's scientific staffers had major safety concerns and wouldn't support a regulation deeming them safe. So HHS officials moved to a different approach that would direct the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.

Ultimately, FDA staffers provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-regulated factories.
Kennedy has said repeatedly that U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans are turning to “gray market” products imported from China and other countries.

Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting Americans from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.

The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.

It’s extremely rare that HHS would take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials have said. However, federal law technically gives HHS authority over essentially all drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.

Many Americans using peptides today don’t deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections. Instead, they often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only,” since the FDA doesn’t regulate research chemicals.

In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.
At a meeting in July, FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.
The policy pending at the White House avoids a direct confrontation with FDA staffers because it only directs the FDA not to enforce certain rules.

HHS ultimately included several safety measures suggested by FDA staffers, according to two of the people. Besides sourcing ingredients from FDA-registered facilities, compounders will be directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the chemical identity of peptides.
Those measures are supported by some industry groups, including the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which recently met with White House officials about the proposal.
