title: South Korea fines Google and Apple over unfair app market practices
summary: South Korea on Wednesday fined Google and Apple a combined $47.6 million, saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews
story: South Korea on Wednesday fined Google and Apple a combined $47.6 million, saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet’s Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country’s media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Apple said it “respectfully” disagrees with the decision, arguing that its current practices comply with South Korean law and that it is evaluating its legal options. Apple said its in-app payment system allows users to make secure transactions while protecting them from predatory tactics and fraud and that such safeguards that could potentially be lost when paying through alternative methods.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

title: Microsoft offers quarter of global workforce voluntary buyouts
summary: Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence
story: Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence
Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence.

The company's voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, the company's Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a blog post Monday.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman wrote. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
The company, which releases its quarterly financial results Wednesday, had approximately 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.
Shares of Microsoft Corp., based in Redmond, Washington, hit an all-time high this month. The stock rose about 1% on Monday.

In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including a large number of workers at its Xbox video game business.

The gusher of investment in data centers — likely topping $700 billion this year — to power artificial intelligence has made memory chips, computer processors and other equipment, as well as electricity, more expensive. Economists expect it will continue to push up inflation at least through the end of this year.

Microsoft has been ramping up its AI capabilities for several years. In 2024 the company revealed a new class of AI-imbued personal computers that centered on fusing its AI assistant, called Copilot, into the Windows operating system for PCs, where Microsoft already has the eyes of millions of consumers.

And in October 2025 Microsoft introduced a new artificial intelligence character called Mico, a floating cartoon face shaped like a blob or flame that embodies the software giant’s Copilot virtual assistant.

title: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
summary: Anthropic expands its support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares publicly for the first time
story: Anthropic expands its support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares publicly for the first time

Anthropic expanded its support for the nonprofit sector Monday, even as the artificial intelligence company filed to sell shares to the public for the first time. The maker of the AI assistant Claude said the moves are all part of its broader strategy for “compounding good.”

Anthropic launched a new Claude for Nonprofits plugin created with 30 nonprofits to be more responsive to their specific needs. It will also broaden its Claude Corps program that embeds fellows with nonprofits to help them better utilize AI by also making consultants available to help organizations with smaller, shorter-term projects.

“This work is so core to who we are as a public benefit corporation,” Elizabeth Kelly, Anthropic’s head of beneficial deployments, told The Associated Press. “We were founded to ensure that we’re both developing AI safely and responsibly and that we’re deploying it in a way that really benefits everyone, including those who are too often left behind.”

Earlier this month, Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund that could be used for large scale donations to nonprofits or directly distributed to groups of people adversely impacted by AI. The fund still needs to be approved by shareholders once Anthropic completes its IPO, which could come as early as November.

Critics say AI companies are using donations and nonprofit pledges as an attempt to generate goodwill with the public at a time when so many are worried about the potential dangers of the technology and its impact on jobs.

However, Anthropic says that as a public benefit corporation, it balances its commercial interests with the interests of the public good. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei told The Associated Press in a May interview that the company works to make that balance clear. “I think there’s something really valuable about that as a construct just to help investors and employees and outside people understand what our intentions are and hold us accountable to them,” she said.
Other public benefit corporations include eyeglass maker Warby Parker, insurance company Lemonade, and Amalgamated Bank.

Bella DeVaan, director of the Charity Reform Initiative at the Institute for Policy Studies, said that public benefit corporations can be meaningful, but the federal government doesn’t currently properly regulate corporations. Without tax reform and a change in what she calls “the public permissiveness toward billionaire power in America,” DeVaan said there is no guarantee that even public benefit corporations will act in the public interest.

“Their wealth belongs to the public in the first place -- it’s created by the country and there’s a sort of social wage owed to people who use their products,” she said. “I hope that when people use the ethos of Silicon Valley that gave birth to these companies that have grand designs of changing the world that they’ll also think about how philanthropy could actually achieve charitable aims.”

Kelly said Anthropic’s work with the nonprofit sector is part of the company’s mission. The bulk of the 25,000 nonprofits currently using Claude for Nonprofits have less than 10 people on staff, so its impact on the organizations is often great. She points to Allies Against Slavery, the Texas-based nonprofit fighting human trafficking, as an example of what is possible, after its only government affairs staffer used Claude to analyze more than 750 state-level anti-trafficking policies and turned them into recommendations for advocates.
“This is basically compounding good,” she said. “That’s the kind of work that we’re so excited to support here at Anthropic.”

Montgomery County Food Bank President and CEO Scott Burns said his organization’s use of Claude has already generated significant savings that allow it to provide food to more people in his Texas county north of Houston.

“Costs have gone up for fuel,” Burns said. “Costs have gone up in every area – for proteins, in particular… I still want to be able to do more without adding a bunch of additional resources and (Claude) will enable me to do that.”

The Montgomery County Food Bank is one of the 30 nonprofits that has been working with Anthropic to better customize Claude for its specific needs. Burns said his team has already used it to optimize scheduling for food pickup and delivery and keeping better contact with donors.

He is looking forward to welcoming two Claude Corps fellows into the organization soon to tackle its outdated inventory system and the scheduling of its volunteers. Burns said he is also hoping to share his findings with other food banks.
“Nonprofits – we’re kind of an open book,” he said. “Why would I not share? It’s only going to help get more people fed, right?”
Taproot Foundation CEO Cat Ward said her nonprofit is excited about working with Anthropic to provide pro bono expertise to nonprofits for specific projects.
“Nonprofits are as lean as they come,” Ward said. “They’ve got the ambition. They’ve got the vision. This is about empowering them with tools that’ll help them go further faster.”

title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says
summary: U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff said in a statement on Sunday.
story: "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Murphy's chief of staff said.
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff said in a statement on Sunday.
The 53-year-old Democrat was taken to a hospital on Saturday after he started to feel numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game, said Allison Herwitt, Murphy's chief of staff.
Upon examining Murphy, doctors determined he had suffered a stroke, Herwitt said, adding that the senator has been transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore.
"The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: 1 dead, 8 injured in Alabama shooting after football game, police say
summary: One of the injured was in critical condition, Birmingham police said.
story: One of the injured was in critical condition, Birmingham police said.
At least one person was killed and eight others were injured in a shooting after a football game in Birmingham, Alabama, on Saturday, law enforcement said.
At least one person was detained in connection with the shooting, according to the Birmingham Police Department.

"Shortly after 7:50 p.m., multiple shots rang out in the 400 block of Grayman Avenue West, officers responded and located multiple gunshot victims," Officer Darrell Freeman said during a press conference.

Freeman said nine people had been hit by gunfire, including "at least one being confirmed deceased." Another of the injured was in critical condition, he added, and seven others were in stable condition.

"Multiple firearms were recovered from the scene by officers and turned into our property room," Freeman said. "One person has been detained and transported to the Birmingham Police Headquarters for questioning. This is an active scene with developing information."
The shooting was near Legion Field, which hosted the Magic City Classic college football game earlier on Saturday between Alabama A&M and Alabama State.
"This did occur after the game," Chief Michael Pickett said. "For the most part, it was off of the property."
In a statement posted on social media, Birmingham Mayor Randall L. Woodfin said the shooting left him and the community "hurt, shaken and rightfully angry."

"There is no argument, no beef, no misunderstanding that can justify this level of senseless violence during a night of celebration," Woodfin said. "But hear me clearly: We refuse to let fear shake the spirit of this community. Justice will be served to those who brought harm to those at one of our most treasured events."
The mayor noted that the Magic City Classic is rooted in the traditions of historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs), including the "traditions of family."

"Tonight, as a family, we grieve. We wrap our arms around neighbors who are dealing with unimaginable pain right now. And just like family, we will stand united as we overcome this tragic night," Woodfin said. "While this crime is under an active investigation, we will not let up until we achieve swift justice for this senseless violence."

title: 1 dead, 6 injured in 'targeted' shooting at California Halloween store
summary: One person was killed and six others were injured in a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store inside the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, California, police said.
story: Police urged the public to remain vigilant on Saturday.
One person was killed and six others were injured in a "targeted" shooting at a Spirit Halloween store inside the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, California, police said.

"Based on preliminary information obtained during the investigation, the shooting is believed to have stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect inside the Spirit Halloween store," police said in a statement Saturday.

Fairfield police responded to the shooting at about 8:30 p.m. local time Friday, according to a statement from the police department. Seven people were found with gunshot wounds, one of whom died from their injuries.
The six other victims were taken to local hospitals, with at least three in critical condition, police said.
"Detectives continue to actively investigate this case, reviewing video footage and other evidence to identify the individual responsible for this heinous act of violence," police said.
Police have identified Constance Hages, a 31-year-old female, as the victim who died of gunshot wounds. Hages was pregnant at the time of her death, family members told police.
A 16-year-old male, a 19-year-old male and a 32-year-old male remain in critical condition, police said. A 23-year-old male remains hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two additional victims, a 19-year-old male and a 43-year-old male, were treated for gunshot wounds and have since been released from the hospital, police said.

"We encourage anyone in the community with information to contact the Fairfield Police Department," Fairfield Chief of Police Dan Marshall said during a press conference Friday night. "I know the mall has cameras, so hopefully we'll get some of that footage."
Police encouraged the public to "remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity" during Halloween celebrations Saturday evening.

"Our department extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the victim who died from their injuries. We also extend our thoughts to the other victims who were injured during this shooting," police said Saturday.

title: Judge says court will investigate government officials in DC golf course case
summary: The judge wants to know if lawyers tried to mislead her over Trump's plans.
story: A federal judge in Washington said Friday the court will investigate whether government attorneys committed ethical violations before the court in the case about the dispute over the East Potomac Golf Course, the public course in Washington, D.C., that President Donald Trump wants to close and renovate.

"The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and [Justice Department] attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated applicable ethical rules," Judge Ana Reyes said from the bench. Reyes said she intends to appoint a special master to assist in the inquiry.

The case involves a lawsuit filed in February by the DC Preservation League to prevent the Interior Department from closing the historic golf course on the Potomac River and replacing it with a championship-style course favored by Trump. While that litigation was ongoing, the government agreed in court it would give notice to the DC Preservation League about any efforts to permanently alter the course.

The government gave notice at 4:55 p.m. on the Friday before the Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples Day three-day weekend that it would commence cutting trees at the course over weekend. It began work early the next morning, cutting down more than 400 trees and drawing the ire of Reyes and sparking a flurry of court activity to determine if the government has misled the court.

Reyes began Friday's motions hearing by reading the D.C. Bar rules of professional conduct, which govern the duty of lawyers appearing before the court to be truthful and to correct any false statements or fact or law that they make. She soon turned to Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, peppering him with questions about the government's representations about its plans to close the golf course on Nov. 15.
At issue was Woodward's Oct. 19 appearance in an evidentiary hearing in which he stated that "[w]ith regard to the November 15th date ... there is no plan to close the course."

But a week later, Trump posted on his social media platform that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons."
Friday's hearing was scheduled to reconcile what Woodward told the court and whether any false statements were made to the court.

On Tuesday, Reyes issued a sharply worded 70-page ruling that criticized the administration over its plans for the golf course and concluded the administration likely violated environmental laws in the process.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," Reyes wrote. "Not to believe him that a cabinet secretary has 'developed' a federal land project. Not to believe him that the secretary's agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land. Not to believe him that 'Restoration work' will begin 'IMMEDIATELY!' Not to believe him that the course 'will be closed' for over a year. Not to believe what the President has repeatedly told the American public. And yet, here we are."
The judge ordered the administration to give the court 10 business days' written notice before making any irreparable modification to the course and East Potomac Park, where it is located.
Under withering questioning from Reyes on Friday, Woodward insisted as a legal matter no plan has been finalized.
Woodward had previously filed a motion to disqualify Reyes on the grounds that she was not impartial. That filing was rejected by Reyes.

The special master, who has yet to be appointed, will have a mandate to investigate whether government lawyers, which could potentially include top Justice Department officials, were involved in making false statements, withholding information from the court, failing to correct false testimony or interfering with the accuracy of written testimony.
The government will have an opportunity to object to the appointment.

title: These House races could determine which party is in control in the next Congress
summary: All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3.
story: There are 16 races that ABC News rates as Tossup going into Election Day.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3. But spread across the political map, there are 16 races that ABC News rates as tossup in which the outcomes are expected to come down to the wire and will be crucial to determining the balance of power in the House for the 120th Congress.
Democrats must net at least a three-seat gain to take control.
Here are the races that ABC News rates as Tossup:
Alabama 2: Incumbent Democrat Shomari Figures vs. Republican Rhett Marques

In this newly drawn district, Figures faces Marques, a state representative, in a competitive race. The district was redrawn after the Supreme Court allowed Alabama to reinstate a 2023 congressional map that a federal court had previously blocked. Figures is counting on strong turnout among Black voters, who make up about 40% of the district’s voting-age population. President Donald Trump rallied in Mobile on Oct. 2 and urged voters to back Marques. Trump would have carried the new district by 14 points in 2024.
Colorado 5: Incumbent Republican Jeff Crank vs. Democrat Jessica Killin

Crank is locked in a tight race against Killin, an Army veteran and former chief of staff for then-second gentleman Doug Emhoff. The district, which includes Colorado Springs and nearly all of El Paso County, has leaned more left over the past three presidential cycles. However, Trump won this military-heavy district by about 9 points in 2024. The Iran war is a key issue in this race. Crank supports the war but believes Trump should have sought congressional approval.
Florida 14: Incumbent Democrat Kathy Castor vs. Republican Mike Beltran

Castor, a 10-term incumbent, is facing off against Trump-endorsed former trial lawyer Beltran. The seat became more competitive after Florida’s legislature redrew this district, putting Castor on the defensive.
Florida 22: Open -- Democrat Pia Dandiya vs. Republican Casey Askar

The battle for Florida’s newly drawn district spanning parts of Palm Beach and Broward counties and the city of Naples puts two political newcomers in the ring: Marine Corps veteran Askar against former teacher and U.S. Education Department official Dandiya.
Iowa 2: Open -- Democrat Lindsey James vs. Republican Joe Mitchell

As incumbent congresswoman Ashley Hinson runs for Senate, this historically red House seat in the Hawkeye State is now up for grabs. James, a state representative and chaplain, is running against Mitchell, a 29-year-old lobbyist and former state representative who worked on Trump’s transition team. Trump won this district by 10 points in 2024, but the economic impacts from the Iran war and tariffs on this agriculture-heavy district have made this race competitive.
Kentucky 6: Open -- Democrat Zach Dembo vs. Republican Ralph Alvarado

GOP Rep. Andy Barr’s bid to fill Mitch McConnell’s long-held Senate seat leaves his Kentucky House seat open. Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy JAG officer, faces Alvarado, a physician and former state senator. This district used to be more competitive, but redistricting in 2022 has made it friendlier to Republicans in recent years – though Barr was a consistent Democratic target since he was elected in 2012.
Michigan 4: Incumbent Republican Bill Huizenga vs. Democrat Sean McCann

Huizenga, who has served in Congress since 2011, is being challenged by McCann, a state senator. Huizenga does have incumbency advantage and outperformed Trump substantively in 2024, but his race appears to be tightening as many pollsters anticipate a sour political environment for the president’s party.
Michigan 7: Incumbent Republican Tom Barrett vs. Democrat William Lawrence

First-term congressman and former Army helicopter pilot Barrett, who has repeatedly bucked Trump by voting to limit his war powers in Iran, hopes to keep his seat and defeat progressive candidate Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement. Despite the split, Trump has campaigned in favor of Barrett’s reelection in the competitive swing district, where Democrat Elissa Slotkin beat a Republican in 2018 to flip this seat before she ultimately won a bid for Senate in 2024.
Michigan 10: Open -- Democrat Christina Hines vs. Republican Mike Bouchard

As Rep. John James runs to be Michigan’s next governor, his open seat in Detroit's northern suburbs is up for grabs. The battle is between Hines, a former prosecutor, and Bouchard, an Army veteran. Trump carried this district by more than six points in 2024.
Montana 1: Open -- Democrat Sam Forstag vs. Republican Aaron Flint

Rep. Ryan Zinke’s retirement has left this Montana seat open with no incumbency advantage for Republicans. Flint, an Army veteran and conservative radio show host, is running against Forstag, a union leader and wildland firefighter smokejumper. Trump won this district covering western Montana by nearly 12 points in 2024.
New York 17: Incumbent Republican Mike Lawler vs. Democrat Cait Conley

Lawler is one of two Republicans running for reelection in Kamala Harris-won districts this cycle -- six others opted against another term in the House. Lawler has kept this seat in a blue state since 2022, outperforming Trump in 2024 by 2.8%. Lawler, who secured State and Local Tax (SALT) deductions during the Trump tax bill negotiations, is running against Conley, an Army combat veteran.
Ohio 7: Incumbent Republican Max Miller vs. Democrat Brian Poindexter

Miller’s reelection bid has been hampered by allegations of domestic assault against his ex-wife Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller, a former Trump aide, has flatly denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with any crimes and refused to drop out of the race despite widespread calls from Republicans. Trump stopped short of calling on Miller to withdraw last summer, calling the situation "sad.” He’s being challenged by Poindexter, a union organizer and ironworker.
Pennsylvania 1: Incumbent Republican Brian Fitzpatrick vs. Democrat Bob Harvie

Five-term incumbent Fitzpatrick, a former FBI agent, is the other Republican running for re-election in a district that Harris won in 2024. Fitzpatrick has repeatedly broken with the president on policy issues and was one of two House Republicans who voted against his mega tax and policy bill. He has established himself as a moderate in the House, helping boost his electoral performance in the competitive district, which includes Bucks County and Montgomery County. Harvie, has served as a Bucks County commissioner since 2020.
Texas 15: Democrat Bobby Pulido vs. incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz

De La Cruz, who was first elected in 2022, is seeking to keep her seat in a South Texas district that is nearly 80% Latino. Redistricting expanded the 15th into Hidalgo County and shifted some of her GOP voters into neighboring districts. Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, is challenging De La Cruz in a race that could test Trump’s standing with Latino voters.
Texas 35: Open -- Democrat Johnny Garcia vs. Republican Carlos De La Cruz

This East San Antonio seat, previously held by Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, is open after the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus changed districts because of redistricting initiated by the Republican-controlled legislature. Garcia, a deputy sheriff, hopes to keep the district blue and is running against Trump-endorsed De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran and brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz.
Virginia 1: Incumbent Republican Rob Wittman vs. Democrat Shannon Taylor

In North Virginia and the Middle Peninsula, 10-term Republican Wittman is battling to keep his seat against Taylor, Henrico County’s top prosecutor. It is one of a few districts across the country where Kamala Harris in 2024 outperformed Joe Biden in 2020, suggesting the district is trending left.

title: Voters weigh citizenship amendments as Trump fans fears of noncitizen election fraud
summary: Civil rights groups warn millions of Americans could get sidelined.
story: Civil rights groups warn millions of Americans could get sidelined.
Voters in six states on Nov. 3 will decide whether to approve ballot measures that would amend their state constitutions or state law to make U.S. citizenship a requirement for voting.
The closely watched popular referenda reflect a push by President Donald Trump to crackdown on noncitizen voting based on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud.
Voting-rights advocates warn they also raise the potential of sidelining millions of eligible American voters.

"Rather than strengthening democracy, [the amendments are] a political maneuver designed to justify future rollbacks of voting rights," said Rashane Hamby with the ACLU of Kansas in testimony last year.
Federal and state laws already prohibit noncitizens from voting in any federal or statewide election, but advocates for the constitutional amendments say even more protection is needed.

"Law can change, as we know,” said West Virginia state Sen. Patricia Rucker, a Republican, at a press conference last month. "This proposed amendment would ensure that no future legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill."

No state constitution currently includes a citizenship requirement for voting. Five states -- Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia -- have amendments on the ballot. An Alaska initiative would create a new state law.
Of particular concern to some supporters: major cities in three states plus the District of Columbia that do allow some noncitizens to lawfully participate in local elections.
"There's nothing that magically stops those bad ideas at that state's borders," said Arkansas state Rep. David Ray in a news conference last month.

Many civil rights groups and nonpartisan voter advocates fear the measures -- and accompanying regulations requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote -- could disenfranchise tens of millions of Americans.
Jemmie Lolita Pepper of Indiana, a former public-school educator who was born on U.S. soil but spent decades unable to prove it, says she empathizes with both sides of the debate.

"I understand the desire to require proof so there won't be voter fraud or anything like that. I truly support that: no voter fraud,” said Pepper, 63, in an interview. "But for those of us who had to live years of not having [any documentation], you couldn’t prove it. I couldn't."

With pro bono legal help, Pepper recently untangled a series of clerical errors in state records -- including a misspelling of her first name and faulty substitution of her last name -- that had prevented her from obtaining an official government ID and, in turn, casting a ballot. She now has one.
"They had my name listed as the boys' spelling, J-I-M-M-I-E," Pepper recalled of her legal odyssey. "I said, 'Well that’s still me. That's still me.'"

An estimated 21.3 million Americans -- or 9% of all eligible voters -- are unable to readily present documentation proving they are citizens because of misplaced or inaccessible records, financial hardship putting replacement fees out of reach, name changes from divorce or remarriage, and clerical errors in state databases, according to a 2025 study by the University of Maryland.
Only 48% of Americans have a valid passport as of 2023, according to the State Department.
Some voting-rights advocates say a proof-of-citizenship requirement would hit elderly, disabled and rural voters particularly hard.

"I’ve been through SCUD missiles, riots, sniper fire. To be unable to keep it together navigating all these processes makes me ashamed to say, but it would be really difficult," said Symmone Ford of Michigan, a 56-year-old Gulf War veteran with severe PTSD who has difficulty leaving her home.

"I can’t afford the money for a lawyer to change my name. I barely have enough to pay my bills," said Ford, whose last name does not currently match her birth certificate because of several marriages and divorces.

Additional paperwork requirements for voter registration could effectively shut down online access, some experts said. Even when people do have proper documentation, many may lack access to copiers, notaries and scanners to submit electronically.

Nine states currently have laws requiring state officials to verify a voter's citizenship status either by looking at documentary proof at time of registration, reviewing voter registration history, or cross-checking with other government databases, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Federal law requires voters in all states to attest with a signature -- under threat of imprisonment -- that they are, in fact, U.S. citizens when they sign up for a ballot.
Still, 83% of Americans, according to Gallup, say people registering to vote for the first time should have to provide documentation to show that they are eligible citizens.

Efforts by Trump and his Republican allies to institute a nationwide proof-of-citizenship standard stalled in Congress earlier this year and later got blocked by federal courts when he attempted to impose it by executive order.
An online tracker of major public claims of noncitizen voting compiled by the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research shows cases of noncitizen voting are extremely rare.

In Michigan, for example, the state attorney general identified 38 credible cases of noncitizen voting in the 2024 general election out of roughly 5.7 million votes cast. That's 0.0000066% of total votes cast.
Six of the Michigan cases have resulted in criminal charges, while 10 were closed without charges and 22 are still under review, according to state officials.

Eighteen states did not publicly disclose finding or removing any noncitizen from a voter registration list in the 2024 election, and no state uncovered any coordinated effort to get noncitizens to vote, according to CEIR records.

President Trump and the Department of Justice continue to push unsubstantiated claims of widespread noncitizen voting as the basis for tighter voter registration rules and ballot segregation in several states, including California and Washington.

The U.S. Supreme Court has previously struck down efforts to add a proof-of-citizenship requirement to federal voter registration forms. Later this year, in a major case from Arizona, the justices will decide whether states can mandate proof-of-citizenship on state forms and for voting in state races.

title: DOJ says election officials could face jail time if they fail to preserve records
summary: The DOJ has warned election officials in multiple states that they could face jail time if they fail to preserve election records in accordance with federal law.
story: The Justice Department sent letters to election officials in multiple states.

The Justice Department has warned election officials in multiple states that they could face jail time if they fail to preserve election records in accordance with federal law, according to copies of the letters obtained by ABC News.

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter framed his letter, sent Thursday to state election leaders, as a "reminder" of their obligation to preserve ballots, pollbooks, precinct sign-in sheets and other election-related materials.
"It is a crime to willfully fail to comply" with the record-retention rules, McCotter wrote. "Such a failure is punishable by up to a year in prison and a $1,000 fine."

The message from McCotter comes as the Trump administration continues threatening election workers in California and elsewhere with jail time for tabulating ballots that the Justice Department claims could belong to noncitizen voters.

Multiple state election officials said McCotter's invocation of criminal liability for election officials who fail to comply with longstanding law marks a departure from how past administrations have communicated such obligations to their state counterparts.
Some state officials ABC News spoke with took issue with the letter's tone.
"While I hope the decision to emphasize criminal penalties was intended simply as a reminder of the law, it could have been handled differently," said Connecticut Secretary of State Stephanie Thomas.

In January, the FBI seized more than 600 boxes of ballots and other election records in Fulton County, Georgia, as part of an investigation driven by allies of President Donald Trump seeking to overturn the outcome of the 2020 election.
A federal judge in May denied a request from Fulton County officials to force the FBI to return the ballots.

title: Peltola denies knowing of 'any other candidate' on ballot besides herself, incumbent
summary: The DOJ is acting to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska said.
story: The DOJ is acting to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe.

Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied that she knew about an effort to recruit a candidate to be on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"I just want to clear the air. I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said during a rally in Juneau, Alaska, on Thursday, according to an Associated Press video.
ABC News has asked the Peltola campaign to clarify whether she is denying knowledge of the reported recruitment effort to find a spoiler candidate.
Peltola later added, "I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan."

Peltola's comments, just days before the high-stakes midterm elections, come after a New York Times report Wednesday that her campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee played a role in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan -- a Republican who almost has the same name as incumbent Sen. Sullivan -- as part of an effort to sow confusion and ultimately benefit Peltola's campaign.
At a separate campaign event on Thursday, Peltola called the New York Times' report "just another distraction."
"It's another diversion. Every day, it's some new, you know, 'look over here' moment,” Peltola said in a social media video verified by ABC News.

Meanwhile, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska held a press conference Friday afternoon to announce the Justice Department's efforts to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe into the Alaska Senate race following that New York Times report.

In the press conference, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman provided little in the way of details about what actions the department was specifically taking -- citing sensitivities surrounding ongoing criminal investigations.
"I do want to say that what we've learned recently has been deeply troubling," Heyman said. "We are acting on it intensely and swiftly."

Heyman said the new information reported on by the Times has resulted in a "significant surge" of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and other law enforcement "around the country" are also taking "investigative steps" regarding information from the article. Heyman said the office has already received "a number of new pieces of information" in just the last 24 hours that investigators are following up on.
Asked during the press conference what specific crime was being investigated, Heyman conceded the department hasn't made a determination one way or another.

"We investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories," he said. "So I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse. I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

Earlier this week, the Justice Department began issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal probe of Democrats' alleged efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. The Trump administration filed a separate civil lawsuit last week seeking an injunction against the state certifying the results of its election in the event Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses, which a federal judge is expected to rule on in the coming days.

Peltola’s campaign earlier this week told ABC News that it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." Former Peltola staffer Elisa Rios told the Times about the reported recruitment effort, saying Peltola wasn't directly involved but that she was "definitely aware."
ABC News reached out to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign for comment on the New York Times' report earlier this week, but has not heard back.

Alaska courts evaluated the dispute over Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy and found nothing illegal about his bid to be on the ballot -- even if it was not entirely in "good faith" or an attempt to "confuse and mislead" as the Trump administration and Republicans contend.

On Friday morning, President Donald Trump, who has claimed Pelota has committed "election fraud," said Alaskans would need to have a "190 IQ" to understand the ballot with two Dan Sullivans, despite the ballot's clear distinctions between the two candidates' names and other distinctive marks like party affiliation and incumbency.

On the general election ballot, Sen. Sullivan is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, a registered Republican, and it is noted that he is the incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. with no party affiliation.

"You need about 190 IQ to figure out the ballot. They put a ballot down where they're talking about incumbent Republican and the other one. Most people don't know in Alaska, in a lot of other states too, what does incumbent mean? They don't know what incumbent means," Trump said when he called into Kansas City's KMCO "Mundo in the Morning."
Peltola won the primary by a larger margin than adding Dan J. Sullivan in could have made up for: 48% to 2%, respectively; Sen. Sullivan earned 43% of the vote in the primary.

GOP Sen. Sullivan on Thursday criticized Democrats' alleged efforts to recruit another Dan Sullivan in the Senate race. Sen. Sullivan, on Fox News, claimed Peltola's campaign ran a "secret operation to put a fake Dan Sullivan on the ballot with the primary purpose, the only purpose, to trick Alaskans."

title: States push back on Trump's noncitizen voting claims
summary: The Trump administration has warned several states that their voter rolls include noncitizens, but many of those claims haven't held up to scrutiny.
story: The administration is making a bid to impose itself on state-run elections.

It was a dire warning, delivered on the biggest stage: Some 278,000 noncitizens were improperly registered to vote in federal elections and were poised to tilt the scales of the election in November, President Donald Trump warned in a primetime address to the nation in July.
"The real number is actually much higher," he added.
The president's bold claim set off a series of events that culminated in recent weeks with an unprecedented bid by the federal government to impose itself on state-run elections.

The Trump administration has sued the state of California and threatened other states over the issue of noncitizen voting, a longtime concern of the president and his administration despite experts saying it is already illegal and "vanishingly rare." Federal officials have demanded action after presenting to states what they say are lists of noncitizens who are registered to vote, gathered using a combination of federal immigration data and commercially available state voter registration rolls.

But in the final weeks of the campaign, as the administration implores state and local officials, both in and out of court, to investigate those individuals, the lists -- and the grandiose numbers Trump and his allies publicly trumpeted -- appear to be buckling under the scrutiny of state and local election officials.

In California, Washington and Nevada -- and beyond -- state and local officials say the lists provided by the Justice Department appear grossly inaccurate and justify the states' reluctance to purge individuals from registration lists so close to the election.

The Trump administration initially accused California of harboring over 190,000 noncitizen voters on its rolls over the summer. That sum was whittled down to 20,000 by the time the Justice Department filed its lawsuit against the state last week.
It's not clear why the administration reduced the figure so dramatically. But even the smaller figure seems inflated, according to state and local officials.

In court filings, officials in Los Angeles County said a preliminary review of 200 individuals on the list showed that nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history."

Judge David Carter, the federal judge assigned to the case, rejected the Justice Department's push for an emergency intervention based in part on what he called the administration's "unreliability" and "lack of credibility."

Late last week, separate from its litigation against the state, the DOJ sent letters to every California county asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News.

"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to the letter sent by Justice Department officials.

Since then, county election officials have been sifting through the lists. According to some county officials, the results so far seem to confirm their skepticism of the Trump administration's claims.

In Butte County, situated just north of the Sacramento Valley, officials received a list of 47 names from federal prosecutors late Friday. The county's top election official, Keaton Denlay, told ABC News that he personally reviewed what he called the Justice Department's "poorly formatted excel spreadsheet with missing and jumbled information."
Denlay found that 32 of the 47 individuals "are not on Butte county's active voter rolls," and another seven "did not have sufficient information for me to match to our voter list with confidence."
Officials in Nevada County received a list of just 10 names. Their review "found no evidence of non-citizen voting in the November 3, 2026 Election," an official said.

Of the 33 names sent to officials in San Benito County, officials there said, "a preliminary review ... indicated that not all listed individuals were currently registered to vote in San Benito County," without specifying how many.
Other county officials contacted by ABC News said they were either still reviewing the list or analyzing their legal obligation to cooperate with the Justice Department.

A Justice Department official told ABC News that, as of Thursday, the DOJ under Trump had charged roughly 200 individuals across the country with either illegal voting or unlawful voter registration-related offenses.

Federal prosecutors in Washington state convened the media on Monday for a press conference where they accused state leaders of knowingly allowing some 400 noncitizens to vote this fall, calling that figure just "the tip of the iceberg."

The top election official in Washington state issued a blistering response on Wednesday, claiming that a preliminary review of the Justice Department's list found a number of U.S. citizens, as well as "several" other individuals who are not registered to vote.

"The information you provided contains several glaring deficiencies," wrote Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state in response the DOJ. "You provide no information about how the information was collected or what sources were used. Nor do you provide any backup documentation supporting your assertions."

Hobbs said this close to an election, the risk of removing individuals from registration lists or sequestering their ballots would risk disenfranchising eligible voters, a sentiment shared by election officials around the country and the judge overseeing the Justice Department's case in California.

"It is almost certain more people named on this list are also United States citizens; those already identified may just be the 'tip of the iceberg' of individuals that would be wrongfully disenfranchised by the actions you request," Hobbs told the DOJ.

In August, federal officials alerted Nevada state leaders, including Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar, that there could be as many as 15,903 noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The two parties met on a video conference to discuss the figure.

According to a recording of the video conference obtained by ABC News, the meeting was not overtly hostile -- but there appeared to be palpable tension and some awkward exchanges, as Nevada officials seemed deeply skeptical of the claims made by Department of Homeland Security officials.
"So what you're saying is the 15,000 number has not been vetted?" a Nevada official asked, according to the recording.
"I probably wouldn't use the sentence, 'It hasn't been vetted,'" a DHS representative responded, adding that each individual has not "had a full manual review."
"So it went from 16,000, and then to the 185, and then down to zero from our perspective," Aguilar said.

"There's no trust in that relationship," Aguilar later told ABC News. "In order to have a working relationship, there has to be trust, and the fact that they continue to tear that trust apart and spread the misinformation and the lies that they are about our elections is wrong."

In response to a request by ABC News for comment earlier this month, DHS stood by its work, which it called "a service to Nevada's citizens," and accused Nevada officials of knowingly harboring illegal voters on its lists.

"Nevada knows the 185 names they keep waving around were never the full list of illegal voters," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email. "They were only the files [that immigration officials] had finished reviewing at the moment of the call. Since then, [immigration officials] have manually confirmed about 2,000 more aliens from the same list."
They concluded: "The review is just beginning."

title: Vote Republican, or else: How Trump is dangling government help on the campaign trail
summary: President Donald Trump is signaling to states that his administration may be far less likely to help if their voters put Democrats in power on Election Day
story: President Donald Trump is signaling to states that his administration may be far less likely to help if their voters put Democrats in power on Election Day

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump says Georgia GOP Senate candidate Mike Collins can call him whenever he wants to ask for help for his state. But if Georgia reelects Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, Trump says it could be another story.

“There’s a big difference between that and Pee-wee Herman calling,” Trump said last week in Perry, Georgia, using his derisive nickname for Ossoff. The president acted out a hypothetical scenario at his rally where Ossoff called to ask for money for his state, with Trump responding, “I don’t give a damn what he wants.”

It’s been a recurring theme at Trump’s rallies this month: From North Carolina to Ohio to Kansas, the president has dangled the idea that his administration would be far less likely to help states where Democrats win in the upcoming midterm elections.

Trump has sandwiched the threats into rallies where he has announced goodies like new semiconductor investments, a submarine repair center and fewer limits on a certain type of diesel, underscoring to the audience the types of tangibles an all-Republican Washington could continue to deliver for voters should his party remain in power after November.

But the president’s utterances — part of a larger political strategy that’s anchored on making the midterms about himself and activating conservative voters — have also injected politics into processes that have traditionally remained apolitical, such as doling out disaster aid and providing benefits for veterans.

“It’s a losing strategy for the failed president to insult and threaten voters while he’s in town reminding them he made everything more expensive,” Ossoff told The Associated Press in response to Trump’s rally comments in Perry.

Asked for further elaboration on the pattern of remarks, the White House said Trump is committed to keeping a Republican majority in Congress so “he can continue to deliver on his winning, commonsense agenda.”

White House spokesman Davis Ingle cited Trump’s policies on taxes, prescription drugs, immigration and other policies and added, “Democrats have made it clear that they have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people.”
Yet some of Trump’s remarks have handed ammunition to Democratic candidates in key battleground races.

A sweeping 2022 veterans law signed by then-President Joe Biden allowed those facing health conditions linked to contaminated water at Camp Lejeune, a Marine Corps base in North Carolina, to file for compensation.

In Greenville, North Carolina, earlier this month, Trump announced that $1 billion in cash settlements had been delivered to veterans and their family members who had been affected by the Lejeune contamination, and that he would direct the Justice Department to settle all remaining legitimate claims expeditiously — “if we win the House and the Senate.”
“So, if we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said. “If we do win, you’re getting it.”

Questioned afterward at the White House, Trump said, “If we’re not there, then somebody else is going to have to settle” the Camp Lejeune claims and he “can’t speak for another administration,” although his own Justice Department is handling the claims.

It wasn’t the first time Trump had made that type of remark in North Carolina, where his handpicked Senate candidate, Michael Whatley, has struggled to gain traction against Democrat Roy Cooper, a well-known former governor.

During a September rally in Gastonia, Trump said North Carolina was still waiting on more Hurricane Helene recovery money and added, “Now, if Michael loses, I’m not sending it,” even though he immediately said he was kidding.

Cooper has described Trump’s Camp Lejeune threats as “insulting and frustrating” while his campaign has gone after Whatley for refusing to denounce them. (Whatley, asked in a local television interview about the president's comments, said caring for the affected veterans and families is a priority.)

The threat angered Jill Steen Dilgard, whose father and other relatives served at Camp Lejeune and were subsequently diagnosed with cancer and other health issues. She said in an interview with the AP that it was “totally unacceptable” for the president to condition care for those who had served in the U.S. military on the results of the midterms.

“It made me physically sick, and it infuriated me,” said Steen Dilgard, who helps advocate for other Camp Lejeune victims and their families. “You're playing politics and trying to bribe for a vote. So many hundreds of thousands have already lost their lives, and hundreds of thousands are suffering, and many have been given a death sentence.”

Trump has frequently announced state-specific perks at rallies, from protecting a steam-powered heat utility in Ohio to investing billions in Montana mortgages through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to pardoning truckers in Alaska who had pleaded guilty to violating federal environmental laws.
But sometimes, he takes it a step further.

During a trip to Kansas to shore up GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, Trump noted to the crowd that he had granted a waiver that would temporarily allow year-round sales of E15, an ethanol-blended gas that is usually restricted during the summer.

“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Trump said during a rally in Park City. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.”

Although there is legislation in Congress that would allow for permanent year-round sales of E15, it can also be done at an administration’s discretion through temporary waivers issued by the Environmental Protection Agency.
In response, Hamilton's campaign did not criticize Trump directly but said, “Kansans are tired of our broken politics that treats public service like it’s all about opposing teams."

“Roger Marshall has been in Congress for 10 years and never passed year-round E15,” said Tyson Brody, a spokesman for the campaign. "When Adam is senator, he will look forward to working with anyone — including President Trump — to finally deliver on this and other important priorities for Kansas.”
Other times, the president’s threats to not help Democratic-led states have seemed less about policy and more about personal relationships.

In Vandalia, Ohio, this month, Trump again was noting how Republican officeholders in the state were pushing him on disaster relief and added that “when you are president, you have a lot of power over states.”

If Democratic gubernatorial candidate “Amy Acton got in, I don’t know anything about her,” Trump continued. “She’s never gonna call me. I’m never probably gonna work the same way. You just can’t. It’s just human nature. But I’m not gonna help her probably.”
Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in response that the candidate is “committed to working with anyone, Democrat or Republican, to make life better for working Ohioans.”
At the Perry, Georgia, rally, Trump made clear he wasn’t joking about his threat to ignore requests from Ossoff.

“People don’t realize what a big difference it makes. And probably I shouldn’t say that because they’ll say, ‘This is not appropriate,’” Trump said, explaining that “having people that you like call you as opposed to people that you can’t stand” makes a big difference.

title: Ahead of midterms, backlash grows over soaring electricity bills
summary: Nationwide, electricity costs have spiked approximately 5% in the past year, government data shows.
story: Electricity costs have spiked 5% in the past year, government data shows.
With less than one week to go before the midterm elections, soaring electricity bills have become a hot topic on the campaign trail.
Over the past year, residential electricity costs have spiked approximately 5% nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
An ABC News analysis found that in the top 10 states where electric bills have increased the most, five are home to competitive races for the U.S. Senate.
In Maine, where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is in a tight race with Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, electricity costs have surged 16% in one year.
In Ohio, where incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown are facing off, electricity costs are up 12% in the past year.
Across the country, 57% of Americans now say their utilities are unaffordable, up from 45% in February, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos' KnowledgePanel.

Electricity prices have been rising for several reasons, including costly upgrades to an aging energy grid, state and local regulations and rising demand from consumers and businesses, including data centers.
Tech companies and data center developers are pledging to cover their own costs amid the backlash. The evidence is mixed -- and community-dependent -- on whether data centers increase power bills.

At an Oct. 20 county meeting in Loudoun County, Virginia, where there are more data centers than any other region in the country, some residents spoke up to say the rise in electricity costs is unsustainable.

"The fact that someone like me, for example, my utility bill is going from an average of about $250 a month to around $850 a month, and we're hearing those same things across the country," Derrick Robinson, a Loudoun County resident, told ABC News.
The U.S. Department of Energy says there are ways for individuals to help cut down on their electricity usage amid rising costs.

The department shares tips on its website, including using power strips and turning them off when not in use; sealing gaps around doors and windows to improve insulation; turning the water heater to 120 degrees Fahrenheit and washing clothes in warm water instead of hot water.

title: Texas Democrats see data centers as a winning issue
summary: Rural Texas voters have overwhelmingly backed Republicans for decades, but Democrats hope voter opposition to data centers could help unseat the Republican governor.
story: Rural Texas voters' opposition pushed GOP governor to back off from his support.

Rural Texas voters have overwhelmingly backed Republicans for decades, but this year Democrats are hoping that voter opposition to data centers could give them a chance to unseat the Republican governor.

The Democratic candidate in that race, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has made opposition to data center construction a central part of her race against Gov. Greg Abbott. That race has become competitive for a state that hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990. ABC News ranks the race as Lean Republican.

Hinojosa told ABC she didn't expect this issue to be so central to her campaign "but the thing about the data centers is it's a physical manifestation of a government, a governor during doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves ... it's also told the story of a larger problem in Texas."
Hinojosa supports a moratorium on new construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks.
She has criticized Abbott for signing tax breaks for data centers and promoting the industry's growth. Abbott once said he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter" of the industry.
Hinojosa says that she has gained support with rural Republican voters who have lost faith in the governor on the issue.
Several rural counties in Texas have sued to stop data center construction, citing concerns about pollution, water usage, and loss of family farmland.
An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted earlier this month found that in 69% of Texans oppose new data center construction in their communities.

For his part, Abbott announced a moratorium on new data center construction in rural communities in September and said he supports more stringent requirements on power and water use by the centers. He told ABC News, "When rural Texans know the detailed strategy that I have, they are coming to my side."
Republican Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, who lost his re-election bid to a challenger backed by Abbott, called those promises from the governor "smoke and mirrors."
He said that voter voters' attitudes about data centers "will cost [Abbott] support because he's wrong on the issue. He's not listening to the people. He's listening to his donors."
Abbott press secretary Eduardo Leal told ABC News, "Governor Abbott has the strongest data center guardrails in the country. Sid Miller is a sore loser and has no idea what he's talking about."
Miller says he will not vote for Abbott or Nate Sheets, the Republican who beat him in the primary for agriculture commissioner. He cites policy on data centers as one of the reasons.
When asked if he planned to vote for the Democrats in those races, Miller said, "That's between me and God, and it's going to stay that way."
Another lifelong Republican told ABC News he planned to cast his first vote for a Democrat this year because of his stance on data centers.
Daniel McCoslin, a Marine Corps veteran living in Centerville in southeastern Texas, says a planned data center near his family's farm mobilized him to vote against Abbott, saying, "He needs to go."
He described his decision to switch his vote as a tough one saying, "I ate the cat turd instead of the dog turd."
One Republican warned that the backlash over data centers might be an overreaction that could hurt rural communities.

Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian, who serves on the body that regulates Texas' energy industry and is not up for re-election this year, argues that data centers provide jobs and revenue to parts of the state that are struggling, saying, "rural Texas is in trouble ... The money is moving out, and the population is going down."

Christian blames the voter backlash on outside sources like China and Democratic Sen. Bernie Sanders, saying that Texans have "been lied to. They've been told half-truths, or they've been told only the problems."
But even he admits this is the issue that could decide the midterms for his party: "The entire swing vote is rural Texas."

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
summary: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations
story: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations

MEXICO CITY -- Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country's Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.

No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.

Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City's main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.

But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.

In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.

In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island's community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery's perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: Flash floods trigger evacuations in Arizona and Colorado amid heavy rains in southwest
summary: The San Juan River is forecast to crest at more than 19 feet around 11:00 p.m.
story: The San Juan River is forecast to crest at more than 19 feet around 11:00 p.m.

More heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a wide swath of the Southwest on Sunday, including a Colorado mountain town bracing for a river to reach historic levels, as weary residents in the normally arid region deal with another round of overflowing rivers and creeks.

In southwestern Colorado, officials in Pagosa Springs, a town in the Rockies located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs, warned in a Facebook post of potentially “catastrophic flooding” as the San Juan River was forecast to crest at more than 19 feet (5.8 meters) around 11:00 p.m. Sunday.

“To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters),” the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office said in a separate Facebook post. “This is a potentially catastrophic flood event. Extensive damage is expected.”

Officials in the tourist destination of Sedona, Arizona, ordered residents in areas near Oak Creek to leave immediately as flood waters were rising rapidly and multiple people were trapped in their homes. Officials in nearby Camp Verde also issued an evacuation order for residents living near the Verde River, West Clear Creek, and Wet Beaver Creek.

“We are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days,” Aaron Hardin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Tucson, said of conditions that have resulted in flash floods, possible river flooding and swift boat rescues in Tucson, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of Sedona.

The latest round of soaking rains started Saturday evening and was expected to bring flash flooding to already saturated areas through Monday. The weather service estimates as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.

The weather service issued flood watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet.
Pagosa Springs officials said anyone in low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra Rivers should head to a designated shelter at a local church.

They said residents should leave immediately, and not wait as emergency crews may be extremely limited during the worst of the storm. The highway entering the hot springs town also would be shut down to inbound traffic Sunday afternoon, town officials added.

In Sedona, officials ordered residents living in affected areas to head to Sedona Red Rock High School. But they urged people not to attempt to drive across roads with rushing waters and to stay away from creek beds and washes.

Sedona Fire District Chief Ed Mezulis said in a short clip posted on Facebook that emergency crews from surrounding communities were coming in to assist as local fire and police officials were already responding to multiple reports of residents trapped in their homes due to the rising flood waters.
“Please stay at high ground, watch your alerts and be careful,” he advised.

A video shared by the fire department showed powerful flood waters inundating vehicles and rushing past homes and other structures. Other videos and photos shared on social media showed people standing on a pedestrian bridge taking photos and videos as churning, brown waters rushed underneath.

title: Andreas Almgren of Sweden finishes first in his marathon debut, taking the New York City Marathon
summary: Andreas Almgren of Sweden finishes first in his marathon debut, taking the New York City Marathon
story: Andreas Almgren of Sweden finishes first in his marathon debut, taking the New York City Marathon
NEW YORK -- Andreas Almgren of Sweden finishes first in his marathon debut, taking the New York City Marathon.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won the women's race of the New York City Marathon on Sunday for the second time.
Chepkirui, who also won the race in 2024, pulled away from countrymate Hellen Obiri in the final 150 meters to seal the victory in 2 hours, 24 minutes and 36 seconds.

American Jessica McClain finished second, passing Obiri — a two-time winner — in the final few strides. It was the first time a U.S. woman finished in the top three since 2018. McClain was 6 seconds behind Chepkirui.

It was the 50th time that the race has run through all five boroughs of the city. There were just over 2,000 competitors in the seventh running of the race, including only 88 women. About 60,000 runners stepped up to the starting line Sunday, with nearly half of them women.
See AP’s full sports coverage here

title: US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
summary: The Trump administration plans to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to Afghanistan via Pakistan
story: The Trump administration plans to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to Afghanistan via Pakistan

President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.

Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

“This is absolutely unconscionable," said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.”

The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.
U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.

In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.
In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.

In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.

Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.

“It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP.

“This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said.
Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this," Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

In September, Trump's administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.

The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution — and had gone through yearslong vetting processes to start new lives in America — stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

title: Heavy rains expected to bring flooding risk to already saturated parts of the US Southwest
summary: The National Weather Service says heavy rains are expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest
story: The National Weather Service says heavy rains are expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest
Heavy rains starting Saturday evening were expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest through Monday, according to the National Weather Service.
