story: Asian trading is mixed as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grow after Alphabet’s stock drop dragged on U.S. markets
TOKYO -- Asian shares were trading mixed Friday, as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grew after Alphabet's stock drop dragged on U.S. markets.

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.3% in afternoon trading to 63,155.94. At the end of its two-day monetary policy board meeting, the Bank of Japan decided to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1.25%. That was widely expected because the central bank raised the rate  last month.

The U.S. has been pressuring Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar inched up to 157.67 Japanese yen from 157.65 yen. The euro cost $1.1186, up from $1.1181.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.2% to 8,908.10. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 4% to 5,701.71, as shares in SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both slipped.

Shares related to the great market interest in AI have tended to be volatile, because some issues, including chip makers, get pushed up because of that interest, but then may decline because of worries about supplies, for instance.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 1.7% to 23,359.06, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.4% to 3,636.60.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 0.3% for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3%.

Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6% for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72.

In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94% from 5.05% late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30% earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 1.15% to $103.17 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 1.05% to $116.09 a barrel.
AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

title: Roof of a water tower in Manhattan where a rare family of barn owls nested removed
summary: The roof of a water tower atop a building in Manhattan’s Upper West Side that was home to a family of celebrity barn owls has been removed
story: The roof of a water tower atop a building in Manhattan’s Upper West Side that was home to a family of celebrity barn owls has been removed

The roof of a water tower where a family of celebrity barn owls had been nesting in Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been removed, sparking outrage among New Yorkers who have been captivated by the elusive birds.

The barn owl family was discovered weeks ago, drawing crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the birds, including nature photographers. It is believed to be the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history.

Jessica Wilson, the executive director of NYC Bird Alliance, said that she saw one barn owl fledgling Thursday on the roof of a nearby building after the roof of the water tower, which is located atop a building, was removed. Barn owl fledglings “should not be out in the middle of the day” because barn owls are nocturnal, she said.
“It had been disturbed from the nest,” Wilson added. “We didn’t see any more fledglings.”

NYC Bird Alliance received reports Thursday morning from residents and birders of work happening at the top of the tower, Wilson said. When Wilson got to the building, no workers were present. Enforcement police with the state's environmental conservation agency also arrived, Wilson said, and they were able to access the building's roof with the permission of the building's superintendent. On the roof, Wilson saw that the top of the water tower where the barn owls had been nesting was gone.

The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation said in a statement that its police officers “investigated the area and found that the roof of the water tower on the building was removed, exposing the barn owl nest.”
The officers told the building owner to “halt demolition of the water tower until further notice” while the department investigates any potential violations, the department added.
Reached by phone, the building's superintendent declined to comment. It's not immediately clear who owns the building or ordered the removal of the water tower's roof.
Thomas Obersteiner, an Upper West Side resident, said he saw a man with an extension cord climbing down from the water tower around noon on Thursday.
The news of the water tower roof removal prompted criticism.

“I am outraged by reports that construction work on an Upper West Side water tower destroyed part of the structure that was home to Manhattan’s first Barn Owl nest, potentially endangering a pair of owls and their several fledglings," state Sen. Erik Bottcher said in a social media post, adding that active "migratory bird nests” are protected by state and federal law.
“Our city’s wildlife deserves protection, and there must be accountability when these protections are violated," Bottcher said.

“That nest was well-known, incredibly well-known, written about widely,” said David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account Manhattan Bird Alert. "It should never have happened.”
Barrett said he observed the water tower Thursday and saw that the roof had been removed.

Birds have captivated New Yorkers in the past. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

Barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl’s range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

Barn owl fledglings depend on their parents to hunt for them because they don't know how to hunt yet, Wilson said. The fledglings' parents bring them food at their nest. Without the nest, Wilson added, "we’re worried that these barn owl fledglings might not survive.”

title: 2 helicopters collide southwest of Portland, Oregon, shutting down highway
summary: Authorities say two helicopters collided near a small airport southwest of Portland, Oregon
story: Authorities say two helicopters collided near a small airport southwest of Portland, Oregon
McMINNVILLE Ore. -- Two helicopters collided Thursday near a small airport southwest of Portland, Oregon, forcing the closure of a key highway, authorities said.
Emergency crews responded around 2:15 p.m. following reports of a crash a few miles east of the McMinnville Airport, according to the Yamhill County Sheriff’s Office.
Officials had no details about how many people were aboard the helicopters or their conditions.
The Oregon Department of Transportation said Highway 233 is closed 1 mile (1.6 kilometers) west of Dayton because of the crash. There was no estimate for reopening.
Local roads were also closed. The sheriff's office urged the public to stay clear of the area.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was aware of the incident but was still gathering information.
McMinnville, about 35 miles (56 kilometers) southwest of Portland, is home to about 34,000 people.
The small airport situated on 650 acres (263 hectares) has two paved runways, according to its website. It’s partially bordered by homes and near the North American Aerospace Museum.

title: Polymarket paused international trading after security issue
summary: Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform Thursday due to a security incident involving a third-party provider
story: Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform Thursday due to a security incident involving a third-party provider
Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said.
Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders.
The prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform.
“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed.
Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.
Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance monitoring tools.

DebugBear's own website was unavailable Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident.” It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were impacted, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was impacted “will be made whole.”

title: Sandy Hook families urge Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on AR-15-style rifles
summary: Relatives whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are urging the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold bans on certain semiautomatic rifles
story: Relatives whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are urging the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold bans on certain semiautomatic rifles

Relatives whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are making an impassioned plea to the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on certain semiautomatic rifles, citing the high body counts and devastating injuries the weapons can inflict.

The parents of five of the 20 first-graders killed in the 2012 Connecticut shooting and relatives of one of six educators who died filed a “friend of the court” brief on Wednesday, weighing in on two cases challenging bans in Connecticut and the Chicago area. Justices are scheduled to hear oral arguments in both cases on Dec. 2.

“The assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School, carried out by an untrained, 112-pound youth armed with an AR-15-style rifle, is graphic proof of the unusual and extreme lethality of that firearm and the harm it is capable of inflicting on American communities,” the relatives' filing says. They added that they “seek to protect other American families from becoming casualties in another AR-15 killing spree.”

Gun rights advocates and groups whose lawsuits led to the two Supreme Court cases are arguing that it's unconstitutional under the Second Amendment to ban semiautomatic rifles, which are legally owned by millions of Americans. Supporters of the bans say such rifles were designed for military use, are too dangerous for civilians and should be regulated like machine guns.

More than 40 other people and groups — most in favor of the rifle bans — also filed “amicus curiae” briefs on Wednesday. Such filings are submitted by parties who are not directly involved in the litigation.

The 20-year-old Sandy Hook gunman, Adam Lanza, shot his way into the locked school in Newtown, Connecticut, and unleashed a fury of more than 150 bullets in about four minutes with a Bushmaster AR-15-style rifle fueled by high-capacity ammunition magazines. The massacre led Connecticut to ban such rifles in 2013 — the same law now before the Supreme Court.

Jennifer Hensel, whose 6-year-old daughter Avielle Richman was killed in the shooting, was quoted in the relatives' brief saying Avielle was shot multiple times in the face and authorities told her that she would not recognize her daughter if she saw her body.

“A moral imperative is truly at hand,” Hensel said in supporting weapons bans. “Please, do not allow more blood to soak our Connecticut soil from assault-style weapons. A fundamental duty to protect all in Connecticut is at stake.”

A similar brief filed Wednesday by Sandy Hook Promise, the gun violence prevention group started by Newtown families, said another victim, 6-year-old Dylan Hockley, was shot five times — “his body destroyed so completely, his mother was told not to touch him to say goodbye as he lay in his coffin.”
“The effects of these weapons on children’s bodies are catastrophic and obscene,” the filing said.
Dylan's mother, Nicole Hockley, a co-founder of Sandy Hook Promise, urged the Supreme Court to consider children's safety.

“I know firsthand the devastation a semiautomatic rifle can inflict in minutes on the bodies, hearts, and minds of children — and the families who love them,” she said in a statement. “No family should have to live with that pain. As the Court considers this case, the consequences being experienced by children and communities cannot be an afterthought.”

Gun rights supporters say that while they sympathize with gun violence victims' families and condemn mass shootings, the solution isn't to curtail Second Amendment rights. They say school shootings happen despite bans on so-called “assault weapons.”

“Solving or at least mitigating school shootings is not about banning a type of gun,” said Konstadinos Moros, director of legal research and education for the Second Amendment Foundation, a plaintiff in the challenges to both the Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, bans.

“While some guns are obviously more capable than others, school shooters inflict harm not because of the capability of their firearms, but because of the helplessness of their targets,” he said in an email to The Associated Press. “The real solution lies in proper school security, which can both more quickly respond to shootings, and deter attacks from happening in the first place, given that the depraved individuals who commit these sorts of crimes tend to pick ‘soft targets.’”

The current Supreme Court, which has expanded gun rights, announced in June that it would hear appeals challenging bans on the AR-15 and similar semiautomatic firearms in Connecticut and the Chicago area. The ban in Cook County was first passed in 1993. Lower courts have upheld both laws.

Similar laws are in place in about a dozen states, covering major cities like New York, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Congress allowed a national assault weapons ban to expire in 2004, but Democrats have supported renewing it in response to mass shootings. States have also continued to pass their own laws, including recent measures in Virginia and Rhode Island.

It is the latest high-profile dispute over guns to reach the court since its conservative majority handed down a landmark ruling in 2022 that expanded Second Amendment rights and spawned challenges to firearm laws around the country. The court said that any gun laws must have a strong grounding in the nation’s historical traditions.

title: Virginia GOP says shooting outside its offices in Richmond appears unrelated to its operations
summary: A woman has been shot just outside the Republican Party of Virginia's offices in Richmond
story: A woman has been shot just outside the Republican Party of Virginia's offices in Richmond
RICHMOND, Va. -- The Republican Party of Virginia said a shooting Thursday just outside its offices in Richmond doesn't appear to have anything to do with its operations.
The party said in a statement posted online that a woman was shot around 1:45 p.m. directly in front of the building that houses its offices.
Frank Loehr, chief financial officer for the Republican Party of Virginia, told reporters that he and other staffers were working inside the office when shots rang out outside.
A woman who had been speaking with two people who had a booth outside the building was brought inside the office bleeding after being shot, he said. The booth was not affiliated with the party.
The woman was conscious and moaning in pain, Loehr said. First responders arrived quickly and took her away, he said.
The status of the woman is unclear. Police have not responded to phone messages, texts or emails.

title: Filmmaker Michael Mann suffers "superficial injury" at gun range
summary: Filmmaker Michael Mann was injured at a gun range in Los Angeles, his representative said.
story: Michael Mann, a filmmaker known for the classic crime drama "Heat," was injured at a gun range in Los Angeles on Saturday, his representative told CBS News.
The representative said on Sunday that Mann had received treatment at a hospital for "a superficial injury" and was being released.
"On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann," the representative said in a statement.
Mann, 83, has apparently been an experienced target shooter for decades, and the accident happened at a sanctioned gun range.

In addition to "Heat," Mann's filmmaking record includes crime classics like "Collateral" and "Thief." He continues to be quite active in Hollywood in his 80s and most recently directed the film "Ferrari," with Adam Driver, and is developing a sequel to "Heat," which is supposed to begin filming early next year.

title: A new Georgia O'Keeffe exhibit opens a window to unfamiliar works
summary: An exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts, "Georgia O'Keeffe: Architecture," is painting a different portrait of the artist, best known for her depictions of flowers and desert landscapes.
story: When you hear the name Georgia O'Keeffe, architecture may not immediately come to mind. "So many people know Georgia O'Keeffe as a painter of flowers, or maybe they know her landscapes, or her paintings of bones; so, something like a barn, I know, is a surprise for many people," said curator Ben Colman. "Curiously, flower pictures represent only about 10% of her artwork."

A new exhibit at the Detroit Institute of Arts, titled "Georgia O'Keeffe: Architecture," is painting a different portrait of the artist, showcasing her architectural works through an autobiographical lens.
"We are looking at the places where she lived and worked, the places that were really formative to her as an individual and as a painter," said Colman.

O'Keeffe was born in 1887 on a Wisconsin dairy farm, a source of inspiration in her works. "When she painted ["My Shanty, Lake George"], she wanted to challenge what she considered misunderstandings of her art," said Colman. "She was very conscious, and maybe self-conscious, about selecting subjects that would not be perceived as typically feminine in their composition."
She would later live in Manhattan, just as skyscrapers began to redefine the city in the 1920s.
"She pays special attention to what she called the sky shapes, the negative space of sky, moon, and clouds that she saw around the buildings," Colman said.
O'Keeffe eventually moved to New Mexico, where she found herself surrounded by adobe structures and desert landscapes.

Over the course of her career, O'Keeffe would go on to complete about 140 architectural paintings. Colman said, "These are pictures where she's asking questions about the nature of the places where she lived, about the qualities of light, atmosphere, and texture of the buildings that she painted."
Georgia O'Keeffe died in 1986 at 98 years old, her legacy grounded in a vast body of work, cementing her presence in American art.
Story produced by Liza Monasebian. Editor: Chad Cardin.

To honor the artist, the Santa Fe Chamber Music Festival had commissioned and dedicated to O'Keeffe a piano quintet by composer John Harbison - music that, like O'Keeffe's paintings, translates stark and unfilled spaces. title: How movie star James Stewart became a war hero
summary: In 1941 the Oscar-winning actor answered his nation's call, serving as a pilot in the Army Air Corps, and came home from WWII a changed man. The film "Jimmy" depicts his decision to enlist, and his emotional post-war return to the screen in "It's a Wonderful Life."
story: It's trite but true; Jimmy Stewart played the Everyman better than everyone. He had the gawky innocence to be an idealistic senator, in "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington"; an eccentric with a six-foot-tall rabbit pal in "Harvey"; and a depth, in "Rear Window" and "Vertigo," that even Alfred Hitchcock found mysterious.

But it was director Frank Capra who gave us the Jimmy Stewart that everyone still depends on every Christmas. "It's a Wonderful Life" is remarkable for a lot of reasons, not the least of which is that Stewart's memorable performance was his first after an almost-five-year absence from Hollywood. Audiences hadn't seen him on screen since 1941, the same year he took home the Academy Award for "The Philadelphia Story." He was a Hollywood A-lister. But not long after, he found himself on another list: the list for the draft.

Stewart could have served safely stateside doing recruiting films and such. But he wanted, or at least felt, he needed to do more. Already an accomplished pilot, Stewart enlisted in the Army Air Corps.
"He knew that America needed good pilots; he was one," said Janie McKirgan, curator at the Jimmy Stewart Museum in his hometown of Indiana, Pennsylvania.

McKirgan said few wanted to let Hollywood's golden boy actually fly: "It took a long time for him to find somebody in the Army Air Corps that was willing to take that risk," she said. "Because if Jimmy Stewart, Academy Award-winning Jimmy Stewart, got shot down, it would be a huge blow to troop morale, to America, to everything."

His fight to be able to fight despite his celebrity is the subject of a new film out this week, called "Jimmy." It stars Max Casella as director Frank Capra, and K.J. Apa as Jimmy Stewart. "We really set out to make the movie that Frank and Jimmy never got to make," Apa said.
Casella said he was only vaguely aware of Stewart's wartime service; Apa did not know about it: "I can't believe it was true," he said. "It was the courage that made me dumbfounded of his story."
Casella said, "He gave up Hollywood at the very top of the mountain."
To watch a trailer for "Jimmy" click on the video player below:

There'a a lot of what you'd want in the film: Old Hollywood, action-packed air battles. But really at its heart, this is a movie about what Stewart's service did to his soul. Stewart flew 20 combat missions over Germany. He lost men, and saw things he wished he didn't. But like most of that generation, he kept those horrors to himself.
"Dad never talked about his military service to us," said Kelly Stewart Harcourt, one of his twin daughters. "Never talked about his war service at all."

Harcourt, an executive producer on the film, says her dad came home from war a different man: "He said, 'I'm an out-of-work actor and an out-of-work pilot, and I don't know what I'm gonna do. Do I even want to make films again?'"
Her dad kept a diary, something she and her sister found in his nightstand after he passed away in 1997. She read from it, having never shared it publicly:
"This was a terrible day. We lost 13 crews out of the group on the mission today. Only half of them came back."
The next day, though, in the see-saw of war, everyone came home safely. That was a cause for celebration.  And yet, Stewart wrote this:
"It's strange that this could practically cancel out the loss of all those boys, but I guess that's the way things have to be in this god-damn, stupid, lousy, dirty war."
Harcourt says her dad suffered from nightmares, depression, anxiety – symptoms that would be diagnosed as PTSD today.  And that, in a way, is what gets us back to "It's a Wonderful Life."
"Dear Father in heaven, I'm not a praying man but, if You're up there and You can hear me, show me the way..."

For years there had been quiet speculation that whatever demons Stewart may have brought home were exorcised in the role of George Bailey, a desperate man also pushed to the edge. Harcourt believes he brought those feelings to the role of Bailey. "You can't pull off that performance without feeling like that," she said.
We'll never know, of course.  Whatever his muse, its effect was unforgettable.

Stewart went on to do more than 50 films after "It's a Wonderful Life." But he was most proud of his service to his country. In 1983, Stewart was honored at the Kennedy Center, where cadets from the U.S. Air Force Academy brought him near tears.
Jimmy Stewart did indeed have a wonderful life, but his sacrifice, and those of others, gave us a pretty wonderful life, too.

title: Heidi Klum reveals a giant severed hand as 2026 Halloween costume
summary: The TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at a party encased in a slithering worm costume.
story: Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday, 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event.

Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.
The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand - specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.
"I looked at my hand and I thought, 'Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,'" Klum said.
The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume.

In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, an 8-foot-tall (2.4-meter-tall) "Transformer," a werewolf from Michael Jackson's "Thriller" music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum-lookalikes, and Kali, the multiarmed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.

Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face.
"Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it," Klum said. "It's quite heavy."

Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins.
"A little bit of Tom is with me," she said.

title: Book excerpt: "Frank Capra: A Life" by Sam Wasson
summary: Returning to movie screens after his service in World War II, Jimmy Stewart was nervous about appearing in Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life" – a film now acknowledged as one of his very best.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Returning to movie screens after his service in World War II, actor Jimmy Stewart was nervous about appearing in Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life" – a film now acknowledged as one of his very best.

In his biography of the director, "Frank Capra: A Life" (published by Harper), Hollywood historian Sam Wasson writes of how Capra helped shepherd Stewart back into the public limelight in a role that was perfectly suited to Stewart's talents – and in the process created a timeless classic.
Read the excerpt below – and don't miss Lee Cowan's report on Jimmy Stewart's post-WWII experience on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 1!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.

Unlike Capra, Stewart refused to promote his return to Hollywood. His contract with Liberty stipulated that he was not to be made to discuss his heroism. "In all advertising and publicity issues by the corporation, or under its control," the relevant clause read, "the corporation will not mention or cause to be mentioned the part taken by the artist in World War II as an officer in the U.S. Army."

By then, Stewart had read the script Capra had given him. George Bailey, the hero of the picture they would call It's a Wonderful Life, was the truest to his own life. Still, he was terrified. It was to be his first film in almost five years. Had he lost the audience? Had they forgotten about him? Leaving a department store in Beverly Hills, he was mistaken by a gaggle of bobby-soxers for MGM's new heartthrob Van Johnson. But more than tastes in movie stars had changed since Stewart went to war. At a Lux Radio Theatre performance of Destry Rides Again, the script he was holding shook so hard, they could see it from the control room.
"No sense running away," Stewart told his friends one night at Chasen's. "The truth is I'm scared as hell."

Scared, and also emotionally fried. "I don't think I'll ever get into an airplane again," he confessed. "I rolled two thousand hours overseas, and that'll just about do me." There was, one journalist observed in 1946, "a trace of weariness" about him now. To another, Stewart said, "It got pretty rough overseas at times."

What Capra would not have told Stewart was that he, the director, was the more frightened of the two. Without [Robert] Riskin, it had been the most chaotic script gestation of his career—a career that had never been more vulnerable. The script he had given Stewart was still changing, and where once he could have turned to [Jo] Swerling or Myles Connolly or Sidney Buchman to pitch in for a polish or, at least, talk story, friend to friend, none of them was available to him. Capra's loneliness was, for him, unprecedented, impossible to describe.

The night before his first day of filming, April 15, 1946, Stewart's worry intensified. He studied the scene, as if being word-perfect—never a requirement on a Capra set (in fact, a disadvantage)—would save him from disaster.

The first day of It's a Wonderful Life was also William Wyler's first day on The Best Years of Our Lives, which would be his last picture with Goldwyn before he joined Liberty. "Last one in is a rotten egg," Wyler had cabled Capra. With its hundreds of partying extras, that scene that first day—the first of several on location at Beverly Hills High School, where George and Mary fall into the swimming pool beneath the gymnasium floor while dancing—would open Capra's production on a happy note. Using his independence to the hilt, Capra would go to the trouble and expense of shooting It's a Wonderful Life, to the best of his ability, in sequence, as was his preference, but in his capacity as social director of a new filmmaking community, he understood that the best way to break the ice was with a bang—three days at a high school dance in Bedford Falls.
Cannily, he also knew it was the setting for the first adult meeting of George and Mary.

Rather than Jean Arthur, who would have added an unnecessary tinge of knowing sophistication to Mary Hatch, Capra cast the fresh-faced midwestern beauty Donna Reed, whom he had first seen opposite John Wayne in John Ford's 1945 They Were Expendable. It was a lucky break for the director who rarely needed luck when casting. One look at Reed grinning with unguarded devotion at the man she loves, and any audience would see just why Bailey, blind for so long, might see her face in the right light, at the right moment, and open his eyes to life.

It was true also of Jimmy Stewart that the first time he saw Donna Reed that day in the gym of Beverly Hills High, "I fell in love with her right off the bat. She just seemed to be everything. ... Everything just seemed to come out of her."
"Jimmy," Capra said, doing a bit of acting himself, "I meant to call you last night to tell you our first scene starts on page 31, not 33. Ready?"

Capra, directing without directing, had surely never intended to call Stewart the night before. But it got the actor just where Capra wanted him: off his guard, a little nervous, that is, to approach Donna Reed as Mary Hatch, for Stewart was meeting both for the first time, nervous enough to fumble his answer to her question—not in the script or finished film, but tossed in just moments before they shot, by Capra—"Are you going to walk me home tonight?"
Stewart didn't have to act the scene. He just did it, perfectly, gulping, "N– n– no."
"That's it," Capra said. "Cut!" He grinned at Stewart. One take was all they needed.

title: Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
summary: Patrick Stewart starred on stage and screen across his decadeslong acting career. He died at his home on Wednesday.
story: Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.
Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.
Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.

Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.
In a 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart said "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry initially turned him away.
"He was talked into employing me by the other producers," Stewart said.

Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."

"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.

Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.
Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."
In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.
In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.

Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."

Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.
In that 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart reflected on what he believed made a successful relationship.

"I think it's being open and a good listener and to make connection," he said. "You don't have to be exactly the same but it's necessary that you can share – I think very important. So sharing and respecting."

Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."

title: Hayden Panettiere's death ruled accidental by South Carolina police
summary: A South Carolina coroner previously confirmed Panettiere died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl.
story: The death of Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, South Caroline police announced Wednesday.

Greenville Police Department said the investigation into Panettiere's death has been concluded "based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation," and the actor's death was officially ruled accidental.
Last month, a South Carolina coroner confirmed Panettiere died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl. There were no signs of trauma, the coroner's office said.

Emergency responders were called to a residence where Panettiere, 36, had been staying in Greenville, South Carolina, on the afternoon of Aug. 16. Despite "advanced cardiac life support measures," she was pronounced dead there, the Greenville County Coroner's Office said.'

Panettiere's on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the scene of her death, according to a police report obtained by CBS News. The Hickersons made the 911 call that brought first responders to the apartment.

Authorities, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, were investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death. Police previously said that a preliminary investigation "has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances."

title: Jay-Z to headline 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
summary: The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
story: The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
The announcement included a short video of Jay-Z sitting in SoFi Stadium surrounded by goats with the caption "GOAT's out of the bag."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his "Jay-Z 30" concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Since then, the headlining halftime show performers have included Shakira and Jennifer Lopez, Rihanna, Kendrick Lamar and The Weeknd, among others.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums "Reasonable Doubt," "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
His 1996 debut, "Reasonable Doubt," was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.

Jay-Z's career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.
Bad Bunny performed at last season's Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.

The next morning, the Puerto Rican superstar held the top six spots on Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart, with another song coming in at No. 8. Eleven other Bad Bunny songs were ranking in Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart at the time.

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: RFK Jr. to ease access to unapproved peptides, draft policy states
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps Wednesday that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.
story: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps this week that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.

In a draft policy filed Wednesday, Kennedy said he had determined that compounding pharmacies could prepare six specific peptides — BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, TB-500 — even though they do not have approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
"By allowing limited compounding of the substances addressed in this guidance under appropriate safeguards, the policy provides patients with a more controlled alternative," Kennedy wrote.
Compounding pharmacies mix ingredients to prepare customized medications for individual patients.
Although they are not FDA approved, the six peptides in Kennedy's new policy are often still marketed with health claims.

The Department of Health and Human Services "did not intend to take action" against licensed pharmacies or physicians that compound "a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product," Kennedy's policy said.

Peptides are small proteins that can have powerful effects. There are several, such as insulin, that are FDA approved as being safe and effective. GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and to treat diabetes also contain FDA approved peptides.

In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend allowing the six unapproved peptides to be used in compounding, although that decision did not constitute FDA approval. That vote, however, went against the recommendations of the FDA's own scientists, who said there isn't enough evidence of safety and effectiveness for each of the six peptides to make such a determination.
Kennedy cited that panel's recommendation in his decision, saying he had determined the policy "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety."

In a statement provided to CBS News, an HHS spokesperson said that pharmacies will have to do quality testing and safety reporting, and that should help patients know what is in these peptide drugs that are currently being sold by unregulated sources.

"The policy does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness," the HHS spokesperson said. "It requires patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing, and safety reporting to hold compounders accountable and give patients an alternative to unregulated sellers."
The draft policy requires an FDA-registered ingredient maker, a lab certificate for the raw ingredients, and reports of serious side effects.

In a CBS News investigation published last week, a laboratory test was conducted on an experimental peptide weight-loss drug known as retatrutide that was purchased from a bodega in Brooklyn, New York.
The lab test, however, found that the sample of retatrutide purchased from the bodega did not contain a peptide at all.

A CBS News investigation last summer found that dozens of clinics across the country, staffed by licensed physicians and nurse practitioners, have been openly advertising retatrutide even though it has not been reviewed by the FDA and remains in clinical trials by drug giant Eli Lilly.

Kennedy's draft policy will be open to public comment beginning Friday through Nov. 13. The policy will remain in place until the FDA finalizes a rule regarding compounded peptides. However, at this point, the FDA has not proposed one.

title: Nearly 75% of ex-NFL players who died from 2008-2023 had CTE, study finds
summary: Nearly 75% of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE, a new study out of Boston University finds.
story: Nearly 75% of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a new study led by Boston University researchers finds.

CTE is a degenerative brain disease that is found in people who have suffered repeated blows to the head. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death. CTE has been discovered in football players as well as other athletes, first responders and military members.
The study published in JAMA Network Open shows how CTE, rarely seen in the general population, is far more common among deceased NFL players, lead author Julia Gallini said in a statement.

"With CTE consistently found in less than 1% of donors to community brain banks, an estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms," Gallini said.
CTE study findings
B.U. said the new findings build on a study released in August, which estimated that anywhere from 25% and 98% of ex-NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE.

"The wide range reflected uncertainty about how representative brain donors were of the overall NFL population," B.U. said in a statement. "Brain donors are more likely to have symptoms believed to be related to CTE, a concept known as selection bias."

In the new study, 362 of 387 deceased ex-players were found to have some form of CTE. But to counter the selection bias, researchers factored in that former NFL players with cognitive symptoms were five times more likely to have their brains donated to science.
"They used this estimated selection ratio to adjust the 94% prevalence of CTE observed among brain donors to an overall estimate of 74.5%," B.U. said.
The authors noted that the study only involved NFL players who have died and does not predict how many living former or active players might have CTE.

"It's hard to learn what the guys who built the game have suffered through," former NFL quarterback Matt Hasselbeck, an ambassador for the study, said in a statement. "We have to learn from this data to make the game safer, because we can't accept these numbers for the next generation of players."
NFL and NFLPA respond to CTE study

The NFL said in a statement that it "continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts." It pointed toward the introduction of better equipment like Guardian Caps and rule changes designed to keep players safe.

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust - and expanding - set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," the NFL said. "We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."
The NFL Players Association said the study is one of many that are "critical" to understanding the long-term health impacts of football.

"The NFLPA remains committed to supporting scientific research, investing in resources that aid players' physical and mental well-being, and expanding access to care so that they can experience improved health outcomes during and after their playing careers," the union said.
Asked about the findings on Wednesday, New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel says he and other football players "knew what the risks were."

"Your kids are going to have to see you maybe be knocked out on the field and laying there unconscious, or getting another surgery, or breaking your arm or breaking your leg," the former linebacker said.
The former linebacker said he thinks the NFL should be doing everything it can to protect players' quality of life.
"I do think that the league in being conscious and trying to make the game safer and better is good," he said. "But I also knew what I was signing up for when I decided to play the game."

title: Binance resumes withdrawals for some cryptocurrencies after heist
summary: The exchange said it would resume withdrawals in phases, pending security checks.
story: Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereal after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X.

As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereal, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."

The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

title: $6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
summary: A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was likely carried out by North Korea, according to a blockchain intelligence firm.
story: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?

In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
The FBI on Saturday also accused TraderTraitor of being behind the attack, saying the hackers have been converting the stolen funds into Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency.
The hackers are preparing the funds for "further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.

Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"

Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
summary: Security experts are calling it the "largest bank robbery in human history." Getting all of the stolen crypto funds won't be easy.
story: After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.

"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.

Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."

TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.

"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.

The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.

Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.

"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.

"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."

Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.

"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.

Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.

"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

title: Nasdaq sheds more than 700 points as tech stocks slump
summary: Disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears on Friday that the AI trade could unravel.
story: The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 700 points on Friday, a rocky close to October trading amid growing investor concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.

The rout followed a series of earnings reports from major tech companies that fell short of Wall Street's expectations. Intel's stock tumbled nearly 29% on the day, the chipmaker's biggest single-day drop since 1974. Shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, also continued to struggle following a 12% slide on Thursday that erased roughly $500 billion in market value.
Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, fell 4.2%.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.
The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 sank 140 points, or 1.8%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572 points, or 1.1%.
Debt reckoning?

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."
Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.

The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.

Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.
A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: Millions of French press coffee makers recalled due to burn risk
summary: Product safety regulators said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, leading to burn injuries.
story: Coffee appliance company Bodum USA is recalling 5.9 million French press makers, warning that the glass carafe can break and cause burn injuries.

Bodum USA is the American subsidiary of a Danish-Swiss company that specializes in coffee hardware. So far, the company has received 70 reports of glass carafes breaking, 48 of which resulted in burns, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The French press coffee makers were sold on Amazon.com, in retailers including Target and Walmart, and other stores between 1974 and October 2026.
The agency said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, which can happen when customers use metal spoons to stir coffee.

"While the rate of reported incidents involving carafe breakage during use is extremely low, especially considering that Bodum has sold millions of these products in the U.S. for decades, this recall will further encourage the safe use of our French Press Coffee Makers," Bodum USA said in a statement.
A Bodum USA customer service representative told CBS News that the company was not offering refunds to customers.

The recall involves a variety of Bodum USA models, including 8-cup French presses and 12-cup Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper and Kenya models, according to CPSA. The recall number is 27-055.

Safety regulators said customers who purchased one of the recalled French press makers should not use metal utensils to stir the coffee and should avoid using the carafes if they are cracked or damaged. Customers can contact Bodum to receive a plastic stirring spoon.

For more information, consumers can contact the company toll-free at 888-879-8213 Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET; email at Bodum3302@sedgwick.com; or online at www.bodumfrenchpressrecall.expertinquiry.com or www.bodum.com (click on "Recall Information").
