title: Transcript: Sen. Bernie Sanders on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Bernie Sanders, Independent of Vermont, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Bernie Sanders, Independent of Vermont, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We are just hours away from voters in 50 states going to the polls for an election that could shift the balance of power here in Washington. We begin with someone who has been on the campaign trail quite a bit, although he is not up for reelection. That's Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders, who joins us from Burlington. Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR BERNIE SANDERS (I-VT): Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I've been told you've hosted telerallies, town halls for Maine and Michigan this weekend. Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed. You're focused as well on Florida and Minnesota. Why Florida, since it is likely GOP according to CBS numbers, and CBS also rates Minnesota as likely Dem. Why focus there?

SEN. SANDERS: Well, I don't take anything for granted. I think Angie Nixon in Florida is running a great grassroots campaign. She pulled off a huge upset in the Democratic primary. I think she has a real chance to win the general election. She is mobilizing working-class people all over this country, and she's talking about the right issues. And those issues are true in Minnesota. They're true in Florida. They're true in Vermont. People are disgusted and frustrated with an economy in which the billionaires have never ever had it so good. Elon Musk now owns more wealth alone than the bottom 53% of American households, while millions of people today are struggling to put food on the table, pay for, you know, pay to fill up their gas tanks, pay for rent. So what Angie is talking about, what Troy is talking about is an economy that works for all. That's resonating.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, out in Michigan, there appears some inner Democratic Party squabbles that are ongoing here around the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. There was a back and forth over the weekend with Congresswoman Haley Stevens. She lost the primary, but she continues to make public her deep misgivings about backing him now, citing concerns about his ads and his views on Israel. At this point, is the Democratic Party just too divided to pull off a win in Michigan? Is it getting in its own way?

SEN. SANDERS: No, I think- No, I think the over, you know, Haley Stevens lost a very, very close primary. I can understand being upset about that, but I think two days before the election, where people all over Michigan understand that this is the most important midterm election, perhaps in the history of the United States, because we are taking on the most dangerous president that we've ever had, somebody who's an authoritarian, does not believe in the Constitution or the rule of law, who wants to give massive tax breaks to billionaires, throw 15 million people off their health care, that they had started an illegal, unconstitutional war in Iran. So, what the people in Michigan understand, sure, we have disagreements with Abdul on this or that issue, but from what I can see, all over the state people are standing up. They're going to stand with Abdul, take on somebody who will be nothing more than a rubber stamp for the Trump administration. That's Mike Rogers.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, just want to clarify there Haley Stevens has been criticizing ads associated and endorsing Abdul Sayed [sic] that he has said are- are not his ads, but she's still criticizing him for them.
SEN. SANDERS: Right. But, I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah go ahead.
SEN. SANDERS: Right, and he had nothing to do with those ads.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SEN. SANDERS: But Margaret, I was in Michigan last week--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. SANDERS: --and I got to tell you, if you want to look at ads in Michigan, I have never in my life seen such disgusting, racist, fearmongering ads as those that are taking place in Michigan right now. They are calling Abdul El-Sayed, who is a medical doctor, they're calling him a terrorist, a jihadist, really disgusting things. And the- the fact that any Republican would stand behind those horrible ads is a disgrace.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, the rhetoric is extraordinary. El-Sayed would be America's first sitting Muslim senator if he pulls off a win here. He has been accused, though, of ties to a Sunni Islamist group known as the mother- Muslim Brotherhood. He has distanced himself. He has disavowed it. But I want to play for our viewers something. Senator Cruz of Texas warned against El-Sayed being given any access to classified intelligence if he wins. Listen.
[BEGIN SOUND ON TAPE]
TED CRUZ: And if I am correct that he is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Michigan does not need a senator who's on the side of the terrorists.

BERNIE MORENO: This character Abdul  El-Sayed can be nowhere near Washington D.C. Do you think he understands that concept that our rights come from God Almighty? That Jesus came here for our salvation.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, do you think that El-Sayed could actually govern if his colleagues in the Senate are this vitriolic?

SEN. SANDERS: I mean that- I just got to say, what Cruz and Trump and Vance and others are saying is disgusting. It really is. And again, I don't care if you disagree with Abdul- he believes in Medicare for all, he believes in taxing billionaires. Fine, you disagree with him on that, that's fine. But that level of racism, overt, absolute racism, is frankly disgusting and should appall every decent American. The fact of the matter is that Abdul is running an extraordinary campaign, and I think what you're going to see is a good victory in Michigan for him. People will rebel against that type of ugliness.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I appreciate your clarity when it comes to racism. I do want to point out that some Americans hear any criticism of sending aid to Israel and the words that the candidate has used as anti-Jewish hate, and they believe that that's scapegoating as well. How do you respond to that?

SEN. SANDERS: Well, you know, for me, it's a little bit personal. I am Jewish. My father's family was wiped out by Hitler. Anti-Semitism is an extraordinarily disgusting and dangerous ideology that has killed millions and millions of lives in the last century. We cannot tolerate anti-Semitism period. But the reality is that right now in Israel you have a right-wing extremist government led by Netanyahu, who, in my view, and the view of many experts, has in fact committed genocide against the Palestinian people. To be critical of a racist extremist government in Israel, and to say that American taxpayers should not spend a nickel supporting that government is not anti-Semitism, it is attacking a right-wing government, and I would say the same about any other government on earth. Does not reflect the nature of the religion of the people who are in that country.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it.
SEN. SANDERS: So I reject that. You can criticize Netanyahu, and you're not anti-Semitic.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it. I want to ask you about the next Congress. Senator Dan Sullivan told CNN today that he will accept the results in the Alaska U.S. Senate race, the certification of which the Justice Department has said it may challenge. But we're already hearing from Republican Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana, that there "was fraud perpetrated against the people of Alaska, and under no circumstances should Mary Peltola be seated if she wins in a fraudulent manner." She argues, as you know, she has no knowledge of this Democratic effort to stack the ballot in Alaska from- and to hurt the incumbent, though an aide told the New York Times that the candidate did indeed know. Bottom line: What do you expect the Senate to do if she wins? And does all this mess really hurt the Democratic argument that they have a moral high ground on election integrity?

SEN. SANDERS: Yeah, frankly, what the Democrats did in Alaska seems to me to be pretty dumb, but it goes- this is- it's not illegal. It's what happens in every election. Right now in Ohio, there is a gentleman who is running, who is, as I understand it, don't know him, claiming to be a socialist, fine. And Republican Super PAC is putting money into his election. So why in Ohio is a Republican, a right-wing super PAC, funding a socialist? The answer is obviously- obvious. They want to take votes away from Sherrod Brown. Is this a good thing to do? No, it is not a good thing to do. It's a stupid thing to do--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Should there be an investigation--
SEN. SANDERS: --What's going on in Alaska is--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --of Alaska?

SEN. SANDERS: No, that's the decision- The federal government does not get involved in state elections. And you have a president who, in fact, denied that he lost the election in 2020 against Biden. For him to be deciding what is a fair election or not is a little bit absurd. People of Alaska can make that decision themselves.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Senator Bernie Sanders, thank you very much for your time today.

title: Shapiro says officials must "lead by example" in heated rhetoric
summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said that officials must "lead by example" amid what he called "dangerous" campaign rhetoric that's escalated as Election Day approaches.
story: Washington — Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said Sunday that lawmakers must "lead by example" amid what he called "dangerous" campaign rhetoric that's escalated as Election Day approaches.

"I think what you do is try and lead by example — as we are trying to do here, as I am trying to do here — try and bring back kindness in the face of the cruelty that we see from this president," Shapiro said  on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Shapiro, who was first elected governor in 2022 and is seeking reelection this year, spoke about the threats against him and his family. He highlighted the arson attack on the governor's residence in 2025 after he and his family celebrated the Jewish holiday of Passover with a Seder in the residence, saying, "It weighs on me, but it doesn't control me."
He said he has "profound differences from the person I'm running against, from the president and others."
"But I don't think engaging in cruelty is the answer," Shapiro added. "I think it makes everyone less safe."
Asked about the rhetoric on the campaign trail in places like Michigan, where a key Senate race is playing out, Shapiro said, "It's dangerous. It's hateful."

Shapiro said that since the attack on the governor's mansion, "even more people have threatened me and my wife, our family — threatened us based on how I worship."While he said "it weighs on you, certainly, to know that there are people out there trying to do you harm," he said, "I would also tell you, it motivates me to keep doing what I do to not let the bad guys win."
Shapiro said he and his family met before he opted to seek reelection, and "everybody agreed — can't let the bad guys win."
"We've got to keep going forward," he said. "You got to stand up against the hate. You got to lead by example, and you got to try and bring some decency back to this country."

title: The issue that could tip the scales in the Texas Senate race
summary: The contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico may determine control of the U.S. Senate. "Sunday Morning" talks with the candidates' supporters and local observers about a race that has drawn interest from around the country.
story: This year's midterm elections in Texas are on track to cost a billion dollars, with more than half of it spent on the U.S. Senate campaign – what could be the most expensive non-presidential race in American history. But whatever the price tag, it's certainly one of the most combative.

Republican State Attorney General Ken Paxton's campaign bus displays a rally cry from the 19th century Texas revolution against Mexico: "Come and take it." Paxton, whose government tenure has been marked by controversy, is President Trump's hand-picked candidate. At a rally October 23, Paxton exhorted the crowd: "Do you believe in protecting Texas and stopping Sharia law? So do I. Do you believe that parents, not the government, should raise your children? So do I."
Paxton's opponent is a Presbyterian seminarian and former middle-school teacher, State Representative James Talarico. Going into Election Day, polls show the two locked in a tight race.

Talarico draws his campaign's closing theme from the TV show about Texas high-school football, "Friday Night Lights." He told a crowd in San Antonio Oct. 24, "To win this election, we have to execute. We have to leave it all on the field. We have to win."

The issues in Texas mirror concerns across the country: high prices, immigration, government corruption, and the power of big tech and billionaires. As the song goes, "The eyes of Texas are upon you." And now, all eyes are on Texas.
"A big, messy, complicated election"

Sarah Adler Hartman and Matthew Watkins are the CEO and editor-in-chief of the Texas Tribune, a non-profit and non-partisan news organization. We invited them to the historic Salt Lick restaurant, just outside Austin, for some Hill Country barbecue, and a little politics.
Asked whether all the attention on Texas is inflating the egos of Texans to be the center of the political universe, Hartman replied, "Everything's bigger in Texas!"
Hartman acknowledges that despite the popular image of Texas, the state has a growing Asian American population, a growing Latino population, and more people moving here from around the country.

"Texas is very different than the caricature that people paint of Texas from outside of the state," she said, "and I think you see this, and you see some of the growing pains, the cognitive dissonance in this."

Watkins noted, "There's more Democratic voters in Texas than there are in Massachusetts. There's traditionally Democratic voters in rural areas of the Rio Grande Valley who are very socially conservative. There's, you know, really liberal white people in Austin. That's how we get into a big, messy, complicated election like we're in now."
"These races are all about turnout"
Last weekend, "Sunday Morning" followed Paxton and Talarico as both stumped in and around San Antonio, and spoke to some of their supporters.

Paxton's backers say the race is about what it means to be a true Texan. One man said of Democrats moving to the state, "They don't understand. They're bringing their point of views here, and it's going to ruin it. It'll be just like California if something doesn't change."
Another woman said she doesn't see Talarico as a Democrat: "He is more for Communism and taking away the rights that we have been founded on in this country," she said, adding he "alarms" her.

Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz has been on the trail campaigning for Paxton. "Look, this race is neck-and neck; it is a dead heat," Cruz said. "These races are all about turnout. The left is going to show up. They hate Donald Trump. They're going to show up. The question is, does everybody else? Do regular people come out and vote? If regular people come out and vote, we'll win Texas and have a good election."
"There are a lot more decent people"
Talarico supporters say GOP attacks on their candidate, over the border and transgender rights, are not working.

One woman doesn't buy the argument that Latino voters in Texas are turned off by Talarico on cultural issues: "I mean, I'm Latina, so I'm Brown and proud," she said. "I just voted this morning for James Talarico, so I am very excited to see, hopefully, the change that's going to happen."

That change won't come easy. Conservative republicans have run Texas for decades. But some Democrats feel their time has come. One woman got emotional telling us, "I'm hoping that this election will see that there are decent people, there are a lot more decent people than there are corrupt and cruel people. It's not about being Republican, it's not about being Democrat right now. It is good versus evil."

Congressman Joaquin Castro, a San Antonio Democrat, says economic concerns are paramount, even if the culture fights get the headlines. "Prices are so high, you know, people are really feeling it economically. They feel like they don't have time for [cultural issue fights]. I mean, all these attacks on transgender or all this other culture stuff? It's like, I can't pay my bills, I can't afford gas.
"Also, you know, James Talarico, he really is a generational talent," Castro said. "I know you hear that. But he's somebody who's trying to unify people."
Although diners back at the Salt Lick didn't appear to give it much notice, rising costs – of beef and gas, and housing – could be the deciding factor here and nationwide.

"There are a lot of people nationwide who view Texas as sort of the beating heart of conservatism for the country," said the Texas Tribune's Matthew Watkins. "There are people on the right who say, 'We can't lose Texas or else we lose the country'; there are people who on the left who say, 'Man, if we win Texas, like, this is a big deal.' There's this sort of psychological weight that is on it that makes people feel like, Okay, we can't lose this, or, What if we win this? That is causing people to really take interest in this race"

title: Midterm elections preview: How might this year's vote change Washington?
summary: With elections to choose all 435 House members, a third of our Senators, and 36 governors, "Sunday Morning" looks at why – with rising costs and a historically unpopular president – this year's midterms may upend expectations.
story: Every four years, we get to choose our own president. But every two years, we have other elections, where we choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives, and a third of our Senators, and a whole lot of governors.
This is a midterm elections year, our chance to steer the direction of the country.

"These are historically viewed as referenda on the job performance of a president," said New Yorker politics columnist Susan Glasser. She believes Tuesday's elections will be historic in a long list of ways.

First, there's the matter of the president's steadily sinking popularity. "The president is the most unpopular American president in the history of modern polling going into a midterm election," Glasser said.

The main reason is the price of everything. "People are so angry," Glasser said. "It's symbolized in how much money they're paying to put gas in their cars at the pump, or how much money they're paying for groceries. But it's obviously much, much broader than that."

Another historic factor: The number of political ads. "This will be a record-breaking year basically any way you slice it," said Wesleyan University professor Erika Franklin Fowler, who studies political ads. "The amount of money that's being spent is enormous."

This year, midterm ad spending will be over $11 billion, a record. But do political ads actually change anybody's mind? "Really not all that much," Fowler said. "No amount of advertising is going to change citizens' minds about the cost of goods in this type of economy."

Also historic is the rise of artificial intelligence in the ads: Computer-generated scenes of candidates that look like real video. Fowler said, "It's having candidates say things that they never said or do things that they never did. Those are particularly concerning because it's not clear to the viewer that this never happened."
How is that legal? "There's no federal regulation of AI in advertising," said Fowler, "so most of it actually doesn't even carry a disclaimer."

And with just days to go before the election, is any ad, or any rally, going to change a voter's mind? "That might be the irony of it all – we're seeing a lot more early voting this year," Fowler said, "and so a lot of the advertising that's on air now is actually too late to make a difference."
The Trump factor

Pollster Anthony Salvanto, who conducts our CBS News polls, said, "We see, overall, the numbers shifting toward the Democrats. It's not historically unusual for a president's party to lose seats in a midterm."
So, what is driving voters: The war? Corruption? Gas prices? Salvanto said, "It all of the above."

Another big factor, according to Salvanto, is the president: "Two-thirds of folks tell us they're going to the polls for Congress either to support him (26%), or, in more cases, to oppose his policies (41%)."

The president is a factor for the candidates, too. Most ads for Republican candidates don't even mention Mr. Trump. Sometimes they even criticize his policies, such as Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers' ad calling for an end to President Trump's tariff war against Canada.
So at this moment, what's the state of play for the House and the Senate? According to the latest CBS News House model, the Democrats are on pace to win 229 seats, giving them the majority.

As for the Senate, Salvanto said, "At the start of the year, there weren't many folks who gave Democrats a chance to take the Senate. Well, what we've seen over time is that a lot of those red Republican states have in fact come into play. Doesn't mean the Democrats are going to win them, but they certainly look to be more competitive."

The idea that Texas and Kansas might elect Democratic Senators is definitely historic. Glasser said, "The last time that Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas was in the 1930s. The last time a Democrat was elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas was Lloyd Bentsen in 1988."
What comes after the election?

So, if the Democrats win control of both houses of Congress, does that change anything? According to Susan Glasser, "I think you would see efforts to restrain the Defense Department from spending more money, for example on Trump's war with Iran. I think you might see very aggressive oversight and investigation hearings. I think you'll see them issue subpoenas."

But Glasser has more immediate concerns about what happens after the elections: "Donald Trump said that he won't accept the results of any election that he personally does not think were conducted the way he wanted them to be."

Asked if she thinks the president might try to invalidate or interfere with the results, Glasser laughed: "I don't think that's a speculative question. Remember that Donald Trump is the only president in all of American history ever to refuse to accept his defeat in a legitimate election. One of the things that Trump and his allies might try to do is to delay or block certification of incoming members of the Senate in close races."

Already, the Trump administration has ordered a criminal investigation into Alaska's Senate race, where Democrats are alleged to have recruited a candidate with the same name as the Republican opponent.

But even if the ride is bumpy, the midterm elections – especially these midterm elections – are a critical part of the American system of government. "I think it's absolutely a crucial midterm," Glasser said. "This is what the system was built to do, to balance and to constrain and to check among the different branches of government. I think we'd be looking at very different paths for our country depending on the outcome on Tuesday night."

title: Former President Obama endorses Booker in Kentucky Senate race
summary: Charles Booker is running against Republican Rep. Andy Barr to succeed Sen. Mitch McConnell.
story: Former President Barack Obama endorsed Democratic nominee Charles Booker in the Kentucky Senate race on Sunday, two days before Election Day.

"I'm proud to support Charles Booker for the U.S. Senate," former President Barack Obama said in a statement shared first with CBS News. "Charles cares deeply about the people of Kentucky, and by sending him to Washington, working families across the Commonwealth would have a leader who understands their struggles and has what it takes to make real change."

Booker said he was 'humbled and honored" to receive the endorsement. He is running against Republican Rep. Andy Barr to succeed Senator Mitch McConnell. McConnell, 84, announced his retirement last year and is Kentucky's longest serving senator.

"Mitch McConnell essentially built a career leveraging Kentucky to become one of the most powerful politicians in our country, and we know that by flipping Kentucky, we flip the U.S. Senate," Booker told CBS News in an interview earlier this year.

While Kentucky is not among the states listed in CBS News Senate battleground tracker, Booker's campaign says it has internal polling that indicates the race could be tightening. The race is considered solid Republican by Cook Political Report.

Aides are also citing an increase in Democratic turnout during early voting last week as a sign of potential momentum. According to the Kentucky State Board of Elections, more than 267,000 individuals had cast ballots. At least 95,645 registered Democrats had already voted compared to 83,726, Secretary of State Michael Adams said in a post Friday.
"A lot of it has been encouraging people to pay attention and to know that there is a race here, that it is competitive, and that there is a path to win," Booker said.

Booker challenged Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul in 2022 and lost by nearly 24 points. Although Kentucky is a deep-red, Democrats are hoping the national envorinment will help them make inroads in some unlikely places.
Barr has cast Booker as a "socialist experiment" and "the most extreme candidate in the history of our state." President Trump has endorsed Barr and visited the Commonwealth last month.
"He's been an amazing congressman," Mr. Trump said during an Oct. 17 rally in Highland Heights. "He'll be one of the great US senators."

Obama's endorsement follows a slew of other high-profile endorsements for the Kentucky Democrat, including from a group of senators, including Sens. Michael Bennet, Mark Kelly, Lisa Blunt Rochester, Chris Van Hollen, Raphael Warnock and Elizabeth Warren, who announced their support on Saturday. Booker is also backed by Govs. J.B. Pritzker and Wes Moore and he stumped with Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and DNC Chair Ken Martin last week.

The former president has issued nearly two dozen endorsements for Democratic candidates and rallied for Senate candidates in Georgia, Michigan and Ohio late last month. He has raised more than $15 million for party committees throughout the midterm cycle.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:00 a.m. on Nov. 1, 2026.

title: Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's planned arch
summary: There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet over Washington, D.C.
story: The legal challenges to President Trump's proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.

There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with Arlington National Cemetery. That would make the arch 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty from its base to the top of the torch.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.

In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington, D.C., and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia."

"The Arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River," the lawsuit says. "During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges."
As the original plaintiffs have, the two states also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration's plans to move ahead imminently with construction.

"Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump," said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, in a statement to CBS News. "From restoring our treasured landmarks after suffering years of abuse and vandalism, to cleaning our parks and the Reflecting Pool and equipping the White House with a much needed Helipad and the finest Ballroom anywhere in the world, President Trump's bold vision is ensuring the People's House and our Nation's Capital will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come."

The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would impact emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, including the January 2025 midair collision between a military helicopter and airliner that killed 67.
Administration wants to get started on construction

Speaking to reporters during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday night, Mr. Trump said the arch "is very important militarily for Washington, D.C., and our country. It's also going to be the most beautiful arc ever built."

"It will be one of Washington's most beautiful things. It's also very important militarily. Maybe more importantly, but I don't think so," Mr. Trump added. "But it is very important militarily, and I think we're doing very well."
He said, "Whether it's Virginia, Maryland, or Washington — it doesn't matter. It's something the region needs militarily, and I think aesthetically also."

The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a favorite of Mr. Trump's, at Thursday's meeting of the National Capital Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the then-two active lawsuits pending.

On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an "occupied roof" and two mezzanines.

Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a "fire command center." The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.

Chutkan asked what the urgency was and how the government would be harmed "apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city" if she issues a preliminary injunction while the lawsuit plays out. Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was "absolutely a high priority project" and were Chutkan to step in, that would impede the work of the government.
Golf course and Kennedy Center projects also have wound up in court
The lawsuits are among several that have been filed against the government as Mr. Trump seeks to remake the nation's capital at breakneck speed, prompting judges and plaintiffs to balk.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Friday she would open a "formal inquiry" to investigate if federal attorneys violated ethical boundaries, including making misrepresentations to the court, during a legal dispute about the East Potomac Golf Link project. Mr. Trump wants the public course overhauled so it could host professional tournaments.

There is a hearing Tuesday before U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper on a motion from Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, seeking the release of communications between the center's management and administration officials. The government has refused so far, citing executive privilege. Mr. Trump is the board chair.

Beatty alleged in a separate filing Friday that the government withheld information from trustees, including an analysis from the construction manager, that would have shown that a closure was not necessary. She is challenging a government request that Cooper dissolve an injunction he put in place to stop plans to shutter the performing arts venue for two years for renovation. That injunction also called for the removal of Mr. Trump's name, which had been placed on the center in December.

title: Daylight saving time ended today. Here's what to know.
summary: Millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep this weekend when the time change commonly known as daylight saving ended for 2026, meaning clocks "fell back."
story: Millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight saving ended for 2026. Most of the U.S. "fell back" an hour when the clocks changed at 2 a.m. on Sunday.
Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ended for the year:
What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it?
Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time.

The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.

For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun rose at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.

The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service. After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.
During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long.

After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the 1970s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark.
Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time?

Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate. The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect.

President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation. Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure.
In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter."

There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office.
If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president.
Did the time change today?
Yes, the time changed at 2 a.m. local time Sunday.

For 2026, the end of daylight saving time came during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun.
But for parents of young children, the time change may have been more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust.
What day and time did daylight saving time end in November 2026?
Daylight saving time officially ended at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect. A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October.
Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ended?
Most Americans gained an hour when daylight saving time ended, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March.
When will daylight saving time start again in 2027?

Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8.
The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April.
Which states don't do daylight saving time?

Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona. The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe.
The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time.
Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically?
Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically.

Apple, Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones.

title: El-Sayed asks fellow Democrat Stevens not to attend final campaign events
summary: Stevens has demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad and apologize for comments he made about Israel. El-Sayed said Stevens is "intent on relitigating" their primary.
story: Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has asked his Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, to stay away from all remaining campaign events in the final days before Tuesday's election, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The pair clashed Friday ahead of what had been a planned Sunday campaign event where they were expected to make a rare appearance together. Politico was first to report El-Sayed had asked Stevens to stay away.

The public rift between the two Democrats comes just days before one of the country's most hotly contested Senate races, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers seeks to peel off centrist Democratic voters. El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.
In a statement Friday evening, El-Sayed said Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

The dig came hours after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for suggesting during the campaign that "Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care."
"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens said in the statement. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

She also urged El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. The video ad features a couple in a grocery store talking about needing to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf because "we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." The man and woman in the ad then complain about the billions in military support that the U.S. has provided Israel.
El-Sayed's campaign said earlier this week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad, which was created by the political action committee Rebellion PAC.
"No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign," his campaign said in a statement.

"You guys love to play the condemn game," El-Sayed told reporters Saturday afternoon following a rally in Sterling Heights, Michigan, when asked if he condemned the ad. "I've already been clear that that ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad."
In her Friday statement, Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring the far-right podcaster and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson.

Stevens had said she planned to appear with El-Sayed at a Detroit church on Sunday, alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Even before asking her to stay away, an announcement from El-Sayed's campaign about his appearance with Clyburn did not mention Stevens.

Earlier this week, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News he would vote for Rogers. Later that day, Stevens said in a CNN interview that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying, "We're a household divided," but she called on his campaign "to shut out the hate and to call it out."
This Sunday's "60 Minutes" will feature Ross Douthat's exclusive interviews with Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers.

title: DOJ calls Alaska Senate allegations "troubling," asks to segregate ballots
summary: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska did not specify what crimes are being investigated by the Justice Department, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."
story: Anchorage, Alaska — The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska said new reporting on the origins of an independent candidate's Senate campaign "has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, as federal officials in a separate civil case seek to segregate some of Alaska's Senate ballots.

Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for the District of Alaska, called the allegations about how Daniel J. Sullivan — a man with the same first and last name as incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan — ended up on the ballot "troubling."

"We are aware of the recent New York Times reporting regarding the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, that they orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate, and we are taking that extremely seriously," he said in a press conference in Anchorage.
But Heyman declined to detail what specific crimes are being investigated, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

"That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.
Asked by CBS News why the Justice Department is choosing to escalate the case ahead of the election, Heyman said, "We're not escalating anything except to the extent that a new article came out."

"This has been going on sort of quietly for several months, with the intent not to escalate anything," he said, adding that investigators are going to take allegations involving election integrity seriously, even if a few days before the election.

Republicans have claimed that Daniel J. Sullivan is a plant by Democrats to confuse voters and boost the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country.

Peltola and national Democrats have strongly denied any involvement in his campaign. Peltola said Thursday she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has argued Republicans have been linked to their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates, including in this year's Senate primary and in other elections.

State election officials initially determined Daniel J. Sullivan was not eligible to appear on the ballot, accusing him of a "deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the decision was overturned by state courts, which ruled that state officials didn't have the authority to exclude a candidate based on their interpretation of "good faith."

The controversy drew renewed scrutiny after the New York Times reported that operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the matter and the Justice Department has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials.
In a separate civil case, the Trump administration has sued to block Alaska from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses because of "voter confusion."

On Friday, the Justice Department asked for a preliminary injunction, saying it wants to "ensure the preservation and segregation of ballots that may be impacted by voter confusion." The government also asked for expedited discovery for the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and requested that a judge rule on the matter by Monday. The filings heavily rely on The New York Times' reporting.

"Daniel J. Sullivan does not seek to serve in the U.S. Senate but rather seeks to confuse voters," the filing says. "Accordingly, there will indeed be voter confusion caused by this frivolous candidacy."

Federal government lawyers said they want to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."

The state of Alaska opposed the request, arguing the Justice Department's lawsuit "lacks any merit." They also said votes are "comingled in the ballot box on Election Day" and therefore can't be segregated without violating ballot secrecy requirements, and noted that "the ballots (whether segregated or not) will not reveal any voter's reasons for voting for Daniel J."
And they said an order to preserve ballots is unnecessary since the state already saves ballots for 22 months.

"The United States' delay further undermines its request for expedited consideration. It waited until two weeks before Election Day to file a lawsuit about issues that arose months ago," the state said.

The Justice Department lawsuit is predicated on allegations that the second Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act. However, in a motion filed Saturday to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit, the Alaska Attorney General's Office argued the DOJ's argument has "no legal basis," and said there is "no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer."
"What's more, the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters' vital right to ballot secrecy," the state wrote in its motion.
Alaskan officials also countered in Saturday's motion that "state officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion."

During the news conference Friday, Heyman also said that he had been recused from the matter some time ago, but that the recusal "has officially been rescinded." Heyman said he had been recused because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, which is no longer the case.

title: Judge dismisses with prejudice Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal
summary: In a 20-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that President Trump did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.
story: A multimillion-dollar defamation lawsuit by President Trump against The Wall Street Journal over a story reporting his ties to a birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein has been thrown out.

In a 20-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice on Saturday, ruling that Mr. Trump did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.
He said the lawsuit was "grasping at straws" as it attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the WSJ's investigative reporting.
Actual malice requires that plaintiffs prove that statements made about a public figure were published with the knowledge that they were false, or with disregard for whether they are true or not.
When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again, and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

"President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," a spokesperson for Mr. Trump's legal team told CBS News in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."
A source familiar with Mr. Trump's legal strategy said that the decision will likely be appealed.

The lawsuit was over a story the WSJ published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Mr. Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The president dismissed the story as "FAKE" and filed a $20 billion lawsuit against the paper, its parent company News Corp, the company's CEO, the reporters who wrote the story and Rupert Murdoch, News Corp's chairman emeritus.

House lawmakers later subpoenaed and obtained a redacted version of the birthday book from Epstein's estate, which included the letter at the center of Mr. Trump's lawsuit. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said: "It's very clear President Trump did not draw this picture, and he did not sign it."

In April, Gayles dismissed the lawsuit, saying the president's legal team failed to clear the legal bar needed to establish their claim. He ruled that the president came "nowhere close" to showing the paper acted with "actual malice" toward him, the standard for bringing a defamation suit as a public figure.
Mr. Trump's legal team refiled the lawsuit.

title: Judge orders DOJ to stop trying to "intimidate" California election officials
summary: A federal judge ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots and threatening criminal prosecution for noncompliance.
story: A California judge late Friday ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots or not count certain votes from alleged noncitizens, and to stop threatening officials with criminal prosecution if they do not comply.

The ruling from U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson came in response to a lawsuit filed a day earlier by labor unions and other groups, accusing the Trump administration of intimidating California election workers and interfering in the administration of the midterms.

The Justice Department has pressed officials in California this month to separate out mail ballots for roughly 20,000 people it alleges are not U.S. citizens, and has issued grand jury subpoenas for officials in Los Angeles County — part of a sweeping campaign by the Trump administration. Federal officials have also suggested for months that election workers could be prosecuted if they fail to stop noncitizens from voting.

The lawsuit cited the head of the Justice Department Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, sending letters to all 50 states and Washington, D.C., threatening to criminally prosecute local election officials in July, and the department's latest demand for lists of names of voters they believe are possibly noncitizens, as examples of unlawful conduct.

The judge on Friday found federal officials have likely violated the Voting Rights Act of 1965's prohibition on "attempting to intimidate, threaten or coerce" people who help others vote. She also said the government was acting outside its legal or constitutional authority.

"One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation," she wrote. "Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy. It requires safeguarding to ensure full participation and public trust in our elections."

Thompson also wrote: "Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters."
The judge issued a temporary restraining order that expires on Nov. 16, and scheduled the next hearing for Nov. 13.

In addition to blocking the Justice Department from threatening criminal prosecutions or demanding that officials separate out ballots, Thompson ordered the Justice Department to inform the court of any pending search warrant applications or subpoenas.

"The judge issued an order against the federal government without even waiting to hear from the United States, while in other cases the Department's own urgent election claims are delayed by judges until after Election Day," a DOJ spokesperson told CBS News in a statement on Saturday. "That is a two-track system of justice. The Department is reviewing the order and evaluating all options."

The ruling was issued after another California federal judge on Wednesday denied the Justice Department's request to compel California to set aside more than 20,000 ballots for alleged noncitizens. He found that it violates "longstanding constitutional principles" giving states the authority to administer their own elections. The Trump administration appealed the matter to an appellate court, which also rejected a request to segregate the ballots on Friday.

title: How to watch live 2026 election results on CBS News
summary: With control of Congress on the line in House and Senate races around the country, here's how to watch the 2026 midterm election results on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
story: Control of Congress and the future of President Trump's agenda are on the line in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters cast their ballots for all 435 House seats and 35 Senate races around the country. Candidates for governor are on the ballot in 39 states, along with some high-profile measures like California's proposed billionaire tax.
CBS News will have extensive live coverage of results and analysis on all platforms after the polls close on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
How to watch election coverage with cable
CBS News' "America Decides: Election 2026" live coverage on TV and cable starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. ET. (Find your local CBS station here.)

Anchors Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell will be joined on the set by "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King, "Face the Nation" moderator and chief foreign affairs correspondent Margaret Brennan, and CBS News' team of political reporters, including Robert Costa, Major Garrett, Nancy Cordes and Ed O'Keefe.

title: As Texas Dems predict a Hispanic wave, Hinojosa takes her pitch ringside
summary: Days before Election Day, Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa is stepping into the ring for a critical voting bloc in the Lone Star State: Hispanic men.
story: Days before Election Day, Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa is stepping into the ring for a critical voting bloc in the Lone Star State: Hispanic men.

Hinojosa's campaign plans to air a 30-second advertisement Saturday during Mexican boxing superstar Canelo Álvarez's fight against Christian Mbilli, an effort to reach Hispanic voters, especially Latino men, who played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 victory.
The advertisement is titled "No Te Dejes," a Spanish expression meaning "Don't let yourself be pushed around," and repeats Hinojosa's central campaign message: "Fight back."

According to her campaign, the spot contrasts Hinojosa's proposals to protect public schools, restrict data center expansion and lower taxes with what she argues is three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's prioritization of wealthy donors and large corporations.
The advertisement will run on DAZN, the sports streaming platform carrying Saturday's fight.
The ad reflects a broader strategy by Democrats to engage Hispanic men through sports and culturally relevant programming rather than relying exclusively on traditional political advertising.
It's an approach that has already been tested in another Southwestern battleground.
During his successful 2024 Senate campaign in Arizona, Democrat Ruben Gallego made a concerted effort to reach Latino men through boxing watch parties, rodeos, cookouts and other community events.
Gallego went on to defeat Republican Kari Lake, becoming Arizona's first Latino U.S. senator, even as Mr. Trump carried the state by nearly six percentage points in the same year.
In an interview with CBS News following his victory, Gallego said his strategy with Hispanic voters was to "talk to them as often as possible."

Abbott has also pitched himself to Latino voters in Texas. His campaign launched a Spanish-language ad that cast Hinojosa as too socially liberal for the state, with press secretary Eduardo Leal arguing in a statement last week that her policies don't match "the values of the Hispanic community." Abbott has also highlighted his wife Cecilia's status as the state's first Hispanic first lady.

Hispanics make up around 40% of Texas' population, and they could play a central role in Hinojosa's push to become Texas' first Democratic governor in over three decades. A CBS News poll earlier this month showed Abbott leading Hinojosa by four points outright, with a 3.4-point margin of error, but Hinojosa led by 23 points among likely Hispanic voters.
But Latino voters in Texas are increasingly emerging as a swing electorate.

Some 55% of Latino Texans voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, according to CBS News' exit poll data. Latino men favored the president by a nearly two-to-one margin. That shift was an earthquake in Texas politics, turning once-reliably Democratic counties in the Rio Grande Valley into GOP-leaning territory and scrambling Democrats' hopes that Texas could be turning their way.

In comments to CBS News, Hinojosa offered her own explanation for Mr. Trump's success with Hispanic voters in 2024, arguing that his message resonated with Texans who felt the political establishment had failed them.

"The reason why Trump won, and why he was able to capture the Latino vote in the Valley and in Texas, is because he said the system is rigged — and he's right. Democrats had been defending a system that is indefensible, that is actually working against us," Hinojosa said.

Democrats are hopeful that the shift will be temporary. Nationwide polling shows that many Latino voters have turned away from Mr. Trump since 2024, and Democratic strategists in Texas have taken solace in high turnout in heavily Latino areas during this year's Democratic primary.
Gallego's former campaign adviser, Democratic strategist and CBS News political contributor Chuck Rocha, is now advising both Hinojosa and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
Rocha told CBS News many Hispanic voters are disillusioned with high gas prices and other cost-of-living worries, though Mr. Trump's immigration policies have also caused frustration.
"Right now, they're more monolithic than I have ever seen in my life, and they're monolithically mad," he said.
But Daniel Garza, president of the conservative Latino advocacy group LIBRE Initiative, said "there is no pro-Democrat enthusiasm" in his home region of South Texas.
"I think most voters couldn't tell you what the Democrat plan is for bringing down prices," he said.
For now, Hinojosa is betting that one of Mexico's biggest sports stars can help her land a punch with the voters both parties are fighting to win.
This story published first on CBS News at 8:04 a.m. on Oct. 31, 2026.

title: Daniel J. Sullivan left his Alaska hometown before Senate election
summary: Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent Alaska Senate candidate whose name is almost identical to the Republican incumbent, left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, multiple sources confirmed to CBS News.
story: Petersburg, Alaska — Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent candidate running for Senate in Alaska whose name is almost identical to the Republican senator running for reelection, left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, multiple sources confirmed to CBS News.

One resident and former student of Sullivan's said she saw Sullivan on a flight to Anchorage on Monday — two days before The New York Times first reported that he was recruited by operatives linked to Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign. The source added she did not know where Sullivan was headed, but another friend said he and his wife are known among friends as "world travelers."
Sullivan's current whereabouts after leaving his hometown are not clear.

Dozens of Petersburg residents also told CBS News they never saw or received any campaign materials like mailers, flyers, brochures or signs since the former elementary school teacher announced his candidacy last spring.
"I don't think it's a serious candidacy," said Andrew Worhatch, a Petersburg fisherman. "I haven't seen a platform."

Just days before the midterm elections, a CBS News crew on the ground in Petersburg likewise found no indication of any active campaigning by the candidate, including outside his own home, which sits adjacent to the main coastal highway.
Still, Sullivan has his supporters — and voters — including Keely Hankins, who said she thinks "Petersburg Dan" is the only candidate capable of representing Southeast Alaska.

"I've known Dan for a long time. I know his family. I know he's raised good children, and he's always been a really great role model for his students," Hankins maintained. "If you intend to vote and intentionally vote, you know who you're going to vote for, and it says 'Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.,' then it says 'Dan Sullivan, incumbent.' Just read the paper. It's not that hard."
But the new spotlight on the town is not welcomed by some. Darla Kowalski said, "It's just embarrassing to think that we, a small fishing village, have such a hoaxer."
The local school district in Petersburg — a town of around 3,000 accessible only by air or sea — said Sullivan taught music and fourth and fifth grade for nearly 20 years before retiring in 2021.

Republicans have argued for months that Sullivan was seeking to confuse voters in one of the country's closest midterm Senate races, with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan calling him a "sham candidate." State election officials initially deemed him ineligible for the ballot, but state courts reversed that decision.

The Peltola campaign and national Democrats have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan, with Peltola telling supporters she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about" the second Sullivan. In interviews over the summer, the Petersburg native insisted he is genuinely interested in serving as senator.

After the Times' reporting on alleged efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation, and the Justice Department ramped up a criminal probe. Nobody has been charged with a crime. The Justice Department is also suing in civil court to block the election from being certified if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion."
This story published first on CBS News at 3:41 p.m. on Oct. 30, 2026.

title: Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election
summary: The Vatican said Pope Leo exercised his right as a U.S. citizen, submitting a mail-in ballot in his native Chicago ahead of the midterm elections next week.
story: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election. The Vatican confirmed Friday that the American-born pope submitted a mail-in ballot in his native Chicago ahead of November's midterm elections, citing his longstanding belief in civic participation.
The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.
The Will County Clerk's Office confirmed to CBS News that he is on the list of voters who requested a mail-in ballot, with a registered address in New Lenox.

The Chicago Sun-Times first reported Leo's vote and quoted the chief of staff at the Will County Clerk's Office as saying the pope requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3. This was just days before his recent lung cancer surgery.
The pope has been recovering and resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17 and is moving ahead with plans for a trip to South America next month.
Last month, Leo told a general audience at the Vatican that the faithful should leave behind "all passivity and indifference" toward current events.

"We cannot remain as unengaged spectators; rather, we must listen with our hearts, allow ourselves to be challenged, and become involved," the pope said on Sept. 2 in St. Peter's Square, according to the Catholic News Service. "With Christ and sustained by the power of his Spirit, believers are called to take on the burdens of their brothers and sisters, especially those who are crushed by injustice, discrimination and violence."

The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.

According to records from the Illinois State Board of Elections, the pope, as Robert Prevost, was registered to vote in Cook County. The Associated Press reports he previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
Illinois has closed primaries, which means voters must declare a party preference to receive a ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.
The pope submitted ballots in every general election since 2000, except in 2020 and 2022, the AP reported, citing Illinois election records.

title: Is the truth really out there? Studying UAP sightings
summary: Seven decades after the first reported sightings of Unidentified Flying Objects, a scientific council is investigating records and video released by the government of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), to possibly answer the question: Are we alone?
story: On a May evening back in 1950, Evelyn Trent had just finished feeding her rabbits when, she claims, she looked up and saw a slow-moving, metallic disk-shaped object hovering above her farm. Though some dismissed it as a hoax, her account was added to a growing list of unexplained events that sparked America's first UFO craze.

At the annual McMenamins UFO Festival in McMinnville, Ore., just a few miles from Evelyn Trent's farm, there are costumes, a parade, and some theories that might be generously described as fringe: "Well, based on what I've read, it could be us from the future visiting us from, you know, the past," said one attendee, "and then it could also be trans-dimensional or inter-dimensional beings."

Fringe, but definitely something Americans seem interested in. According to a CBS News Poll, nearly one in five Americans (17%) has seen a UFO, which has led to an explosion in podcasts and documentaries on the topic.

Matthew Szydagis, one of the UFO festival's invited speakers, teaches physics at the State University of New York at Albany. He spoke to us about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (or UAPs), or what we used to call UFOs back in the old days: "I think the possibility that at least some small fraction of UFOs or UAPs represent a non-human intelligence," Szydagis said. "That will be the greatest discovery in human history. So, of course that's going to fire people up and get their imaginations going."

Szydagis would like to believe in aliens, but he also knows that extraordinary claims demand extraordinary evidence, especially in the world of "UFOlogy," where the more extreme the claims, the more attention they get.

"We still don't have definitive evidence," Szydagis said. "We haven't been provided with a dead alien body, for instance, although claims of the existence have been made. But I think we have enough indirect evidence to say that the existence of non-human intelligence is no longer laughable, that it's not irrational."

Szydagis is part of a new Scientific Advisory Council, established by the Trump Administration, to study UAPs. The person in charge of that council is none other than respected Harvard professor Avi Loeb, former chair of the university's astronomy department.

"Now, there are some objects the U.S. government cannot figure out," Loeb said. "I would like to figure them out. Because at the very least, as an American citizen, I will be helping the Pentagon and the intelligence community fulfill their mission of, if these are human-made technologies, if they come from adversarial nations, then I can help them identify what they are and where they came from."

The things Loeb and the other council members are trying to identify are the many sightings over the years of lights and objects and movements in the sky that defy simple explanation. Someone who's experienced it firsthand? Former U.S. Navy pilot Ryan Graves, whose testimony in front of Congress got the nation's attention back in 2023, when he recounted an experience during a training mission ten miles off the coast of Virginia Beach: "Two F-18 Super Hornets were split by a UAP," Graves said. "The object, described as a dark grey or a black cube inside of a clear sphere, came within 50 feet of the lead aircraft."

For many people, seeing no-nonsense U.S. military personnel calmly describing things they'd seen and couldn't explain, along with actual images, made the whole thing seem a lot less crazy. Graves told us, "We were seeing these things, we were nearly hitting them, and yet we're still unwilling to talk about them in our safety briefs and incorporate them into the conversation."

Graves was also recently added to the Advisory Council, tasked with getting to the bottom of things, and there are a lot of things that have been released in the last eight months: seven tranches of first-person accounts, photographs, and lots of grainy video, more than 155,000 pages of files overall.

But not enough of the good stuff, says Graves: "What's being released is not satisfactory to me. What you are seeing are very short clips from infrared sensors aboard different platforms. And ultimately, these are not the high-end sophisticated tools that are used by pilots in order to make critical decisions about whether [an] object in the air is hostile, whether it's a decoy, whether it is a threat or not. And so, I think we're left with more ambiguity."

Loeb said, "The mistake that is often made about science is the belief that, 'Oh, the data will come and guide us.' But the problem is that to collect the data, you need to put in effort. And it's often a heroic effort to get the high-quality data."

Questions linger about what exactly the government knows about UFOs, after former Air Force intelligence officer David Grusch testified to Congress that he was told of the existence of recovered UFOs.

When Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) asked whether possession of a crashed craft also meant possession of the bodies of the craft's pilot(s), Grusch replied, "As I have stated publicly already in my News Nation interview, biologics came with some of these recoveries, yeah."
Of course, evidence for all of this is "classified," leading some ufologists to call Grusch and others making claims about government conspiracies "Trust Me Bros."

Loeb, who's floated a number of controversial theories on possible alien life, says the Advisory Council is working to get access to as much information as possible, starting with what's been publicly released. "My role is really simple, because it's like a detective," he said. "And the worst that can happen to a detective is that the detective is starved of data. So, if I don't have data, the quality of my deliberations [is] poor. I mean, only in politics, with very little data, you can make a huge story!"

For his part, Ryan Graves started an organization called Americans for Safe Aerospace, which encourages everyone (but especially pilots) to share their stories of UAPs. And of course, he's got a podcast.

"Recently I've been astounded, in fact, that almost everyone is willing to talk about this," said Graves. "It is fighter pilots. It is commercial aviators. And I think that really speaks to how this conversation has changed over the past few years."

Asked whether he believes he'll get answers within his lifetime, Graves replied, "My lifetime, yes. We are moving towards a point in time where we're perhaps not going to get every answer we want, but we're going to potentially have the confirmation that something truly strange is happening."
Until that conformation, the truth will have to remain (as they say) out there.

title: Meteorite found in the Sahara Desert turns out to be piece of Mars
summary: A meteorite found in the Sahara Desert has been determined to be 4.1 billion years old and from Mars.
story: A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert in 2022 has been identified as a 4.1-billion-year-old chunk of the Red Planet, a NASA study determined.
The nearly two-pound meteorite was found in Mali. It was named Teghaza 001, after the salt plain where it was discovered, NASA said in a news release.

Study of the meteorite allowed NASA scientists to determine it was one of roughly 435 from Mars. Meteorites can be verified as having been part of Mars by comparing their chemical and mineral makeup to samples and data collected by NASA's Martian missions.

Age-dating of the meteorite led researchers to conclude it was about 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth, NASA said. That provides "a rare snapshot" of the planet's crust and formation, the agency said.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the lead author of a paper detailing the age-dating process and related discoveries. Liu is part of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Previous ancient Martian meteorites provided narrower glimpses into the planet's history. But Teghaza 001 shows how Mars' crust formed from cooling magma and was then changed by water on the planet's surface.

The meteorite is made of a unique mix of volcanic minerals, including zircon crystals, NASA said, matching samples observed by the agency's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's southern highlands. Francis Tissot, a geochemistry professor at Caltech, helped the researchers use a pioneering age-dating method that studied a piece of meteorite smaller than a fingernail. The precise method allowed scientists to analyze single grains of minerals.

That analysis showed the rock had been altered by Martian water about 4.1 billion years ago. The rock itself may have been formed even earlier, NASA said. The data also showed that early Mars may have had a more dynamic water cycle than scientists previously believed.

Paper author Lee Saper said that the meteorite "records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." Another study of the meteorite, published in June, focused on the rock's water content and considered how water might have shaped the early topography of Mars.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," Lee, a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center, added.
Liu said that further research on the meteorite is likely.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.
