title: Transcript: David Becker on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with David Becker, CBS News election law contributor and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with David Becker, CBS News election law contributor and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by our CBS News election law contributor and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, David Becker. David, good to have you here. So each state- they have their own systems, their own timeline for poll closings--
CBS NEWS ELECTION LAW CONTRIBUTOR DAVID BECKER: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and for vote counting. Some places, early votes already in, but when will we know results?

: Well, we're going to know results, not because of the factor of how fast states are counting- look, the election officials in every county in every state are going to be working all night long trying to get the ballots reported out. The biggest variable is how close the elections are, because when you talk to someone like Anthony Salvanto, who will tell you if it's really close, they just need more ballots in before they can make a call to say for sure the person in second place can't come in- can't win the race. So, in a lot of states where we haven't seen close elections before, we're going to see close elections in all likelihood, and it might take days. A day like- a state like Alaska in particular, where they're already well behind Eastern Time, they've got very remote voting all over the place. They're going to bring ballots in from all over the place to count them. And if the election's really close, it could be several days. That's normal. And everything that's going on in the election offices all over the country is under observation. There are Republican and Democratic observers at all times watching the ballots counted, watching the mail ballots being opened, et cetera. So people should know there's nothing going on. This is just the normal process and elections might be close. It might take a few days.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And who are those monitors?

: Usually people who are appointed by the parties, either the Democratic or Republican Party, representing candidates in many times or campaigns. That's very normal. That's the way it was in 2020. Even during COVID, there were literally thousands upon thousands of monitors and observers all over the place. So the parties are well represented. They're seeing everything that's going on, and as soon as the results come in and we see them, they're aware of them.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let's talk about Alaska. It is ranked choice voting. It's a little different in that way. This morning on CNN, Republican Dan Sullivan, the incumbent senator, said he will accept the results of the election if he loses. As we discussed on this program last Sunday with Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Justice Department is seeking to stop certification of a possible Democratic win due to ballot confusion with what the New York Times has reported is this Democratic scheme to stack the ballot in accusing- in a confusing way to disadvantage the senator. Yesterday, just to update everyone, Alaska's Republican-led state government urged a federal judge to dismiss--
: That's right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --the lawsuit that the DOJ filed. They said it was meritless.
: That's right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, doesn't this need to be settled by a federal judge before election day?

: It really does, and I mean, it'd be nice if a federal judge dismisses the DOJ's lawsuit, as so many courts have across the country in these last-minute lawsuits that have been brought seemingly, mainly to create an impression of chaos. They're failing, but in Alaska in particular, it would be nice if we got a federal court ruling. We might get one, but Alaska's courts have ruled on this, including their Supreme Court.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

: They ruled that both Dan Sullivans can be on the ballot. We've shown- seen the ballot. You've shown the ballot before. It's pretty clear that the Alaska Division of Elections, run by the Lieutenant Governor- Governor, there, a Republican, has done a really good job of making it as- as unconfusing as it can be. And with that ranked choice voting, if- even if someone still wasn't sure and they ranked both Dan Sullivan's first and second, by the second round, all of those votes would go to the- to the- whatever candidate got the most, presumably the incumbent senator. I'm not surprised Senator Sullivan says he will accept the results. Of course, this is Alaska defending its state sovereignty and its right and authority over elections in the state of Alaska, as guaranteed by the United States Constitution. It's good to see the Republican governor and Republican lieutenant governor there in Alaska defending their sovereignty as strongly as they are.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But even Democrats, as I've said before, have said this does look bad. This looks like dirty pool. Looks like they're playing dirty.

: There's dirty pool. Both parties do this. It shouldn't happen. Right now, in Nevada, there are two candidates named Ford running for governor, we're not sure what the circumstances of that are. One of them is the major Democratic candidate. We've seen Elon Musk bankroll Cornel West's presidential campaign in 2024. These kinds of things shouldn't happen, I don't think there's any question, but it's pretty normal politics, unfortunately. And Alaska's courts and Alaska state law has already ruled on this.
MARGARET BRENNAN: There are other states, California, Washington state, where we're seeing federal scrutiny. What are you monitoring here?

: Well, what's really remarkable is there's so much last-minute litigation alleging- allegedly non- non-citizens on the voter lists, alleging problems with the process coming from the DOJ. This Department of Justice has been in power for nearly two years. They have had the full power of the federal government to investigate any claims. And as you heard from Governor Shapiro, when they've made political statements on this in the press, when they've been asked to show their work, they've hid the ball. They have not shared information with California, with Pennsylvania, with other states. And now they bring these last-minute lawsuits, and they are being rejected soundly by every court, including by Trump-appointed judges in most cases. I think this is a good sign. I think this is a good sign that the administration is running out of gas here on this effort to sow confusion in the election, and the courts are holding firm. And most importantly, the election officials are holding firm. As you and I are talking right now, the last time I checked, it was over 53 million ballots already cast all over this country.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wow.

: We're going to see- the record, by the way, in a midterm election is 118 million ballots cast. We are definitely going to get well over half that before the- before election day even comes. We might see a record turnout. It looks like that's highly possible. We're certainly seeing it in places like Texas, where 7.7 million ballots have already been cast as we're sitting here talking.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wow.

: And their record for a midterm election is 8.375 million total. So they're about- they're just over about 600,000 or so ballots away from their highest turnout ever, and we are days before the election. Election day hasn't even happened yet. That's remarkable.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's fascinating level of participation.
: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: David, thank you for breaking it down. And I know we'll be talking to you in the days and weeks to come. We'll be back in a moment.

title: Transcript: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
summary: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
story: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: All right. So, Governor, you're campaigning for re-election, and you're also trying to help some of these Democrats get elected to Congress. According to our CBS polling, 57% of likely voters believe Democrats have not offered a clear plan for what they would do if they do win control of Congress. What is it that Democrats are running for, or is it simply in opposition to President Trump?

GOV. JOSH SHAPIRO: Well, certainly for me, it's not about opposition to Trump. I'm running as a GSD Democrat—a Get Stuff Done Democrat. I think what people have seen in my leadership here in Pennsylvania is someone who listens, who goes back to the Capitol, and then delivers, executes for the people of Pennsylvania, and I'm working hard to elect these members of or these challengers to the members of Congress here in Pennsylvania who run on a similar platform, common sense things, making sure people have access to health care, making sure that there is actually accountability in Washington D.C. so that the corruption doesn't take money out of people's pockets here and enrich the folks in D.C. Those are just two examples of the kinds of things I see from our challengers here in Congress. And as I crisscross this Commonwealth, what they're seeing from me is a Democrat who understands how to win, but more importantly, understands how to deliver for them. And that's what these candidates are running on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How optimistic are you that you're going to be able to take four seats I think you've said?

GOV. SHAPIRO: I mean, look. Right now, it seems like there might even be five competitive congressional districts here in Pennsylvania. Obviously, four have received the most attention. I think we're seemingly ahead in at least three of them. But look, I never pay much attention to these polls. I think it's all a jump ball, and the most important thing is to do what we're doing on this bus: show up everywhere, talk to people, let them know what's at stake, how important it is to not just re-elect their governor, but that we can finally have a check on Donald Trump's chaos, cruelty, and corruption in Washington D.C. If they get out and vote for their candidate for Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And they're still going to have to work with a Republican president for those next two years when they get there. If they get there.

GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. But there'll be a check on his corruption, and hopefully have real leverage to roll back the Medicaid cuts, to roll back the SNAP cuts, to make sure that there's real responsibility and accountability in Washington D.C. Something we have not had when Republicans have had a trifecta there.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about what's going to happen here in this state in terms of administering the election. Homeland Security claimed earlier this year that as many as 14,576 non-citizens could be registered to vote here. Has the federal government provided enough information to you–
[STOP DOWN]

MARGARET BRENNAN: So Homeland Security said that in this state there are as many as 14,576 non citizens that could be registered to vote in Pennsylvania. Did they provide information to back up that claim? And what did your own investigation find?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah, could is the operative word. As soon as we received that from the federal government, we immediately responded and said, "Look, if you have information of illegal voters who are on our rolls, we want that information because we don't want them casting a ballot here in Pennsylvania." I'm very serious about it. Look, I'm the former chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I have prosecuted election fraud cases. I don't want anyone voting who's not a legal eligible voter–
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did they back that up?

GOV. SHAPIRO: And of course, of course, when we responded to the Trump administration, they provided no backup. So it was a press release designed to get some attention for their false narrative. Listen, the first appointment I made when I was elected governor was the Secretary of State. That's the person that administers elections here in the state. A Republican named Al Schmidt. I chose him, even though I'm a Democrat, because I think the administration of elections should be nonpartisan. Al Schmidt, in his career of running elections, has done more to root out corruption than anything that's ever been done in the Trump administration. We take that very, very seriously, and the Trump administration has never provided a shred of evidence to suggest that there are people on our rolls who are ineligible. If they have it, I want it, and we will act on it immediately.

MARGARET BRENNAN: A recent CBS investigation found Pennsylvania was one of the states where Homeland Security has been going door to door. They've been knocking on doors and asking about the immigration status of people who live there. What can you tell us about what DHS has been doing here? And did the administration coordinate with you as governor in any way?

GOV. SHAPIRO: No. And I want to make very very clearly the Pennsylvania State Police does not do DHS's work for them. Does not do ICE's work for them. We do not ask immigration status. In fact, when ICE came here and tried to bully their way into building two massive detention centers here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, one in Berks County, one in Schuylkill County, I fought back and won and drove those detention centers out of Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How many non-citizen voters did you find?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, what they said was that there were, whatever the number was, over a thousand people. So we said, great, tell us who they are, so we can check their status. They never told us who they were, and so it is impossible for us to be able to check the people that they claim to have identified. I will tell you, we've got very, very strict guardrails in place, led by Secretary Schmidt, constantly making sure that the people who are on our voter rolls are legal, eligible voters. And if we find that someone is not, if a mistake was made in a county where someone was registering, as an example, we immediately get on that. We work with prosecutors to ensure that they are not in a position to cast a ballot. As I said, I was the chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I prosecuted election fraud. It was a handful of cases. By the way, some were Republican, some were Democrat. None of it impacted any elections. But still, we can't allow that to happen here in our Commonwealth. And what I would ask of the Trump administration is, instead of sending me a press release, send me actual evidence, actual data, and we will review it promptly.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you did speak recently with Philadelphia Inquirer's editorial board, and you told them that you think President Trump and his allies are going to try and stop votes from being counted.
GOV SHAPIRO: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You also said you expect Speaker Johnson to make efforts to delay seating new members if Republicans lose the majority. Why are you raising these concerns now? And do you think at all that you might be undermining faith?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. Well, respectfully, I was answering their question as to whether or not I thought the Trump administration would take steps to try and undermine our elections. So just to offer some context to that, and I did issue those answers, and I'll tell you why. Because I have lived through this before with the Trump administration. Back in 2020, I was the attorney general, and Trump lost the election here in Pennsylvania and tried to undermine the counting of the vote. In fact, he and his enablers sued me 43 different times to try and throw out the votes of certain Pennsylvanians. Heck, even my opponent went to court to throw out the votes of people in Bucks County. I won every single one of those cases. Went 43 and 0, Trump went 0 and 43. And so we are prepared should they try to do that again this time. In fact, we put together a task force more than a year ago when Trump began to hint at the idea that he would once again take that tack. So we are prepared in the courtroom. Should they go forward and try and undermine the right to vote. Now, more recently, we've seen further evidence of this president trying to undermine the right to vote in signing that bogus executive order, trying to make it so people here in Pennsylvania and across America couldn't vote by mail. I sued him. I won, and we protected the right to vote. So again, this was A) in response to a question, and B) based on a history of dealing with a guy who is constantly trying to undermine the right to vote here in our Commonwealth.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I want to ask about you. Brian Fitzpatrick, who represents Bucks County, Republican here in Pennsylvania, describes you as a good man, a friend. He said you're smart, competent. He said he thinks you're going to run for president. And Senator Chris Coons, who was just here earlier, of Delaware said a Democrat. If you win Pennsylvania, you win the whole presidency. It's a good argument for you as a candidate. It's a Republican, It's a Democrat speculating. Are they wrong to speculate like that?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, I wouldn't be focused on speculating. I'd be focused on these midterms, which is all I'm focused on. You know, we talked here today not just about my re-election, but the fact that I'm working hard to elect four more Democrats to Congress to tilt the balance of power, take the gavel away from Mike Johnson, working hard to win a trifecta here in Harrisburg, something that hasn't been done since 1992. We have some gerrymandered state senate districts, but I'm hopeful that we're going to be able to get that done this time. So my focus has only been on these midterms, both getting myself reelected, but importantly providing a check on this president, a check to his his chaos, his cruelty, and his corruption, and to show that here in Pennsylvania, when you run on a GSD Democratic platform, that you can win up and down the ballot.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you are close to winning re-election. You said you're focused on the midterms, but how soon after you're going to make a call on your own presidential run?
GOV. SHAPIRO:  I appreciate the confidence you have, or Brian has, or Chris has, but the reality is—
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm just talking about the polls.

GOV. SHAPIRO: I always run like I'm 20 points behind. I'm running through the tape. I'm on this bus for 10 days, crisscrossing this Commonwealth. I showed up in a district yesterday that I think Donald Trump won with about 80% of the vote in the last presidential election. I take absolutely nothing for granted. I'm competing everywhere for the support of certainly Democrats, but Republicans and Independents as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're laying out an agenda that would require some time to achieve.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I'm not sure I follow your question.
MARGARET BRENNAN: If you win re-election in this position now to be governor, to get everything done you want to get done, do you have to serve the whole term?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, I'm going to focus on getting done what I've pledged to get done here, and continuing to listen, see, and do, and make a lot of good things happen for the people of Pennsylvania as their governor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: People like me are just going to continue to ask you.

GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, and you're welcome to ask. And look, I'm humbled that you would ask that question. I'm humbled by the responses the senator and the representative gave you. But the only thing I'm focused on is here in Pennsylvania, winning up and down the ballot.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you spoke to the editorial board recently, you said six people were recently charged in the past nine months. They reported as making terroristic threats or ethnic intimidation against you or your family. You've said it has—it's weighed on you.
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What did you mean by that?

GOV. SHAPIRO: You know, a year and a half ago, my family and I finished celebrating our Passover Seder with the community. And you know someone broke into the governor's residence, threw Molotov cocktails throughout the home, destroyed about a third of the residence, and was running through the residence with a metal hammer that he said he was going to use to beat me to death when he found me. And he's behind bars now for the next 50 years. But since that time, even more people have threatened me and my wife, our family. Threatened us based on how I worship, and it weighs on you, certainly, to know that there are people out there trying to do you harm. But I would also tell you, it motivates me to keep doing what I do to not let the bad guys win, to not let those—
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, you look at this campaign right now, some of the rhetoric in states out now- Ohio, in Michigan, it's downright hateful.
GOV. SHAPIRO: It's dangerous. It's dangerous. It's hateful.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, how do you get rid of that? How do you lower that?

GOV. SHAPIRO: I think what you do is- is try and lead by example, as we all here- as we are trying to do here, as I am trying to do here. Try and bring back kindness in the face of the cruelty that we see from this president. I've got profound differences from the person I'm running against, from the president and others, but I don't think engaging in cruelty is the answer. I think it makes everyone less safe. But what I was saying in response to your question a moment ago, it weighs on me, but- but it doesn't control me. In fact, my family and I met before, you know, we decided to run for re-election, and everybody agreed, can't let the bad guys win. We've got to keep going forward. You got to stand up against the hate. You got to lead by example, and you got to try and bring some decency back to this country.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to get to some of the politics here in Pennsylvania in a moment, but I want to ask you quickly about what is happening in Alaska. The Justice Department has now issued subpoenas to people believed to be connected to what the New York Times reported was the Democratic effort to stack Alaska's Senate ballot with candidates to siphon off votes. I know you must have been following this story. The Democratic candidate said she had no knowledge of the scheme. What do you think this does to election integrity, and do you think that this undermines Democrats' argument that they are the party trying to protect election integrity?

GOV. SHAPIRO: I've been focused, obviously, a lot more on Pennsylvania than Alaska, but what we're seeing from Trump is not super different from what we have seen from him here in Pennsylvania- trying to prejudge an outcome, file a bunch of lawsuits to silence the voices of the voters before they've had their say, and he's already showing that he is going to go to court should the result not be what he wants. Because what Trump doesn't like is when someone thinks different than you, or votes different than you, or has a different perspective than you- he tries to go to court to silence those voices.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But in terms of what has been reported by the New York Times, as one Democrat said to me, "may not be illegal, but it looks like dirty pool." Does it look like "dirty pool" to you? I mean, if you saw something like that in this state, you were an attorney general.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I- yeah, well--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Would you try to prosecute?
GOV. SHAPIRO: You're asking- respectfully, I think you're asking two different questions. Is there something illegal here, or is there something that seems sort of political?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

GOV. SHAPIRO: I don't know enough to be able to weigh in on this, but what I do know is that- to weigh in with any new information- I want to be clear, happy to answer your question. But what is clear to me is that Donald Trump tries to use the Justice Department to silence people who disagree with him, to try and silence the voices of those who might make a different choice in the ballot box than he would want.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But I can't imagine you condone these kind of tactics on the Democratic side.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I'm not engaged in it, I'm focused on these races here in Pennsylvania.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let's talk about Pennsylvania. This state is in the midst of one of the worst measles outbreaks the United States has seen in three decades. In this county, a school here had to close for a day earlier this month--
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --because of a confirmed case of measles. This is highly transmissible. How do you get this under control?

GOV. SHAPIRO: We've got five deaths in Pennsylvania. 1,500 people sickened by measles, a disease that was eliminated in the year 2000 in the United States of America, and it's come roaring back, largely because of vaccine misinformation and disinformation promoted by quack conspiracy theorist RFK, who Donald Trump has now put in charge of our nation's healthcare system. Now, here in Pennsylvania, I believe in making sure people have access to the information, that there is vaccines available to them, it is a personal choice if they wish to get it. But what is critically important is that they hear from an actual medical provider, an actual medical expert, not RFK, who can explain that the MMR vaccine, that's the measles vaccine, is highly effective, and the best way to protect yourself against this measles outbreak. Make no mistake; you can draw a straight line between the nonsense that RFK has been spewing for years and now his work as the leading public health official in this country, and people getting sick here in my state and across the country. How do we get control of it--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

GOV. SHAPIRO: --now, it's the second part of your question. You do what we're doing here in the Commonwealth, bringing all of our healthcare partners together, and working to provide actual medical information to people in our Commonwealth, and making sure they get access to the vaccine, and encouraging them to take it. Now, here's some data for you. Typically, our Department of Health, working with our healthcare partners, would vaccinate around 25,000 people a month. Since the measles outbreak and my encouragement, and Dr. Bogen, our health secretary's encouragement to get vaccinated, we're now up to 55,000 vaccines being administered a month. So, Pennsylvanians are doing what we do best: coming together, looking out for our neighbors, and trusting science- something RFK continually tries to undermine.
[STOP DOWN]

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you clashed with HHS Secretary Kennedy in September, pretty publicly. You had a back and forth over what happened, what was driving the measles problem in the state. The CDC now recognizes three measles-associated deaths. That's fewer than the five--
GOV. SHAPIRO: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --that your state health department has seen. You just accepted CDC help. Do you have any regrets about how you handled this?
GOV. SHAPIRO: No, and respectfully, that's not accurate. First, RFK denied that anyone died here in Pennsylvania. Literally poked his finger in the eye of these families here in Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he disputed deaths due to the measles or--

GOV. SHAPIRO: No, first he said- respectfully, first he said I fabricated it. First he said I lied about it, which we didn't. We know these people died. It's been confirmed not just by our state health department, but also by independent coroners. Then they tried to play games with the number of deaths, and you correctly point out that he's only acknowledged three of those deaths. As it relates to working with CDC, we've had people embedded here from CDC in our state Department of Health before the measles outbreak, and we did accept one additional person that they were asking us to accept.
MARGARET BRENNAN: An Intelligence Service Officer, right?

GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah, one- one person to help with tracking. By the way, this isn't like they're sending 1000 people here to vaccinate folks. It was one additional person, and we gladly accepted them and CDC had been here for, you know, again prior to this outbreak. The fact that RFK claims that we're lying about this, he's doing that because it doesn't fit his narrative. Remember, he's the guy who went to Lancaster, the epicenter of this outbreak, and said, "You don't need the vaccine. Just take a bunch of chicken soup, and you'll be fine."
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're talking about before he was HHS Secretary?
GOV. SHAPIRO: This guy- this guy is not fit to be the head of public health in this country. He's not a health expert. He's not a doctor, and he preaches fabricated--
[STOP DOWN]

GOV. SHAPIRO: Look, he is not qualified to serve as America's top public health official. He is not a health expert, and he is constantly undermining public health here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and across the country. He's unfit to lead. Donald Trump should remove him, and that will help all of us do a better job of beating this disease that was eliminated in the United States back in the year 2000, but has come roaring back sadly because of his vaccine misinformation and disinformation campaign.
MARGARET BRENNAN:  But do you worry at all that the degree to which this has now become a political fight or the politicization of health will make it that much harder--
GOV. SHAPIRO: To be clear--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --for you to persuade people to go get the shot, that are so--

GOV. SHAPIRO: Not at all. Not at all. RFK politicized this. RFK is playing games with this. And in fact, if you look at the work we're doing here in Pennsylvania, it's working. We went from vaccinating about 25,000 people a month to over 55,000 people a month because people trust actual public health experts here in Pennsylvania, not the nonsense that is being spewed by RFK Jr.

title: Transcript: Rep. Mike Lawler on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Republican Congressman Mike Lawler. He joins us today from New York. You are in this home stretch of campaigning in one of the most closely watched districts this cycle. Leader Jeffries has singled out your district as a top target for Democrats. Where do you see this headed?

REP. MIKE LAWLER: Well, I think we're going to be victorious on Tuesday night, Margaret. I've done the work, over the last four years, between my staff and I, we've closed over 10,000 constituent cases, brought back over $140 million to the district, passed over two dozen bills, 17 of which have been signed into law. Ask AOC how many she's had signed into law. The fact is, I show up, and my constituents know me. And unlike my opponent, who parachuted into this district from Virginia, I own a home here. I pay taxes. I'm raising my family here. And I think my constituents respect the fact that I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress. I'm the only sitting member of Congress endorsed by a member of the opposing party. Jared Golden endorsed my re-election just a little over a month ago, and I think people know that I've delivered for them, especially when it comes to the issue of affordability, delivering the largest tax cut in American history, including lifting the cap on salt and leading the housing bill, which will increase supply and bring down prices.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, as you just mentioned, affordability is a top issue for voters, no matter what party they are in. We are seeing the economy growing. We're still seeing consumers spend, but for the last six months, we are seeing that wages are not keeping up with inflation. Republicans campaigned on bringing prices down. Why do you deserve re-election? Why does the party deserve trust when prices have only continued to climb?

REP. LAWLER: Well, as we saw under the prior administration, inflation cumulatively rose 21%. So the baseline price of everything went up. Obviously, with the war in the Middle East, it has caused volatility in the oil markets, which- which has resulted in a- in a spike in inflation. But as you just pointed out, we saw significant growth in Q3, 3.4%. Over a million private sector jobs have been created over the past year. We are seeing purchasing power rise, but there's still work to do. And that's why I have focused extensively on what we can do to bring down prices. Number one, we did deliver the largest tax cut. Number two, we did pass the largest housing bill in 36 years to increase supply and bring down prices and increase access to capital. Before the end of this Congress--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The president didn't love that bill.

REP. LAWLER: --we will finalize a permitting- before the end of Congress, this Congress, we will finalize a permitting reform bill, which will increase domestic supply of energy, which directly impacts the prices of everything from manufacturing to transportation to groceries. And one of the problems in New York, Margaret, utilities are up 58% under Kathy Hochul because they shut down nuclear power, they ban natural gas, they blocked pipelines. We are working to rectify that. That will drive down energy prices significantly, which is critical if we're going to bring down inflation and bring down costs.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Healthcare is one of the top three issues for voters. You are one of the Republicans who tried to secure a short-term extension of those Obamacare subsidies that expired at the end of the year. In this cycle, many Democrats are promising that if they win the majority, they will restore some of those lapsed subsidies. Do you support that? Would you work with Democrats to do that?

REP. LAWLER: Oh, absolutely. Look, I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan members of Congress. My best friend in Congress is a Democrat, Josh Gottheimer. We led that effort to negotiate a bipartisan extension of the ACA enhanced premium tax credit. Frankly, Margaret, it was Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer that rejected the bipartisan agreement. They wanted to go for a clean three-year extension with no reforms. The fact is, since the Affordable Care Act took effect, health insurance premiums are up 150% while insurance company profits are up over 2,000%. We need to fix the system.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. LAWLER: I am fully committed to addressing the healthcare costs in this country. It's the biggest driver of costs facing most Americans, and we need bipartisan solutions to actually deal with it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The OBBB, the Big Beautiful Bill, was projected to have increased the uninsured population in your state by about 860,000 people through 2034, so that tax bill also may have hurt that case. But let me ask you about something else--

REP. LAWLER: Well, respectfully, that's just- that's just not an accurate- that's just not an accurate number at all. But moreover, New York spends 80% more on Medicaid than the average of the other 49 states. Even Kathy Hochul admits they have waste, fraud, and abuse in the system with the CDPAP program that went from $10 million to $11 billion in three years.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, that's the Health Research Group KFF. Let me ask about something else. Elon Musk's Political Action Committee has put forward hundreds of thousands of dollars to support you, and your opponent, Cait Conley, has criticized you for your ties to Elon Musk. She says you're refusing to legislate on artificial intelligence or "superintelligence" to protect Elon Musk. How do you respond to that allegation?

REP. LAWLER: Well, first of all, Cait Conley is the AI candidate for the AI industry. She's the one being paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by two AI companies that she won't even tell the voters what she did to earn those contracts--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, what does Elon Musk expect for that?

REP. LAWLER: --secondarily, I'm leading on this issue- second, wait a minute. Well, first of all, it's an outside group, so I've had no communication with anybody that's spending in this race. Second of all, I'm the one leading on these issues with Josh Gottheimer, the Stop Rogue AI Act to set national standards with respect to these rogue agents and bots, and secondarily for the frontier models to require mandatory testing. Third, Cait Conley has violated federal election law by setting up a JFC with the House Super PAC, the House Democrat Super PAC, and she is spending out of that on campaign ads, millions of dollars. And lastly, Margaret, in the last week, a Democrat Super PAC popped up. They have not filed with the FEC in clear violation of election law, spending millions of dollars saying that I support amnesty for criminal illegal aliens. It is a straight-up lie--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who is behind that?

REP. LAWLER: --they are trying to drive down Republican turnout. These are Democrats supporting this. They did this two years ago, and they're doing it again. American Forge Group. This is a straight-up fraud perpetrated on the voters, like they're doing in Alaska.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. LAWLER: And frankly, the FBI and the Department of Justice have informed us that they are investigating it--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
REP. LAWLER: --and it should be investigated.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Alright.
REP. LAWLER: They are violating election law, so people should be focused--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REP. LAWLER: --very clearly on what is actually happening in our elections.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, we did ask the Conley campaign about that, and they told CBS they had nothing to do with the mailers being sent out. But we will ask the Justice Department as well. Thank you, Congressman Lawler.
REP. LAWLER: And they didn't condemn it either. Yep. Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We will be watching your race, sir. Back in a moment.

title: Creditor has "taken control" of forever cruise
summary: Residents of Villa Vie Odyssey, which remains stuck in Cambodia, have been informed the cruise ship is now under control of its lender, CBS News has learned.
story: Residents of Villa Vie Odyssey — which remains stuck in Cambodia —  have been informed the cruise ship is now under control of its lender, according to a message sent to residents and obtained by CBS News.

The ship will soon be moved from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned off, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Company leadership, however, said they're optimistic they can get the ship back — if they find an operational partner.
"This is a 30- to 90-day process, and, during that process, we have time to get a restructure done," Mike Petterson, the company's founder and executive chairman, told CBS News.
Passengers had only the weekend to remove all of their belongings from the ship before it became inaccessible to them, as the lender took over the operational costs of the ship.

"They have now the responsibility to pay the crew, fuel and the operations of the vessel and safekeeping of the vessel," Petterson said, stressing that they're exploring options to keep the ship going. "They would be willing to work with a funded plan — they're not out of negotiations — it's not like you get your car repossessed and you can't get it back."
Some passengers expressed frustration with the company's optimistic tone and worried it gave some residents a sense of "false hope."

"The lender has taken possession of the ship, but that does not mean the Odyssey's future has been decided," the message to residents read, in part. "No sale has been scheduled. We believe there is time to bring forward a viable plan and are working to do that."

An effort by a group of residents to buy the ship from the company also failed, after a lender denied them funding, according to sources who spoke with CBS News. The effort had received pledges from 169 residents who were willing to put more money into the project.

Internal communications reviewed by CBS News showed the ship was in financial distress for at least three months prior to Cambodia. Now, additional documents show that the company had a sense of urgency in getting more residents to provide even more funds.

During a meeting that took place in early August, the company wrote in an internal PowerPoint presentation: "A significant new line of inquiry is the need to distinguish actual inability to contribute from unwillingness to contribute further."

Joel Greiff from Naples, Florida spent $350,000 on a cabin on board, but he spent just 26 days on the ship after moving into it in October. Greiff told CBS News he paid an initial deposit in August 2025 and paid the remainder in May 2026.
In late July, Greiff said he received a message from the company about its financial woes. At the time, the company was asking residents for more money to keep the ship afloat.
"I sell my RV on August 3rd and I'm like — oh," Grief said. "This is gonna fail. Every sign is there."
Since being kicked off the ship, he has found a place to live in Kompat, Cambodia.
"I went and found a place to stay for $200 a month. Beautiful place," he said. "It's right on the river. It's what I wanted and what I needed."
Greiff said he has come to terms with the fact that he may never see the money he invested in the ship again.
"I do not feel ill will, I just feel that they don't know how to run a business whatsoever," he said. "They might want to contemplate never running a business again."

It is still unclear what will happen to the Odyssey next, but, prior to becoming stranded in Cambodia, Residential Cruise Holdings, the parent company of Villa Vie, was in the process of acquiring at least one additional cruise ship and working on two residential cruise projects.

"I don't have any update on that," said Petterson. "Our focus is 100% on the Odyssey. Villa Vie was entirely capitalized by the residents themselves. There is no stakeholder outside of the residents."
A Chapter 11 bankruptcy for Villa Vie would cost the ship about $3 million for the first 60 days of the process, according to the message sent to residents.

"The plan we are pursuing is to support those operations through DIP financing and resident maintenance collections," the message read. "The debt and legal issues are serious, but they do not erase the value of the ship, the resident community or the opportunity to build a stronger operating model. A structured transition with new capital and experienced operators can address the challenges and create a path forward."

Petterson said the company is entirely owned by employees and residents, "so, when there is a financial need, residents are by definition the shareholders of the company and are naturally asked as shareholders to contribute."
This story published first on CBS News at 2:42 p.m. on Nov. 1, 2026.

title: Transcript: Sen. Bernie Sanders on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Bernie Sanders, Independent of Vermont, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Bernie Sanders, Independent of Vermont, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We are just hours away from voters in 50 states going to the polls for an election that could shift the balance of power here in Washington. We begin with someone who has been on the campaign trail quite a bit, although he is not up for reelection. That's Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders, who joins us from Burlington. Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR BERNIE SANDERS (I-VT): Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I've been told you've hosted telerallies, town halls for Maine and Michigan this weekend. Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed. You're focused as well on Florida and Minnesota. Why Florida, since it is likely GOP according to CBS numbers, and CBS also rates Minnesota as likely Dem. Why focus there?

SEN. SANDERS: Well, I don't take anything for granted. I think Angie Nixon in Florida is running a great grassroots campaign. She pulled off a huge upset in the Democratic primary. I think she has a real chance to win the general election. She is mobilizing working-class people all over this country, and she's talking about the right issues. And those issues are true in Minnesota. They're true in Florida. They're true in Vermont. People are disgusted and frustrated with an economy in which the billionaires have never ever had it so good. Elon Musk now owns more wealth alone than the bottom 53% of American households, while millions of people today are struggling to put food on the table, pay for, you know, pay to fill up their gas tanks, pay for rent. So what Angie is talking about, what Troy is talking about is an economy that works for all. That's resonating.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, out in Michigan, there appears some inner Democratic Party squabbles that are ongoing here around the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. There was a back and forth over the weekend with Congresswoman Haley Stevens. She lost the primary, but she continues to make public her deep misgivings about backing him now, citing concerns about his ads and his views on Israel. At this point, is the Democratic Party just too divided to pull off a win in Michigan? Is it getting in its own way?

SEN. SANDERS: No, I think- No, I think the over, you know, Haley Stevens lost a very, very close primary. I can understand being upset about that, but I think two days before the election, where people all over Michigan understand that this is the most important midterm election, perhaps in the history of the United States, because we are taking on the most dangerous president that we've ever had, somebody who's an authoritarian, does not believe in the Constitution or the rule of law, who wants to give massive tax breaks to billionaires, throw 15 million people off their health care, that they had started an illegal, unconstitutional war in Iran. So, what the people in Michigan understand, sure, we have disagreements with Abdul on this or that issue, but from what I can see, all over the state people are standing up. They're going to stand with Abdul, take on somebody who will be nothing more than a rubber stamp for the Trump administration. That's Mike Rogers.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, just want to clarify there Haley Stevens has been criticizing ads associated and endorsing Abdul Sayed [sic] that he has said are- are not his ads, but she's still criticizing him for them.
SEN. SANDERS: Right. But, I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah go ahead.
SEN. SANDERS: Right, and he had nothing to do with those ads.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SEN. SANDERS: But Margaret, I was in Michigan last week--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. SANDERS: --and I got to tell you, if you want to look at ads in Michigan, I have never in my life seen such disgusting, racist, fearmongering ads as those that are taking place in Michigan right now. They are calling Abdul El-Sayed, who is a medical doctor, they're calling him a terrorist, a jihadist, really disgusting things. And the- the fact that any Republican would stand behind those horrible ads is a disgrace.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, the rhetoric is extraordinary. El-Sayed would be America's first sitting Muslim senator if he pulls off a win here. He has been accused, though, of ties to a Sunni Islamist group known as the mother- Muslim Brotherhood. He has distanced himself. He has disavowed it. But I want to play for our viewers something. Senator Cruz of Texas warned against El-Sayed being given any access to classified intelligence if he wins. Listen.
[BEGIN SOUND ON TAPE]
TED CRUZ: And if I am correct that he is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Michigan does not need a senator who's on the side of the terrorists.

BERNIE MORENO: This character Abdul  El-Sayed can be nowhere near Washington D.C. Do you think he understands that concept that our rights come from God Almighty? That Jesus came here for our salvation.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, do you think that El-Sayed could actually govern if his colleagues in the Senate are this vitriolic?

SEN. SANDERS: I mean that- I just got to say, what Cruz and Trump and Vance and others are saying is disgusting. It really is. And again, I don't care if you disagree with Abdul- he believes in Medicare for all, he believes in taxing billionaires. Fine, you disagree with him on that, that's fine. But that level of racism, overt, absolute racism, is frankly disgusting and should appall every decent American. The fact of the matter is that Abdul is running an extraordinary campaign, and I think what you're going to see is a good victory in Michigan for him. People will rebel against that type of ugliness.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I appreciate your clarity when it comes to racism. I do want to point out that some Americans hear any criticism of sending aid to Israel and the words that the candidate has used as anti-Jewish hate, and they believe that that's scapegoating as well. How do you respond to that?

SEN. SANDERS: Well, you know, for me, it's a little bit personal. I am Jewish. My father's family was wiped out by Hitler. Anti-Semitism is an extraordinarily disgusting and dangerous ideology that has killed millions and millions of lives in the last century. We cannot tolerate anti-Semitism period. But the reality is that right now in Israel you have a right-wing extremist government led by Netanyahu, who, in my view, and the view of many experts, has in fact committed genocide against the Palestinian people. To be critical of a racist extremist government in Israel, and to say that American taxpayers should not spend a nickel supporting that government is not anti-Semitism, it is attacking a right-wing government, and I would say the same about any other government on earth. Does not reflect the nature of the religion of the people who are in that country.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it.
SEN. SANDERS: So I reject that. You can criticize Netanyahu, and you're not anti-Semitic.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it. I want to ask you about the next Congress. Senator Dan Sullivan told CNN today that he will accept the results in the Alaska U.S. Senate race, the certification of which the Justice Department has said it may challenge. But we're already hearing from Republican Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana, that there "was fraud perpetrated against the people of Alaska, and under no circumstances should Mary Peltola be seated if she wins in a fraudulent manner." She argues, as you know, she has no knowledge of this Democratic effort to stack the ballot in Alaska from- and to hurt the incumbent, though an aide told the New York Times that the candidate did indeed know. Bottom line: What do you expect the Senate to do if she wins? And does all this mess really hurt the Democratic argument that they have a moral high ground on election integrity?

SEN. SANDERS: Yeah, frankly, what the Democrats did in Alaska seems to me to be pretty dumb, but it goes- this is- it's not illegal. It's what happens in every election. Right now in Ohio, there is a gentleman who is running, who is, as I understand it, don't know him, claiming to be a socialist, fine. And Republican Super PAC is putting money into his election. So why in Ohio is a Republican, a right-wing super PAC, funding a socialist? The answer is obviously- obvious. They want to take votes away from Sherrod Brown. Is this a good thing to do? No, it is not a good thing to do. It's a stupid thing to do--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Should there be an investigation--
SEN. SANDERS: --What's going on in Alaska is--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --of Alaska?

SEN. SANDERS: No, that's the decision- The federal government does not get involved in state elections. And you have a president who, in fact, denied that he lost the election in 2020 against Biden. For him to be deciding what is a fair election or not is a little bit absurd. People of Alaska can make that decision themselves.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Senator Bernie Sanders, thank you very much for your time today.

title: Rioters loot stores in Germany amid cost of living protests
summary: After a largely peaceful protest, violence broke out between police and demonstrators in Germany.
story: Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.

The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.

Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

title: Inside the U.K. movement to pardon women executed for witchcraft centuries ago
summary: In total, across England and Scotland, around 5,000 women convicted of witchcraft were executed, some by hanging and some by burning.
story: Just outside of London sits Maidstone, a quiet country town in a peaceful corner of southern England.
But around 400 years ago, Maidstone was the scene of witch hunts in the literal sense of the phrase.
Records show that more than 20 women convicted of witchcraft were hanged in Maidstone. Witch hunts reached their peak in England in the 1600s.
In total across England and Scotland, around 5,000 women convicted of witchcraft were executed, some by hanging and some by burning.

"They were usually single women, spinsters, or widows, usually without a man to stick up for them," Claire Kehily, a member of the Maidstone Borough Council, told CBS News. "... They were easier to target."
Inside Maidstone's town hall, Kehily showed CBS News a prison cell, reconstructed from an earlier medieval building where accused witches were held before trial.
Now Kehily and her fellow councilors are lobbying the U.K. government and planning to petition King Charles III for an official pardon for all of Maidstone's convicted witches.

"It matters because it was a miscarriage of justice," Kehily said. "The crimes they were accused of they couldn't have been guilty of. And they had no way of being found innocent in many of the cases. This is 400 years ago. But there are still miscarriages of justice. There are still, to these days, people being scapegoated for things."

America's most famous witch trials were in the 1690s in Salem, Massachusetts. Their memory was revived by Arthur Miller's play "The Crucible," an allegory for the political witch hunts led by Sen. Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s.
All of the falsely accused witches in Salem have since been pardoned. But in the U.K., not a single convicted witch has been exonerated.
Samantha Harris, the collections manager at Maidstone Museum, showed CBS News the official record of a witch trial in the town in 1652.
"There had to always be someone to blame," Harris explained, saying that natural disasters or illnesses were often blamed on these women.
"Death of pigs, cattle," Harris said. "... We were scapegoating and blaming people that were often quite vulnerable."
Harris said that for her, getting the women pardoned is personal.

"Being single, being independent, these are things that would have been seen as threatening," Harris said. "I probably would've been targeted absolutely as a witch at the time … If we don't learn from the past, what's to say things won't be recurring again in the future? There's a lot to learn from history."

title: Residents evacuated from Russia-occupied city back in Ukraine
summary: The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus before returning to Ukraine, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
story: Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war. It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.

Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.

Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

title: French police clash with some protesters again as demonstrations continue
summary: Police said about 70,000 people demonstrated in Paris alone. France's interior ministry said about 320,000 people rallied nationwide.
story: French police fired tear gas and clashed with some protesters on Saturday as thousands marched across France again in largely peaceful demonstrations against soaring living costs and police violence.
Police said about 70,000 people demonstrated in Paris alone. France's interior ministry said about 320,000 people rallied nationwide.

In the southern port city of Marseille, demonstrators clashed with police. In Lyon, France's third-largest city, people threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire tear gas, according to a journalist at the scene. In the southern city of Toulouse, police used water cannon against an unauthorized protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators, some of them in costume.

Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night, The Associated Press reported. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays.

In Paris, thousands of people, some wearing costumes ranging from Spider-Man to Frankenstein, walked through eastern Paris as a helicopter circled overhead. Placards read: "No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak" and "Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween." Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has accused French President Emmanuel Macron's government of "taking an increasingly authoritarian turn," joined the march.
"We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students' demands, yes to giving citizens a voice," Camille Guerin, 31, said in the western city of Nantes.
In the northern French city of Lille, 47-year-old Aurelie Herrmann danced at the protest.
"I dance because on television they only show damage and destruction, whereas you can perfectly well demonstrate in good spirits," she said.

An aide to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that police had prepared for street violence on a scale "comparable" to the unrest two weeks ago, when shops were looted and public buildings set ablaze. Nunez said authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening that urged protesters to spark a "revolution."
Some shopkeepers again prepared by barricading their businesses.
"Everyone is staying home. No one is going to come and buy anything," said Wael Boubaker, a cafe employee in eastern Paris, as he covered a storefront with plywood panels.
Alain Di Crescenzo, president of France's chamber of commerce, said business owners were worried.
"Shopkeepers can't wait for Saturday to be over," Di Crescenzo told broadcaster France Inter.
Protests come as elections near
The demonstrations come in a febrile political climate, with presidential elections less than six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading the polls.

The protest movement, bringing together activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on the rising cost of living, inequality, and deteriorating learning conditions.

Following a security clampdown and serious injuries to some protesters, the movement broadened its demands to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest. This week, student protesters complained that the police did not authorize a march through the center of the French capital, and vowed to stage new blockades of high schools and universities next week.
With the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in its debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.
Similar youth-led demonstrations have been seen across Europe in recent weeks. Thousands of young Germans took to the streets nationwide on Saturday.

title: $6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
summary: A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was likely carried out by North Korea, according to a blockchain intelligence firm.
story: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?

In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
The FBI on Saturday also accused TraderTraitor of being behind the attack, saying the hackers have been converting the stolen funds into Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency.
The hackers are preparing the funds for "further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.

Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"

Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: Pro-Palestinian protesters arrested outside U.S. Embassy in London
summary: More than 100 people took part in the protest, with many holding signs reading: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
story: Dozens of people were arrested at a protest outside the U.S. Embassy in London on Saturday in support of the proscribed group Palestine Action, police said.
London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement that 48 people had been arrested and the majority of the arrests were related to individuals expressing support for a proscribed organization.
"Officers remain at the scene and are continuing to make arrests," it said.
More than 100 people took part in the protest, with many holding signs reading: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
Some protesters could be heard applauding and chanting "free, free Palestine" when people were taken away to police vans.

The U.K. government outlawed the direct-action protest group last year as a terrorist organization. The ban makes membership in or support for Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Demonstrators also held a vigil in support of Palestine Action outside the U.S. Consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland, holding placards akin to those in London. No arrests were reported there, but Police Scotland said inquiries to identify people seen wearing T-shirts and holding banners showing support for a proscribed organization were ongoing.
"Evidence is being reviewed and further action will be taken as appropriate," it said.

The protests came before an appeal on Nov. 4 at the Supreme Court against Palestine Action's designation as a terror group. Supporters say the ban is draconian and it violates their freedom of speech.
In August, the U.S. government announced sanctions against Palestine Action, designating it as a terror group.
Palestine Action, founded in 2020, aims to stop U.K. military support for Israel, which it says is committing genocide against the Palestinians — an accusation Israel strongly denies.
The group says it aims to stop genocide by disrupting "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex."

In 2024, its activists broke into a factory owned by Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems UK, smashing equipment with sledgehammers and crowbars. In June 2025, activists broke into a Royal Air Force base, sprayed red paint into the engines of two tanker planes and caused further damage with crowbars.

title: Family of real estate CEO wounded in Toronto home invasion, officials say
summary: A search is underway for three armed men who broke into a mansion in Toronto belonging to a real estate CEO in the early morning hours Thursday and attacked and injured the family inside, authorities said.
story: A search is underway for three armed men who broke into a mansion in Toronto belonging to a real estate CEO in the early morning hours of Thursday and attacked and injured the family inside, authorities said.

The suspects, who were masked, forced their way through a back entrance of the five-bedroom home in the Bridle Path neighborhood at around 3:40 a.m. local time, wielding guns and a hammer, Toronto police said.
Once inside, police said they went to the second floor of the home and confronted 75-year-old David Morton; his wife, 64-year-old Doriana Morton; and their two adult daughters, Maggie and Cristina.
"There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."
The home invasion is believed to have been an attempt to steal property, Smith said in an update Saturday, as opposed to an attempt to target the individuals who lived there.
Police said David Morton, CEO of the MAC Group, and his daughters, ages 28 and 26, tried to fight off the intruders when shots were fired.
All three sustained gunshot wounds, Smith disclosed. And in a separate statement Friday, David Morton said that all four family members were also attacked by the suspects with the hammer.
David Morton said that he and his two daughters were still hospitalized Friday with gunshot wounds, but he did not provide details on their conditions.

"What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience," David Morton said in his statement. "... It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home."

The three male suspects, all believed to be in their 20s and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene in an SUV, police said. On Saturday, Smith said one of the suspects they are looking for is 23-year-old Dejon Richards.

Richards is believed to have been accidentally shot in the shoulder by one of his accomplices during the incident, according to Smith. Richards went to the hospital, where he was interviewed by police, but they could not establish a connection to the incident and he was later discharged.
"All these houses have good security," Cecil Hawkins, a former resident of Bridle Path, said. "So I'm kind of surprised. Shooting people in the house, it just seems mind-boggling."
According to Toronto police, there have been 119 home invasions so far in 2026, up 32.2% over this time last year.

Thursday's home invasion happened in the same neighborhood where a mansion belonging to rapper Drake was targeted in multiple break-in attempts in May 2024. A security guard for Drake was also wounded in a shooting outside the home at that time. Superstar singer Celine Dion also owns a house in that neighborhood.
