title: Blood sugar spikes may be tied to everyday habits you can control, expert says
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how post-meal glucose spikes, insulin resistance and sleep apnea are deeply connected, plus the 10-minute walking habit.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
Everyday habits — from what you eat for breakfast to how much you sleep — can have a significant impact on blood sugar levels, according to a metabolic health expert.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic health, while frequent or prolonged spikes and drops can contribute to health complications.

Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert, told Fox News Digital that understanding how food, exercise, sleep and stress affect blood sugar is key to keeping levels in check.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE
LaValle recommends monitoring blood sugar after meals, known as postprandial glucose, to better understand how different foods, beverages and eating habits affect blood sugar levels.
"Do I spike more from eating rice, or do I spike from eating quinoa? How much can I eat?" he said. "I think that's a foundational issue."
Stable glucose levels are essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic balance, while spikes and drops can contribute to long-term health effects. (iStock)
The metabolic health expert noted that insulin resistance occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin, a process that can be influenced by inflammation in the body.
Normally, insulin helps move glucose from the bloodstream into muscle cells, where it can be stored as glycogen for later use.
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE

LaValle said he’s a "big believer" in eating a higher-protein breakfast rather than one that’s heavy in carbs, pointing to naturally elevated cortisol levels in the morning and their potential impact on blood sugar.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," he added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

One of the simplest lifestyle habits to help lower blood sugar, according to LaValle, is taking a 10-minute walk after eating. Regular exercise is an "obvious" healthy practice, he added, although he acknowledged that it's not easy for everyone.
The expert recommends taking a 10-minute walk after eating to balance blood sugar levels. (iStock)

"It’s easy to say, ‘eat better, exercise, sleep better,’ but then people are working 16-hour days or are single parents, they get home, they open up their pantry and destroy a bag of cookies because that's the first thing they can eat and their blood sugar’s plummeted," he said.
Even a little movement after eating can be beneficial, LaValle said, particularly in a modern world that’s "eliminating the need to move."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
LaValle also emphasized the importance of managing stress, which can contribute to insulin resistance.
Along with healthy eating, exercise and stress management, getting adequate sleep is "huge for glucose regulation," he added.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," the expert advised. (iStock)

"When you don't sleep, and you don’t get enough rest to reset your body for the next day ... all those hormones that are supposed to be getting released get skewed," LaValle said, noting that insulin regulation is particularly affected by inadequate sleep.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
LaValle noted that sleep apnea is often associated with conditions such as diabetes, prediabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, emphasizing the importance of healthy sleep habits.
Hyperarousal of the brain can contribute to insomnia, LaValle added.
Sleep hygiene is important for keeping weight and stress in check, the expert said. (iStock)
For someone who’s "jacked up all day long," feeling overcommitted and anxious, that heightened state of stress can disrupt sleep and, in turn, interfere with glucose regulation.
Inadequate sleep can also affect appetite and eating behaviors, potentially making blood sugar management more difficult.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Then you're going to start to put weight on and then, when you don't get enough sleep, you’ve got to eat more to fuel your brain," LaValle cautioned.
"So you eat more, you're not efficient at packaging that fuel up, you're moving less ... and those are the things that you have control over."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Diagnostic test could flag which men need aggressive prostate cancer treatment and which don't
summary: The Decipher genomic test could help doctors decide which high-risk prostate cancer patients need abiraterone hormone therapy and which can skip it.
story: Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.
A new diagnostic test could improve the prostate cancer experience for millions of men.

Researchers at University College London (UCL) analyzed a tissue-based molecular test called Decipher to determine which men with high-risk prostate cancer were most likely to benefit from stronger treatment — and which might avoid unnecessary medication and side effects.
The analysis focused on abiraterone, a hormone therapy that was shown in the STAMPEDE clinical trial to cut the risk of death in half among men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer.
JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid, held Oct. 23–27.
Not every cancer is alike, and treating someone more aggressively than necessary could have "increased side effects and poorer quality of life," noted a UCL news release.
Adding a hormone therapy called abiraterone to standard treatment for men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer could cut the risk of death in half, the trial found.
Because prostate cancers differ at the molecular level, not every patient benefits from adding hormone therapy.

To determine whether Decipher could help guide that decision, researchers examined test scores from more than 27,000 patients in real-world data and 401 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer who had participated in the STAMPEDE abiraterone trial.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Higher Decipher scores predicted worse outcomes, meaning the cancer is more likely to spread and additional treatment may be valuable. A low Decipher score suggested more intensive treatment may be unnecessary.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Howlett of UCL Cancer Institute commented in a statement that for men with very high-risk prostate cancer, preventing spread of the disease is "critical."
"Understanding who benefits most from additional treatment can make a meaningful difference," she added.
A genomic test could help to personalize treatments for prostate cancer patients, the researchers suggested. (iStock)
The findings suggest that genomic testing could help tailor treatment, according to the researcher.

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment.
Identifying the same pattern in both a large, real-world dataset and a randomized clinical trial strengthens the findings, Howlett noted.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE
"But further validation in other datasets is needed before the test is used routinely to make these decisions," she said.

Elai Davicioni, medical director of urology for Decipher test maker Veracyte, also commented, "We believe this growing evidence gives physicians a stronger reason to use Decipher before making decisions that can affect both cancer outcomes and patients’ quality of life."

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel, who was not involved in the study, also commented on the findings.
"Prostate cancer varies from person to person," he said. "Medical science is increasingly aware that it is not one size fits all."
Localized prostate cancer, which has not yet spread, may contain mutations that predict how aggressive the disease will be and indicate whether it could respond to targeted therapies, Siegel noted.
About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, according to the American Cancer Society. (iStock)

Certain targeted therapies are being used more with widespread prostate cancer, according to the doctor, as they include "more powerful anti-androgens, which works not just on the testes, but on the adrenals as well."
Hormone therapies have "significant side effects," including fatigue, and "don’t always help," he added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Siegel said the study’s strength was its combination of a randomized treatment group with Decipher testing, which helped identify in advance which patients were most likely to respond to intensive hormone therapy.
"This is the personalized, precise approach of the near future," he said.
Many men, but not all with high-risk localized prostate cancer, will have a cancer recurrence after local therapy, according to the doctor. (Getty Images )
Dr. William Dahut, M.D., chief scientific officer at the American Cancer Society, noted that many men with high-risk localized prostate cancer will have a recurrence after local therapy.

"This study shows that by combining drugs that interfere with the male hormone testosterone with standard therapy, the risk of cancer recurrence decreases," the Maryland-based doctor, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Traditionally, if a more intensive therapy benefits some patients, it is offered to all men — even though only a subset may actually benefit, according to Dahut.

"However, a diagnostic test can greatly improve the treatment experience for a patient by potentially only subjecting patients to more intensive therapies whose genomic test predicts the greatest risk of recurrence," he said.
Dahut encouraged patients to speak with their doctors about intensive therapy to decrease the risk of cancer recurrence, as well as to ask about available genomic testing.

The doctor noted that since the study was conducted with a drug to block testosterone and the oral drug abiraterone, it's "unclear whether the Decipher test would be as accurate with other possible combinations that a patient might receive."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death behind lung cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits
summary: National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.
story: Blue Zones Founder Dan Buettner explores why women in a small Italian village are reaching age 100 at remarkable rates, highlighting the importance of friendships, shared responsibilities and everyday movement.
National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.
In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.
PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS
A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.
The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.
Bolotana’s hilly streets encourage residents to walk as part of their daily routines. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.
They move throughout the day: Residents walk steep streets to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes.
They eat a largely plant-based diet: Beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil are traditional staples.
They stay socially connected: Residents regularly gather with friends, family and neighbors through meals, church and community activities.
"Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better."
The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.
AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED
"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."
The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.
Bolotana, Sardinia, is home to ancient olive groves. (Marisa Montibeller)
What sets Bolotana apart

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.
Dan Buettner, middle, is pictured with two centenarian women of Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."
Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.
GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."
As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.
Bolotana church culture connects its residents to faith and to each other. (Marisa Montibeller)

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.
"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."
The Bolotana diet
Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.
DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT
"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."
Dan Buettner prepares a traditional minestrone with Anna Maria Filia in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.
In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Giaccomo Nieddu maintains an ancient olive grove in Bolotana. The oil contains unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids, which researchers are studying for possible links to longevity. (Marisa Montibeller)
Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.
‘Not chasing’ longevity
Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.
"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."
Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.
"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."
Bolotana residents walk steep hills for everyday tasks and socialize regularly. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.
Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.
Centenarians Salvatore and Nina spend time socializing daily in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Connecticut Dem Sen Chris Murphy hospitalized Saturday for stroke
summary: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was rushed to Johns Hopkins after suffering a stroke Saturday while attending his son's hockey game, his chief of staff says.
story: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke and was taken to a hospital on Saturday. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized after experiencing a stroke, his chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement released Sunday.

Murphy, who is not running in the midterms but has been stumping for Democrats, began feeling numbness in his arm Saturday afternoon while at his son’s hockey game and was taken to a local hospital before being transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring, according to Allison Herwitt.
WHAT TO DO IF SOMEONE IS HAVING A STROKE, AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALED DEBATE-NIGHT FEARS
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., talks with reporters during votes in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," she said in a statement.
"The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery."
Murphy was first elected to the Senate in 2013 and has been viewed as a potential 2028 Democratic presidential primary candidate.

He has spent the past several weeks on the campaign trail with Democrats as he stumped to help retake control of the Senate majority in the midterm elections. He had been scheduled to campaign for Democrats in New Hampshire on Sunday.

title: 'Squad' rakes in record $2.35M while slamming the door on cop donations
summary: The Squad Victory Fund raised a record $2.35 million this cycle while explicitly barring donations from the Fraternal Order of Police union.
story: Panelists Meghan Hays and Tiffany Smiley discuss how Democratic socialist candidates receive millions in progressive political contributions on ‘America Reports.'
Hey cops, your money's no good here.

A joint fundraising committee for four progressive House Democrats has raised a record $2.35 million so far this election cycle, while barring donations from the Fraternal Order of Police, according to federal filings and the committee’s disclosure.

The Squad Victory Fund is authorized by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.; Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.; Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass.; and Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. The fundraising gives the four lawmakers and their allied political groups a shared vehicle to collect and distribute campaign contributions.
ILHAN OMAR’S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME
"Squad" members of Congress Tlaib, Omar and Ocasio-Cortez. (AP Photo/Amanda Andrade-Rhoades, File; Photo by Scott Heins/Getty Images; AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis)

The fund’s donor rules also make clear which groups it says it will not accept money from, and one is the Fraternal Order of Police, the nation’s largest police organization. It also bars donations from corporations, federal lobbyists and fossil fuel interests. The disclosure does not explain the FOP exclusion.
SOCIALIST PRIMARY SWEEP SPARKS LAUNCH OF NEW RESOURCE LAYING OUT WHAT’S AT STAKE IN 2026
The Squad Victory Fund says it will not accept contributions from the Fraternal Order of Police, the nation’s largest police organization. (Tom Brenner/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

The fund’s other participants include four allied PACs. Contributions are generally divided equally among the eight participants, with each slated to receive 12.5%, though donors may designate their contributions for a specific participant.
The fund has raised $2,351,388.02 in the 2025–2026 election cycle, its highest total to date, according to its FEC summary.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., US, on July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Through March 31, 2026, it had spent about $1.6 million and reported roughly $68,000 in cash on hand. The committee remains active, so those figures may change.
Contributions are not tax-deductible, the disclosure notes.

title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers at Detroit church
summary: Haley Stevens stood next to Mike Rogers at a Detroit church after Abdul El-Sayed's campaign withdrew her invitation over the antisemitic ad dispute.
story: Dem Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks after Rep. Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers
Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday amid Democratic infighting that has roiled the Michigan Senate race.

The endorsement came on the heels of Stevens' appearance alongside Rogers at Detroit’s Perfecting Church, where Fox News confirmed she attended a service. Stevens lost in the primary to fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and has been critical of his unwillingness to condemn the overt antisemitism of some of his supporters.

"Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul [El-Sayed] said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away and he's right. And that's why I'm endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said in a video posted on X.
Stevens said she remains "a very proud Democrat" who loves Michigan but could not support El-Sayed, citing his backing from political streamer Hasan Piker.

"I'm honored to have Haley Stevens support today. I'm honored to have earned that vote," Rogers told reporters gathered outside the church. "This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else," he added.
The appearance came after Stevens was disinvited from a planned church event with El-Sayed, the man who narrowly defeated her in Michigan’s August Democratic primary.
The reversal left Stevens at the same church as Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent.
HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'
Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens appears alongside GOP rival Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Nov. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Rogers for Senate)
Stevens has pressed El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices, which she called antisemitic.
El-Sayed said the ad was not produced by his campaign and that he disagreed with its contents.
Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., who helped organize the planned appearance, said Stevens was asked to skip it after the dispute became a distraction and upset the church’s bishop.
FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY

Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan and Abdul El-Sayed faced off in the Aug. 4, 2026, Democratic Senate primary in the Great Lakes battleground state. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
El-Sayed’s campaign also asked Stevens to stay away from its remaining events.
Stevens fiancé, Jason Turkish, has previously endorsed Rogers and appeared at a Rogers campaign event, saying he could not support El-Sayed because of his positions on Israel.

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has faced criticism over his stance on Israel, but some Jewish leaders think members of their community should put aside their differences and vote for him. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
The dispute has put a spotlight on Democratic divisions in a close Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber.

title: Inside top Trump bulldog’s plan to save House GOP majority and defy history
summary: Jim Jordan has barnstormed 115 districts across 34 states this election cycle, raising millions for House Republicans fighting to keep their majority.
story: GOP congressional candidate Mike Beltran and Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, discuss Republican momentum in Florida’s 14th district on ‘Fox Report.’
Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, was jumping into the car with his wife on the way to the airport when he took a call from a Fox News Digital reporter on Thursday morning.

It’s a microcosm of what the House Judiciary Committee chairman’s recent weeks and months have been: a seemingly endless series of planes, trains and automobiles across the U.S. campaigning for fellow Republican lawmakers.

House Republicans’ senior leadership is crisscrossing the country raising money and support for their members to win Tuesday’s midterm elections. Jordan, though he’s not part of the trio, has much the same schedule.

"Sometimes they’re fundraisers, sometimes they’re rallies, sometimes they're both," Jordan said. "We're doing everything we can just to help our team win, because… if these Democrats get in there, my real concern, I gotta be honest, is what they're gonna try to do to the structure of our government."
MAPPED: TRUMP’S NONSTOP CAMPAIGN BLITZ SWEEPS KEY STATES
Rep. Jim Jordan leaves a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 10, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

A source familiar with Jordan’s travel schedule said he’ll have gone to 115 districts across 34 states during this election cycle. That includes 19 consecutive days on the road in the lead-up to Nov. 3 in states such as Washington, Oregon, Texas, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois and South Carolina.
And despite the diverse areas, Jordan said his message is mostly the same: Republicans cut taxes, secured the border and Democrats will make it all worse.

"We understand things cost a little too much, and we're working on that. But remember, most of that's because of the Biden administration and their record inflation. We're bringing that inflation rate down, but you know, we still understand things, things cost too much, and we're gonna keep working on that," Jordan said.
TRUMP VOTERS REVEAL THEIR BIGGEST FEAR HEADING INTO MIDTERMS — AND IT'S NOT RISING PRICES
"But the big issue we talk about is, if these radicals that now control the Democrat Party, if they get control of the government, the crazy things they're gonna do are just frightening."
And because he’s not a member of leadership, he’s not afforded the same charter flights and police motorcades that come with that job.
While he’s had some private flights, most of Jordan’s travel has been comprised of commercial airlines and long drives between destinations — including sitting in traffic.
He said his favorite travel tunes include the greatest hits of late country star Glen Campbell.
But Jordan said he also uses much of that time texting or calling colleagues, asking how their races are going, and talking to staff about what issues to raise at his next event.
House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, speaks at a press conference with other members of House Republican leadership in Washington, D.C., on May 20, 2025. (Getty Images)
He’s also raised a significant amount of cash for their campaigns, donating $1.97 million to Republicans across the country and $2.65 million to the House GOP campaign arm.
10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY
It comes as House Republicans fight an uphill battle to retain their majority, as multiple political forecasts show Democrats poised to take over the chamber.
Jordan’s volume of travel is notable for someone who is not in senior House leadership, but it’s not a surprise, given his years-long high profile.
"His celebrity status is very helpful," one House Republican previously told Fox News Digital. "When Jim Jordan comes to town for you, you put 300 butts in seats."
Another lawmaker shared a similar figure. Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital that Jordan reached out to him about doing an event in his district that wound up a success.
DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS

"We had a fundraiser in Gastonia and it was very well attended.  A huge crowd, nearly 300 people there — raised a lot of money, a lot of excitement, a lot of enthusiasm, and so I appreciated him coming down to do that," Moore said. His district also saw a visit from House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., which Moore said also raised a significant sum.
Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on March 17, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Jordan has appeared alongside conservatives in deep red districts and moderates in battlegrounds — walking out to Survivor’s "Eye of the Tiger" for many of those appearances — painting a picture of party unity that’s a far cry from his roots as an anti-establishment rebel leading the House Freedom Caucus.
"It’s kind of a Jordan 2.0," the first House Republican said. "He’s just a great citizen of the conference."

A second House Republican told Fox News Digital that a wide range of members see Jordan as a "mentor." They said Jordan’s travels are a mix of Republicans asking him to come out and him extending those offers himself.
"Jim doesn't care if you're moderate or even if you have to lean left to keep your seat, you have to represent your people," the second House Republican said.
Asked whether he’s changed or the party has, Jordan said it was "the overall picture."

"Any differences that exist in the Republican Party are pretty small compared to the differences between Republicans and the left, the hard left, the radical left, which now controls the Democrat Party," Jordan said.
It has also inspired questions about what he wants out of it.
House Republicans and members of the media are widely expecting that Jordan is eyeing a bid for senior leadership after failing to clinch a position in the past.
The U.S. Capitol building on Aug. 7, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
If Republicans lose the majority, he’s expected to run for minority leader, where he’d be Trump’s top defender in Congress.
But Jordan himself has publicly dismissed those notions.

"I’m focused on… Tuesday," he told Fox News Digital. "The way you stop the radicals from making these structural changes to our constitutional form of government, these radical policy positions that they have, the way you stop them is at the ballot box, and that happens on Tuesday."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
And then the conversation ended, because Jordan had to catch a flight to campaign with Republican candidates in Florida that night.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Trump's DOJ makeover hasn't changed where the political cash is flowing — and the gap is growing
summary: Over 75% of Department of Justice employee donations still go to Democratic committees despite Trump administration efforts to root out partisan bias.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on two former FBI officials being charged by the DOJ with lying in the investigation into Hunter Biden's taxes.

The Trump administration has sought to eliminate what it alleges is partisan bias within the Justice Department, but the vast majority of political donations from individuals identifying themselves as DOJ employees are still going to Democratic-aligned committees, according to a Fox News Digital analysis of federal campaign finance records.

Between January 2025 and August of this year, just over 75% of campaign contributions from individuals identifying themselves as Department of Justice employees went to Democratic committees, the analysis of federal campaign finance records found.

Fox News Digital analyzed roughly $300,000 in political contributions recorded by the Federal Election Commission between January 2025 and August 2026 from donors who listed their employer as "Department of Justice," "DOJ" or a variation of those names. Contributions were categorized by the political affiliation of the recipient candidate or committee, while independent-expenditure committees were classified according to the candidates or parties they supported. When exporting data from the Federal Election Commission's dashboard, an option to include donations from "unique individuals only" was selected to filter out duplicative records.

As the Trump administration has progressed, the partisan slant of DOJ donations has become more pronounced. Through 2025, about 70% of donations from those identifying themselves as DOJ staff went to Democratic committees, a figure that rose to just under 90% in 2026, according to Fox News Digital's findings.
TODD BLANCHE EXPOSES HOW AGGRESSIVE BIDEN DOJ TARGETED LOW-LEVEL MAR-A-LAGO EMPLOYEES
Attorney General Todd Blanche listens during a news conference at the Justice Department on Aug. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Attorney General Todd Blanche and his predecessor, Pam Bondi, both claimed that the Trump administration inherited a deeply corrupt DOJ, pointing to allegations that the agency was inundated with political bias under President Joe Biden's tenure.

"There are a lot of people in the FBI and also in the Department of Justice who despise Donald Trump, despise us," Bondi said in early 2025. "Right now, we’re going to root them out; we will find them, and they will no longer be employed."

Critics have pushed back against claims of political weaponization during the Biden administration, arguing that high-profile investigations into President Donald Trump and other conservatives originated from legitimate legal concerns.
DOJ DANGLES MASSIVE SIGNING BONUSES FOR LAWYERS READY TO FIGHT ‘LAWLESS’ CITIES FAR BEYOND DC

Former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi arrives to testify at a closed-door interview with the House Oversight Committee on Capitol Hill on May 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Both of Trump’s attorneys general under his second administration have made strides to recruit a greater number of ideologically aligned lawyers while attempting to push those out who may not be willing to advance the administration’s interests.

In early February 2026, DOJ chief of staff Chad Mizelle publicly encouraged lawyers who "support President Trump" to contact him about becoming federal prosecutors. Stephen Miller amplified the appeal on social media with the caption "patriots needed," and sitting U.S. Attorney Jason Quiñones reposted the appeal alongside the phrase "we are hiring!" Mizelle later defended the approach as ensuring that executive-branch lawyers were in line with the elected president’s agenda.
LEGAL WAR ON TRUMP’S AGENDA GAINS FIREPOWER AS FEDERAL LAWYERS DEFECT TO DEMOCRATS
Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks before President Donald Trump at the David Mack Center for Training and Intelligence on Aug. 14, 2026, in Garden City, New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
The administration's personnel overhaul has coincided with a substantial exodus of attorneys from federal service.
Over 10,000 attorneys have left federal service since Trump took office for a second term.

Fox News Digital reported in July that well over 100 federal attorneys had left the Trump administration for roles in Democratic-run state attorneys general offices. Many of these lawyers took decades of experience with them, prompting concerns that the Trump administration could be depriving itself of the ability to handle highly technical legal matters.
Some of these seasoned former federal lawyers have since joined legal action against the Trump administration.

While a significant number of government lawyers have left federal service under Trump, and some prominent conservatives have joined the administration, campaign finance records show that Democratic committees continue to receive the overwhelming majority of political contributions from donors identifying themselves as Justice Department employees.

Among the most common recipients of donations from those identifying themselves as DOJ employees were Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Emily’s List, a pro-abortion group associated with the Democratic Party. Some conservative committees, such as those in Trump’s network of PACs, were also common targets for Justice Department donors.
DEMOCRAT POLITICOS RERUN UNDERHANDED LEFTIST PLAYBOOK IN EFFORT TO TORPEDO TRUMP’S AG NOMINEE
President Donald Trump speaks during a midterm campaign rally at the Guardian Centers on Oct. 24, 2026, in Perry, Georgia. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Much of the DOJ's work concerns investigations and prosecutions unrelated to partisan politics, and the campaign finance records do not establish whether employees' political preferences have influenced the department's day-to-day operations.
Progressive critics, to the contrary, have alleged that the Trump administration is using the Justice Department to target its political enemies.

"Those who were fired from the Department were fired for a reason. Those who resigned or took the fork in the road option likely aligned more with the priorities of President Biden and would naturally leave, which is common during transitions," a DOJ spokeswoman previously told Fox News Digital. "The administration gave career employees the fork in the road option to intentionally reduce the size of the government and eliminate unnecessary layers of staff who don’t effectively contribute to the mission of aggressively tackling crime."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

title: Americans forced to change clocks again as Senate stalls Trump-backed daylight saving time bill
summary: Trump shared Sen. Tom Cotton's cellphone number to pressure him on the Daylight Saving Time bill, but the Senate still has no clear path forward.
story: Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the ‘Gutfeld’ panel discuss why President Donald Trump called out Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., for a disagreement over daylight saving time.
Daylight saving time has dodged the wrath of President Donald Trump — for now.
As Americans again participate in the twice-yearly ritual of fiddling with their clocks — this time rolling back an hour on Sunday morning — Congress has fallen short of tackling the issue in time.

Earlier this year, the House passed legislation that would allow states to voluntarily observe daylight saving time year-round. But progress on the legislation has ground to a halt in the Senate, even though it’s a popular issue with voters and Trump.
BATTLE OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME ERUPTS AS PUSH TO STOP CHANGING CLOCKS HITS SENATE WALL
President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 23, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

But it’s not for lack of trying. Trump has routinely pressured the upper chamber to pass the bill and re-upped that call earlier this week in the midst of traveling across the country to rally in key states and safe red bastions to urge voters to keep Republicans in power.

"The United States Senate is letting the daylight saving bill die when a vast Majority of the Country want it," Trump said on Truth Social. "Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore. TAKE A VOTE!"

Trump wants the Senate to pass, or at least take a vote on, the Sunshine Protection Act, but it’s facing heavy headwinds from a broad swathe of lawmakers in the upper chamber on both sides of the aisle.
TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END

His pressure campaign got to the point that he shared the cellphone number of one of his top allies, Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, urging supporters to call the lawmaker and demand he work on passing the bill.

"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said in response. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first."

The House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act along bipartisan lines in July. Majorities of Democrats and Republicans voted in favor of the bill, which passed 307 to 117. Just 22 Republicans and 95 Democrats opposed it.

But it’s one of several pieces of legislation that House lawmakers complain has fallen by the wayside in the upper chamber. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., pressed the Senate to take up that bill in comments to Fox News Digital in early October.
TIME ENOUGH AT LAST: WHAT'S NEXT AFTER THE HOUSE PASSES BILL TO DO AWAY WITH DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME?
As Americans turn their clocks back an hour Sunday morning, Congress has once again failed to address the twice-yearly practice of changing the clocks. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Scalise told Fox News Digital, "There's no reason Americans should lose an hour of sunlight at the end of the day when more daylight means more time with our families, more activity for our businesses and safer communities."

"President Trump has been pushing to make daylight saving time permanent, and House Republicans delivered by overwhelmingly passing the Sunshine Protection Act. It's a commonsense change and the Senate should take it up," Scalise said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

And when the Senate returns after the election, lawmakers will have a densely packed schedule crammed with leftover legislation. With floor time being the top commodity in the upper chamber, squeezing the Sunshine Protection Act onto the floor may be a challenge, even without the resistance it already faces.

"The president feels strongly on it like he does a lot of issues," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters earlier this month. "It’s something we’re having conversations about, but there’s no clear path forward or consensus on it yet."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Everything to know about House and Senate control, ballot measures and 2026 Election Day poll closing
summary: Republicans defend slim congressional majorities as toss-up Senate races in Alaska, Texas and Iowa could decide control of the chamber in 2026.
story: Plus, the latest controversy surrounding Troy Jackson’s business dealings, shifting prediction markets, and Mary Katharine Ham joins the program to discuss the midterms, Democrats’ messaging problems, and what comes next for both parties.
In two days, Americans voting in the midterm elections will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years.
Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate.

"If you elect a Republican House and a Republican Senate on Nov. 3, we will continue to put America first every single day," the president pledged on the campaign trail last week. And he claimed if the Democrats take control, "this country will go to hell."
CHECK OUT THE FINAL FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

President Donald Trump looks on as Kentucky Republican congressional candidate Ed Gallrein speaks during a midterm rally at Truist Arena on the Northern Kentucky University campus on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Ky. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

Also up for grabs in this year's midterm elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states (as well as the territories of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands). Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast.
Here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026.
SENATE
Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, with the final Fox News Power Rankings ahead of Election Day rating the race for Senate control a toss-up.

Both parties are three seats short of a majority, according to the forecast. Democrats are favored in 48 seats and Republicans are ahead in 47. The GOP needs to hold 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate.
WHO'S UP AND DOWN IN THE FINAL FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLS
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

If Democrats ride a blue wave to victory by winning most or all of the competitive races, they could potentially come away from the midterms with up to 54 seats. But if Republicans have a good night and defy expectations, the GOP could hold the majority with up to 52 seats, according to the forecast.

Republicans are playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat.
Democrats are on defense in Michigan, which is rated a toss-up, and in Minnesota and New Hampshire, which are listed as Lean Democrat.
HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, and the Power Rankings point to the Democrats retaking control of the chamber.

A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future.

"Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said.
GOVERNORS
There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors.

The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up.
The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings.
DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Five other races are also seen as competitive and rated Lean Democrat. They are Arizona, Michigan and Oregon, where Democrats are playing defense, and Iowa and Ohio, where the GOP is defending open governor's offices.
BALLOT MEASURES

Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia.

Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024.
But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race.
Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release.
More than a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines.
The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare.

Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax.

Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations.

Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions.
California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development.
POLL CLOSINGS
The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET on Election Day, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET.
6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.
7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close.
7:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.

8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.
Voters across the country will cast ballots on Election Day. (Rawpixel/Getty Images)
8:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arkansas.

9 p.m. PT: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.
10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California and Washington state, with the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon also closing.
Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Fox News Power Rankings: Kansas moves to Toss-up, Nebraska moves to Lean R
summary: The Ohio Senate race shifts to Lean D as Sherrod Brown leads Jon Husted, while Kansas and South Carolina move to toss-up in the final rankings.
story: 'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host Griff Jenkins analyzes new Fox News Power Rankings and discusses pathways to Senate control ahead of the midterm elections.
Updated Nov. 1:
We’re updating this forecast to move Kansas from Lean R to Toss-up, and Nebraska from Likely R to Lean R.
Kansas is a conservative stronghold, but Republicans are spending too much time and money relative to other states to conclude that Sen. Roger Marshall has an edge over Democrat Adam Hamilton.
The odds remain in Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' favor in Nebraska. A larger-than-expected swing against the GOP could open the door for independent Dan Osborn to pull off an upset.
We still consider Senate control a toss-up.

Seven states are most likely to decide the majority. On a good night for the Democrats, their ceiling rises to 55 seats. A good night for the Republicans could see them retain control with up to 52 seats.
TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS
It seems like there are two electorates in these midterms.
SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: DEMOCRATS COULD BE RIDING A MIDTERM WAVE. THESE NUMBERS SHOULD TERRIFY THE GOP
The first is frustrated with President Donald Trump and ready to reject Republicans. It includes growing numbers of independent, rural and Hispanic voters who say they’ll vote for a Democrat.
That’s what the latest round of House polling shows, including a survey last week that had Democrats up 11 points on the generic ballot, and Fox’s most recent national poll.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The second electorate is wavering on Republicans but won’t necessarily hand Democrats the Senate. These are the voters in the Midwest and a few other places. They say they prefer the Democrat or Republican in their states by a point or two at most.
Fox News Power Rankings on key issues in the election. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
That’s the right conclusion from most of the battleground Senate polling.
How could both things be true? In other words, if Democrats have such a wide lead in the House, won’t the Senate fall too?

Both are true, and a big lead in the House doesn’t necessarily translate to the Senate. These voters are all in the same electorate, and they only seem divorced from each other because the House and Senate maps are so far apart this year.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG?
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
The president’s declining approval rating and Democratic advantages on the issues will likely deliver them the House, and possibly by many seats.
Those advantages have also allowed the blue team to play in a lot of Senate races that Republicans thought were unreachable, but only to the point of making them battlegrounds.
GOP SENATE MAJORITY FACES FRESH UNCERTAINTY AS 2 KEY RACES TIGHTEN DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS

The road to a Senate majority goes through several states that Trump won by 11 points or more. Democrats can win any of these races. If Republicans turn out and stay loyal to their party, the climb for the left will be steep.
That’s why the Senate is a toss-up. Voters could give Democrats a majority, and maybe with several seats to spare. They could also let the Republicans keep control.
We’ll find out next week.

In his 11-year political career, Trump has triumphed over almost all the threats to his power. The exception was the coronavirus pandemic, which was the top issue for voters in the 2020 election and ushered in the Biden presidency.
It was also one of the few threats that Trump has faced from abroad.

This time, Trump and the Republicans face a new foreign opponent: Iran. The administration’s decision to start joint U.S.-Israeli military strikes against the nation in February has cast a shadow over the GOP.
Fox News Power Rankings on Trump. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

First, it has impacted Trump’s approval rating, which will decide the fate of many congressional Republicans and has fallen since the war began. It was 44% in the last pre-war survey and sits at 36% now.
Fox News Power Rankings on top issues leading up to elections. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The war has also given Democrats advantages on the top issues. In Fox’s October survey, Iran played a role in four issues that more than two-thirds of voters said they were concerned about: inflation (85%), gas prices (83%), government leadership (79%), and the war in Iran itself (75%).
Fox News Power Rankings on political parties. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Most voters said they preferred the Democrats to handle those issues: 16 points on inflation, 12 points on gas prices, 11 points on leadership, and 9 points on foreign policy.
Still, voters are not convinced that the Senate should change hands.

That comes down to the territory. Trump won seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, and seven of them by double digits. That includes Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.
Democrats don’t need to win all of those states to take the Senate, but it’s hard to see how they get to 51 seats without at least two of them.
While former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown leads in Ohio, the other states are close. Turnout, a polling error in either direction or both could decide them.

There are also a lot of undecided voters. In Alaska, Iowa and Kansas, three states with recent high-quality polling, an average of 10% of voters say they haven’t decided who they will support or won’t support the major candidates.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Any guess on how those voters will break at the ballot box is only a guess. All we know from prior results is that the overall electorate leans conservative, so the Democrats have the tougher assignment to bring them over to their side (or keep them at home).
There are far fewer undecided voters in Texas, where last week’s Fox News Poll showed a tied race at 49%-49%.

If Democrats only win two Trump-won battlegrounds, they’ll need to win three other races where former Vice President Kamala Harris delivered single-digit victories in 2024: Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire.

Democrats are ahead in the latter two. Maine could go either way. While Democrats win its presidential races, it could just as easily be considered a Republican state when Susan Collins is on the ballot.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Both parties are short of a majority in this forecast. Democrats are favored in 48 seats and Republicans are ahead in 45.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

On a good night for Democrats, the party would win most or all the toss-ups, taking the majority with up to 55 seats. In that scenario, other competitive states would also come into focus, including Nebraska, and possibly Mississippi.

A good night for the Republicans would see them simply hold on to most of the states they already have, up to a ceiling of 52 seats. The party also has opportunities to flip a couple of states, including Minnesota and New Hampshire.
Five states have moved in Power Rankings forecasts this week.
In Ohio, Brown has enjoyed a lead in three Fox News polls this year, including last week’s survey, which had him five points ahead of Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted at 52%-47%.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Ohio voters are very familiar with Brown, having sent him to the Senate three times. That has made it hard for Husted to campaign on socialism and woke politics, themes that Republicans elsewhere see as their strongest cards to play.
Ohio moves from Toss-up to Lean D.
("Lean D" means the Democrat has an edge, but it’s still a highly competitive race. We define every ranking and the process for setting them on FoxNews.com.)
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
As this week’s Power Rankings previously reported, Republicans already viewed this as an uncomfortably close race. That belief is now widely shared.
The president headed back there to help Sen. Darline Graham in the Upstate, where she underperformed in her primary runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman.
South Carolina moves from Lean R to Toss-up.
Kansas is a conservative stronghold, but Republicans are spending too much time and money relative to other states to conclude that Sen. Roger Marshall has an edge over Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Kansas moves from Lean R to Toss-up.
The odds remain in Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' favor in Nebraska. A larger-than-expected swing against the GOP could open the door for independent Dan Osborn to pull off an upset.
Nebraska moves from Likely R to Lean R.
Mississippi is a Republican stronghold, but Trump’s decision to rally there over other deep red states is a sign that the party thinks it’s competitive.
GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith faces Democratic District Attorney Scott Colom in a race where protein choice has become a breakout issue.
Mississippi moves from Solid R to Likely R.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Democrats are still likely to flip the House this November, and in this forecast, they’re predicted to take at least 223 seats.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Since a good night for the Democrats would see them take most of the toss-up races, they could end up with as many as 240 seats.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
(On a great Democratic night, the party would pick up most of the Lean R districts as well, taking them as high as 252 seats.)

Republicans have 195 seats in their columns. A good night for them would take that total up to around 212. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Nineteen more races have shifted in the Democrats’ direction this week, all on the same themes outlined in the last House update: national and district polling, top-of-the-ticket strength, and rural voter erosion.

The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future. Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle. The district moves from Lean R to Toss-up.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Finally, Ohio’s gubernatorial race is also on the move. The campaign between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was the top story in politics last week after Ramaswamy ran an ad featuring Acton’s mother, who called her daughter a liar.
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Acton has been estranged from her mother since age 12, when she says she and her brother left her family home because her mother’s husband was sexually abusing her. Acton’s brother now appears in a response ad discussing their family history.
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

This ratings change is less about the response to the ad (Ramaswamy and President Trump are supportive of the commercial; most others, including Husted and Gov. Mike DeWine are against it) than it is about the fact that the Ramaswamy campaign felt the need to run it.
While Ramaswamy sat only two points behind Acton in last week’s Fox poll, he’s an average of seven points behind in other high-quality polls since September.
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
The businessman and onetime presidential hopeful has struggled in favorability ratings throughout his political career. This ad is unlikely to help.
