title: Trump prosecutions under Biden set precedent for DOJ’s Alaska ‘Decoy Dan’ probe, ex-FEC chair says
summary: Hans von Spakovsky says Jack Smith's Trump indictment set the precedent for the DOJ's criminal probe into Alaska's "Decoy Dan" Senate race scheme.
story: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy discusses a federal investigation into an alleged ballot-stacking scheme involving Mary Peltola's campaign. The Department of Justice launched a probe into the recruitment of a decoy candidate named Dan Sullivan. Dunleavy comments on the controversy and its impact on the integrity of the state's election.

The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democratic operatives recruited Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, dubbed "Decoy Dan," to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, prompting liberal-leaning election law experts to accuse the Trump administration of federal overreach.

But former Federal Election Commission member Hans von Spakovsky argued that the Biden-era Justice Department’s prosecution of Donald Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election laid the groundwork for the Alaska probe.

"The Justice Department has talked about a potential conspiracy to defraud the voters of Alaska and people are saying, 'Oh, he's got no case. That's a weak case,'" von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital.
"Well, I suggest you do a Google search and pull up the indictment that Jack Smith got against Donald Trump in the District of Columbia. He set a precedent for this."
MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT

Joined by FBI officials and Alaska State Troopers, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman announced at a news conference Friday that the Justice Department has been investigating whether Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired school teacher who will appear on the ballot without a party affiliation, was colluding with Democratic operatives tied to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign.
The Justice Department previously sued Alaska election officials, seeking to block certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses re-election by fewer votes than those cast for Daniel J. Sullivan.

The lawsuit was amended Friday to include reporting by The New York Times that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and senior aides of Peltola's campaign allegedly worked to recruit candidates who could pull votes away from Sen. Sulllivan. Heyman mentioned the Times reporting repeatedly at the news conference.
Mary Peltola launches her campaign as a Democratic candidate for Senate in Anchorage, Alaska, Jan. 17, 2026. (Reuters)
"We are taking that extremely seriously," Heyman said.

Sources at the Justice Department told Fox News Thursday the Trump administration had issued more than 30 subpoeanas in a span of 24 hours as part of its criminal investigation into the alleged collusion, but Heyman did not say at the news conference what criminal charges are being pursued.
"I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not," Heyman said. "That's why we are conducting that thorough investigation."

Von Spakovsky, a former Federal Election Commission commissioner, said potential indictments of Democratic operatives in the Alaska Senate race could rely on federal statutes similar to those Smith, the former special counsel, used in his 2023 indictment of Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the election.

Von Spakovsky pointed to charges of conspiracy to defraud the United States and conspiracy against rights. In Trump’s case, prosecutors alleged that he used fraud and deceit to obstruct the federal government’s process for certifying the 2020 election and conspired to deprive voters of having their lawful votes counted and honored.

Von Spakovsky said prosecutors could potentially apply similar theories in Alaska if they determine that Democratic operatives knowingly recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to confuse voters and divert votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)
ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME

Smith's "indictment is basically along exactly those same lines, claiming that Donald Trump was trying to defraud U.S. voters from fair and honest elections. So, Jack Smith and Democrats, they set the precedent for the kind of investigation Justice Department is doing now."

Aubrey Wieber, executive director of 907 Initiative, a progressive advocacy group running critical ads against Sen. Sullivan, told Alaska Public Media that the news conference announcing the investigation "on the eve of the election" may be stemming from ulterior motives.
"One could say it appears that they are trying to interfere in an election and put their thumb on the scale," Wieber said.

The Justice Department's lawsuit was filed Oct. 22, prompting a parade of condemnations from those who argued the federal government had "no authority" to intervene, with many pointing to the Alaska Supreme Court rejecting the state's push to disqualify Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot.
Special counsel Jack Smith delivers remarks on an unsealed indictment, including four felony counts against former President Donald Trump, Aug. 1, 2023, in Washington. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)
GOVERNOR PROBING 'DECOY DAN' SULLIVAN ELECTION SCANDAL WARNS SYSTEM FLAW HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

"DOJ's theory: Two candidates named Sullivan might confuse voters. The Alaska Supreme Court settled that in June, and the ballot labels the incumbent. DOJ has no role in state election law," Omar Noureldin, senior vice president of policy and litigation at Common Cause, a self-described non-partisan watchdog organization.

Von Spakovsky called recruiting a candidate with the same name as a political opponent a "dirty trick" but said the recruitment itself was not necessarily a criminal violation. He said the legal analysis could change if operatives paid the candidate or provided services to help organize his campaign.

"The place you run into potential issues is not only if you just recruit a candidate, but you’re being paid to recruit that candidate, and you then provide services to help him run his campaign and organize it," Von Spakovsky said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Providing campaign assistance outside of being a volunteer is an in-kind contribution subject to federal reporting and contribution rules. Von Spakovsky said any failure to properly report such contributions could create a separate campaign-finance violation.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Major US children's hospital opens historic detransition clinic after $10M legal showdown
summary: Ken Paxton announced Texas Children's Hospital opened the nation's first detransition clinic as part of a settlement over gender care practices.
story: Kayleigh McEnany and the 'Outnumbered' panel discuss a landmark settlement requiring Texas Children's Hospital to halt gender-transition services and open a first-of-its-kind detransition clinic for youth.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday that the nation’s first-ever detransition clinic has opened at Texas Children’s Hospital after a $10 million settlement with the state.

The announcement comes after Paxton reached a settlement with TCH in May, finalized in August, requiring the hospital to pay $10 million to resolve government claims and separately establish and fund a detransition clinic.

The new clinic provides "detransition-related medical care to patients through age 21, along with detransition-related obstetric and gynecologic care to patients older than 21," according to Paxton's office.

"In accordance with my settlement with Texas Children’s Hospital, the nation’s first-ever Detransition Clinic is now open," Paxton said in a statement. "I will continue to ensure that this clinic provides the care and support that victims of the radical left’s gender ideology deserve.
A LANDMARK TEXAS RULING BREATHES NEW LIFE INTO ONE DETRANSITIONER'S QUEST FOR JUSTICE
Ken Paxton, Texas attorney general and Republican U.S. Senate candidate, during a "Come and Take It Tour" campaign event in San Antonio, Texas, Oct. 18, 2026. (Christopher Lee/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
"Together, we will protect our children and defeat the dangerous ideology that has inflicted irreversible harm on innocent kids."

Paxton is running for election in Texas' 2026 Senate race. President Donald Trump campaigned in two separate Texas cities, Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Tuesday in an effort to boost Paxton's Senate bid.

The Trump administration has been targeting initiatives related to transgender people in recent months. Trump announced in August that his administration will cease providing funding for gender transition surgeries using Medicaid for minors.
Paxton's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
A TCH spokesperson told Fox News Digital Wednesday the hospital prioritizes providing patients "the highest standard of care," including through the detransition clinic.

"First and foremost, patients and families are at the center of all we do, and we will always provide the highest standard of care, including through this clinic, which formalizes the supportive, multidisciplinary services we have and will continue to deliver," the TCH spokesperson said.
"Given the multidisciplinary approach, care may be delivered in multiple locations, depending on individual patient needs.

"All services provided will be within our hospital’s existing licensure and scope," the spokesperson added. "Services will include endocrinology, surgery, primary care, fertility counseling, psychiatry, psychology, social work/case management and speech pathology. The clinic is operational, and we are complying with all requirements in the settlement agreement."
The TCH spokesperson also told Fox News Digital the hospital is "actively triaging prospective patients" for the detransition clinic.

"Protecting the privacy of our patients and their families is a top priority, thus we are unable to share patient information," the spokesperson stated. "We are actively triaging prospective patients through our established intake process. We can tell you that, thus far, we have not yet had clinical appointments with patients."
President Donald Trump, left, listens as Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks during a campaign rally at Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio on Oct. 7, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
INSURANCE COMPANIES PUT ON NOTICE FOR STRANDING TRANS PATIENTS WHO WANT TO REVERSE SURGERIES

TCH is required to fully fund services provided through the detransition clinic for its first five years, ensuring patients receive those services at no cost, and must also publicize the clinic on its website, according to the settlement.

The May settlement also required TCH to pay $10 million to resolve claims brought under the Texas Health Care Program Fraud Prevention Act and the federal False Claims Act over allegations that the hospital improperly billed Texas Medicaid for gender-transition treatments, according to Paxton's office.
A demonstrator holds a transgender pride flag during a President's Day protest near the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Feb. 17, 2025. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Do No Harm, a medical advocacy organization critical of gender-transition treatments for minors, estimates 13,994 minors received gender-transition-related medical interventions between 2019 and 2023, based on its analysis of insurance claims data.
A Fox News poll published Oct. 21 found that Democratic candidate James Talarico and Paxton were tied at 49% among likely voters in the Lone Star State.

title: Who are Ilhan Omar’s lawyers? Meet the high-powered Dem attorneys the embattled rep hired
summary: Ilhan Omar has hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, attorneys who represented Biden, House Democrats during the Trump impeachment and E. Jean Carroll.
story: Legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes a letter from 175 House Democrats, led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, demanding the administration stop its investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar. Democrats warn that the ongoing probe could negatively impact her re-election campaign in Minnesota. The segment explores the allegations regarding Omar's immigration history and citizenship status.
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has tapped two high-powered Washington, D.C.-based attorneys who have previously represented elected officials at the highest echelon of American politics.

Amid dueling federal investigations — one for immigration fraud and another for financial disclosure discrepancies — the embattled Somali-born lawmaker hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, according to a CBS report. Both are partners at Hecker Fink LLP.
The attorneys have in the past represented Democrat clients and taken on left-leaning cases especially those taking aim at President Donald Trump, his administration and his supporters.
ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C.   (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
Amy Jeffress

Jeffress is a former federal prosecutor whose biography says she tried more than 40 cases during a decade in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the District of Columbia, where she was chief of the National Security Section. She has also been a Department of Justice (DOJ) attaché.

She served as former President Joe Biden's attorney in his lawsuit against the DOJ earlier this year. In that case, Biden sought to halt the release of audio recordings between himself and his "Promise Me, Dad" book ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer.
The audio was recorded in 2016 and 2017 and was subject to a FOIA request from the Heritage Foundation in 2024.

It was cited during special counsel Robert Hur's investigation into whether Biden illegally retained classified information from his term as vice president and piqued the interest of conservatives demanding answers about Biden's mental acuity.
The court declined to block the release of the recordings, in which Biden had frequent memory lapses, and they were made public in July.

U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar speaks during the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party Convention in the Mayo Civic Center in Rochester, Minn., May 30, 2026.  (Alex Kormann/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Before her time at Hecker Fink, Jeffress, a 1992 Yale Law graduate, served as counsel for then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and the Democrat-led House January 6 committee, which spent two years investigating the riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. She represented the committee when it was sued by a Trump campaign spokesperson, Taylor Budowich, after the committee subpoenaed his bank records.

Jeffress also represented Trump foe and former FBI attorney Lisa Page, a key figure in the left's Russiagate conspiracy theory, during congressional scrutiny into the FBI's handling of the matter. Page later sued the DOJ for releasing her text messages with her FBI colleague and lover at the time, Peter Strzok.

In the messages, Strzok assuaged Page's concerns that Trump would become president by vowing that the FBI would stop it and referred to an "insurance policy" against his presidency. That case was settled in 2024.
ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

Jeffress is married to U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of Washington, D.C., who in May ruled that it was illegal for the John F. Kennedy Performing Arts Center to add Trump's name. Trump publicly criticized Cooper as "highly conflicted" due to his relationship with Jeffress.
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., center, and Karmel Mall of Somalia owner Basim Sabri inside the dining area in the mall. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)
Joshua Matz
Matz is also a partner at Hecker Fink. He graduated from Harvard Law and clerked for former Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy.
"Joshua’s practice has long included a focus on democracy and elections," his biography page says.
He represented the state of Pennsylvania in defending the certification of its election results, including arguing before the Supreme Court.
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
He was counsel to House Democrats during both failed impeachment attempts against Trump during his first term in office.

Matz also represented E. Jean Carroll in two separate civil cases against Trump related to his denial of her sexual assault claims against him. He was never criminally charged. In 2022, Carroll accused Trump of defaming her in his denial of her account of an incident she claims happened in 1996. A New York jury found Trump liable for defamation and for sexual assault.
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
Prior to that case, in 2019, a jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million for defamation stemming from other comments made by Trump.

Matz represented students, parents and teachers who opposed Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act, which his biography describes as the "Don't Say Gay" law, which restricted teaching students about sexual orientation and gender identity.

He also successfully represented Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear when he was sued for COVID-19 lockdowns, including school closures, and victims of the 2017 "Unite the Right" rally in Charlottesville.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Now, Matz and Jeffress are representing Omar as she seeks to battle two federal probes. In a video message posted to her social media earlier this month, the lawmaker pleaded with her supporters to keep sending money, noting that her fight against the investigations would be costly.
Omar's attorneys did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Neither did the White House.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Why the Ilhan Omar saga isn't going away
summary: Trump claims Ilhan Omar must resign from Congress over alleged immigration fraud, but the Constitution grants that power solely to the House.
story: Reports indicate the Obama administration investigated allegations about Rep. Ilhan Omar’s past marriage in 2016, including claims that she married her brother to help him obtain immigration benefits. The allegations have resurfaced amid renewed federal scrutiny and questions surrounding the handling of the investigation.
President Donald Trump has his favorite riffs during campaign rallies.
He recently complimented the physique of Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
He still calls out former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris.

But, in recent weeks, the president spun Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., into heavy rotation on his playlist. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department are probing Omar for alleged immigration fraud and financial disclosure reports.
TRUMP SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD GO TO JAIL OR BE DEPORTED, CALLS HER ‘A DISGRACE TO OUR COUNTRY’
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference in which she blamed President Donald Trump for death threats and attacks against her. (AP Photo/Adam Gray)
"What she did was use a fake name and other things that are fake," the president groused about Omar. "She used the fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately resign from Congress."
Trump argued that Democrats "just conceded her seat."
They didn’t.
And the president declared that "she will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body of politicians."
Not accurate.

The president doesn’t decide who gets to sit in Congress. Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution grants that power to the House and Senate. It charges both bodies with authority to "be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members."
The Constitution goes on to say that the House and Senate may "punish its Members for Disorderly Behavior; and, with the Concurrence of two thirds, expel a Member."
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a field hearing at the Minnesota Senate Building on Jan. 16, 2026, in St. Paul, Minn. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

We bring up those responsibilities because it’s possible that the House may need to tangle with the "qualifications" of Omar. Especially since The New York Times reported that the Minnesota Democrat faced scrutiny by the Obama-era Justice Department in 2016. Moreover, that inquiry says the feds found evidence that she may have entered into a fraudulent marriage.

If that’s the case, there could be questions about Omar’s citizenship and, thus, whether she’s even permitted to serve in Congress. Especially if it’s found she was naturalized as a citizen via bogus means.
Republicans have been after Omar for years. Across the aisle, Democrats are concerned this could be a distracting headache. Especially if they seize control of the House after the midterms next week.
THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS

The inquiry into Omar began in 2016 when she ran for the state legislature. Former President Barack Obama was in office. The investigation continued into the Biden administration. The feds terminated the inquiry in 2021.
After the Trump administration raided Omar’s home in October — seizing electronics and documents — Obama defended the congresswoman.

"It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say," the former president said. "But that’s exactly what the Trump administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar."
Obama said the current inquiry flipped her life "upside down" and characterized it as an effort to "intimidate someone."
Controversial influencer and livestreamer Hasan Piker asked Omar about how her week was going amid the investigation.
"It tracks for me," replied Omar. "That’s kind of what I’m used to."
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., pictured walking and talking in the U.S. Capitol basement. (Fox News Digital)
A spokeswoman for Omar said she "has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory."
But indications that Omar faced scrutiny ten years ago make it harder to characterize this as wild, right-wing conjecture emanating from the blogosphere.
"Who ordered [the investigation] closed?" Fox contributor Paul Mauro asked. "Reportedly, both administrations had opened cases into this. We now know how much smoke there is."
Omar campaigned for the state legislature in 2016. Her campaign released a letter from the U.S. attorney saying it "wasn’t investigating" nor requesting an inquiry into Omar.
So was she cleared? Or does word of the old probe pour petrol on the flames?

"Omar will talk about it and say, ‘They've looked into this. Nothing came about it,’" said University of Minnesota political science professor Kathryn Pearson. "But I think it's also a talking point that Republicans will use. So, I think sort of both sides will try to use that to their advantage."
John Nagel is Omar’s Republican opponent on the ballot next week. Nagel views the new investigation as a political wedge.

"With the raid on her home, people should keep this in mind. It's a very serious accusation," Nagel said. "As far as I'm concerned, Somalia comes first in her life. And we are nothing more than a piggy bank for her."
TRUMP PUSH TO OUST OMAR FACES HISTORIC SUPREME COURT TEST, BUT LEGAL EXPERTS SEE ‘UNCHARTED’ TWIST
At least one Republican is ready to bounce Omar from the House.

"If the evidence shows that she is not an American, she has to be removed immediately and probably put in prison," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "I think the idea that a foreigner might be actually serving in Congress should be terrifying to Americans."
But another House Republican urges caution.
"We just need all the facts," said Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J. "I hope that the investigation is thorough, fair, and absolutely aboveboard."
And then there is the question of due process.

"The Ethics Committee should commence an investigation. It takes two-thirds of the House to expel a sitting member. I would highly doubt the Democrats would agree. And certainly not without findings," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox.
"I think, at a minimum, the Ethics Committee should move forward with an investigation immediately upon our return."

This could develop into a real hornet’s nest for the House when lawmakers descend on Washington after the midterms. That’s to say nothing of questions about seating Omar when the new Congress starts in January. If Democrats win the House, would House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. — perhaps as speaker — be forced to grapple with the question of seating Omar if Republicans move to exclude her?

In fact, such a motion to exclude comes right before the new speaker swears in the entire House on Jan. 3. The speaker would swear in 434 members then take votes related to the potential member in question. If Democrats win the House, new, moderate House Democrats might take their first formal floor vote on whether to seat Omar.

Voting against Omar might be good for some of these new members, considering the political nature of their battleground districts. But would the Democratic brass pressure new members to vote with the caucus on such a nettlesome issue?

Democrats who vote to seat Omar give Republicans an immediate opportunity to build a case against newly christened members representing swing districts. A vote to exclude or expel Omar would go down as one of the most important roll calls of the entire two-year Congress.

We haven’t even explored how progressives and democratic socialists — new to the House — might rage at moderate Democrats for not supporting their colleague. That could produce a serious schism among Democrats.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
This isn’t going away. Omar is a lightning rod. The GOP believes it can continue to milk this. President Trump has his favorite riffs about Omar. And it’s possible that House Republicans may as well.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Christian group touts 'ethical' tech features as concerns over out-of-control AI tools persist
summary: Ligonier Ministries built its Grow app with an AI assistant that deflects vulnerable users to real humans and the suicide hotline when needed.
story: A Christian ministry is on the cutting edge of developing a more ethical AI tool, one that sets boundaries for itself and protects the safety of its users.

The leader of a Christian ministry that built its own artificial intelligence application to guide users in their spiritual journey warns companies developing AI systems need to implement "ethical guidelines" to ensure their technology doesn't harm people.

Ligonier Ministries President and CEO Chris Larson says the true highest intelligence is God and shared a new tool his group created to help answer questions people may have from a faith-based perspective.

"It's interesting that [President Donald Trump] even referred to artificial intelligence now as 'superintelligence,'" Larson told Fox News Digital. "Of course, Christians — and, really, all of us — have access to the 'superintelligece,' the one who has created the universe."
A holy Christian cross lying on an open Bible with an American flag in the background. (iStock)
CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

The mission of the Florida-based organization, founded by the late Christian theologian R.C. Sproul, is to proclaim, teach and defend the holiness of God "in all its fullness to as many people as possible."
Part of accomplishing that mission was building an app that the organization calls Grow.

"It's dedicated to helping Christians to better understand the Bible and theology and to go deeper in their faith, put down roots, if you will," Larson said of the new tool. "And, so, this app has 50 years of teaching in it from more than 800 different teachers, of course, grounded in Dr. R.C. Sproul's lifetime of teaching."
The app draws from a library of tens of thousands of pieces of content to help users in their faith journey looking to obtain answers to critical questions.
Inside Grow is an "intelligent answer assistant" that can answer questions from users from a faith-based perspective.
But building Grow for Christian users required putting a great deal of thought into the ethics of the model, Larson explained.
ChatGPT Work, OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse and Google Gemini Spark offer ways to automate time-consuming tasks using artificial intelligence. (Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL
"Now, it's not trying to pretend it's a person or anything like that. It is just trained on our library, and then helping Christians to trust the answers, and [it] will only go so far," he said.

"And, again, I think that's an important guard as well. Because, for us, making sure that we have trusted theological answers and that the intelligent answer assistant is acting with integrity and not going outside of that."
When users push the boundaries of the application, it directs them to real human support, a feature most large language model AI tools refuse to implement.
"And, so, we've given it a sandbox to work within. And any time that somebody tries to push it beyond the borders, we're going to deflect or defer to a real human. Imagine that," Larson said.
A Christian cross against the sky (Godong/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
For example, if a user discusses suicide in Grow, the intelligent answer assistant will direct them to the suicide hotline or other real-world resources.
BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: POPE LEO SEES THE AI AGE CLEARLY — AND WARNS WE MUST SAVE OUR SOULS
Over the past several years, there have been a flurry of suicide deaths that victims' family members say AI chatbots were at least partially responsible.

In one case from last year, a teenager named Adam Raine died by suicide after months of discussing his suicidal thoughts on ChatGPT. According to a lawsuit from his parents, the chatbot provided him information about methods of suicide, validated aspects of planning the suicide and offered to help him draft a suicide note. OpenAI, ChatGPT's parent company, disputes the characterization and says the chatbot directed him to crisis resources multiple times.

"So, we understood that it's important to provide safety guardrails, but also we did not want this intelligent answer assistant to pretend that it was a person," Larson said. "We don't want it to take the place of a pastor or a local church elder or even a parent."
WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT?
Larson said companies developing AI need to consider guardrails for their technology.
"Anybody developing AI tools today needs to think through ethical guidelines, and that's more of the self-regulation and guardrails that we've been talking about," he said.
A laptop shows the letters "AI" beside a smartphone displaying a chat AI app logo in Frankfurt, Germany, Jan. 2, 2025. (Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images)

"I think there's a real concern today because you have great power that's been entrusted to these different companies, and they're not really disclosing their worldview," he continued. "How do they know right from wrong?"
For Ligonier, the absolute truth upon which its AI model is built is the Christian faith.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"How are you determining what is right and wrong? As Christians, we believe we have a true answer — a source that we can turn to."
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: How Obama appointee and Trump nemesis Boasberg ended up overseeing Ilhan Omar warrant, other key cases
summary: Judge James Boasberg oversees the Ilhan Omar search warrant fight, deportation flights, and California voter rolls, raising assignment questions.
story: Former DOJ prosecutor Jim Trusty joins 'America's Newsroom' to analyze the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home. Trusty discusses the DOJ search warrant executed by Homeland Security Investigations and reviews potential immigration charges.

Federal Judge James Boasberg, dubbed a "Radical left lunatic" by President Donald Trump, is presiding over several high-profile cases challenging actions made by the Trump administration, raising questions about how judges are assigned to cases.

The scrutiny comes as Boasberg, an Obama-appointed chief judge of the Washington, D.C., district court, oversees a challenge brought by several media outlets seeking to force the Justice Department to unseal the search warrant on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

"Judge James Boasberg is now involved with the Ilhan Omar case," Steve Ferguson, a self-described business owner with more than 250,000 followers on X, wrote in a social media post. "Is everything rigged?"

In the federal court of the District of Columbia, cases are assigned to judges randomly by an electronic system managed by the clerk's office operating under the direction of the Calendar and Case Management Committee, according to the rules of the court. The committee consists of three to five judges appointed by the chief justice.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Judge Boasberg (Getty)

There are exceptions to the random-assignment process. For example, criminal grand jury matters are assigned to and overseen by the chief judge, currently Boasberg. This means Boasberg’s assignment to oversee the fight over unsealing the search warrant for Omar was "not a surprise" to Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general.
"But there are a lot of cases that seem to be going to judges maybe based on those cases having similarities, which is not what the local rules say," Wessan told Fox News Digital.
When a case needs to be reassigned, the Calendar and Case Management Committee will determine how the reassignment is made.
Wessan suggested that concerns over how case assignments are made are valid, considering some of the high-profile cases against the Trump administration which have appeared in Boasberg's docket.

"If one is just following anecdotally, there does seem to be a lot of high-profile cases in front of judges that seem to be expressing unusual amounts of frustration or disagreement with the administration," Wessan said, urging greater transparency in how case assignments are made.
TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18THCENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH
Federal law enforcement agents confront anti-ICE protesters during a demonstration outside the Bishop Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis Jan. 15, 2026. (Getty Images)

The fight over unsealing the release of Omar's search warrant is just one of several cases involving the Trump administration and now on Boasberg's docket. Boasberg is also overseeing California’s lawsuit against the Trump administration over voter roll disputes.

On Friday, he ordered the administration to provide the state with the names and supporting information for roughly 20,000 people whom the DOJ claims are noncitizens on California’s voter rolls by the end of the day.

Boasberg has issued several consequential rulings against the Trump administration, including a high-profile March 2025 order directing the administration to turn around deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador. The Trump administration fought against the order, pointing to the Alien Enemies Act as legal justification for the deportations.

The dispute over the administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act eventually reached the Supreme Court, which vacated Boasberg's temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, ruling that the case was brought in the wrong jurisdiction.

That same month, Boasberg was assigned a lawsuit seeking to preserve Signal messages after top Trump administration officials discussed plans for a Yemen strike in a group chat that accidentally included Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg. The judge later ordered the administration to preserve the messages.

The string of cases prompted Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio; Darrell Issa, R-Calif.; and Chip Roy, R-Texas, to send a letter in May 2025 to the court clerk asking for greater clarity on how judicial assignments are made. The lawmakers questioned whether assignments were truly random as the court’s rules state.
"The Committee cannot independently verify the randomness of case assignments because the composition of assignment decks is kept secret," the lawmakers wrote.

"We must understand the nature of the case assignment process in the District Court — which is considering a number of cases challenging the Trump Administration’s policy decisions — to consider and develop appropriate legislation."

Venezuelan migrants flown from Guantanamo Bay via Honduras walk up a ladder after arriving on a deportation flight at Simon Bolivar International Airport in Maiquetia, La Guaira State, Venezuela, Feb. 20, 2025. (Reuters/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria)
FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE

Meanwhile, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced legislation in July that would require federal district courts to assign cases randomly, without exceptions, naming it the Boasberg Act. The bill is stalled in committee.

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system. Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts," Schmitt said in a statement.

Under the rules of the D.C. Court, the chief justice does not have the power to reassign a case. The Calendar and Case Management Committee handles case reassignments. The court must notify the judges and attorneys involved, but it does not have to publicly explain why a case was reassigned. Wessan has called for greater transparency.

"The rules shouldn’t say one thing if it’s not true. But if it is true, they could just say so. I think the issue is with the exceptions. What happens in those exceptional cases and how often do they occur?" Wessan said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Given the frequency of the concerning episodes in the district court, erring on the side of transparency is probably prudent to the extent that there are exceptions to the normal random-assignment system."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: CodePink leader adds muscle to well-funded fight to ban restaurant delicacy
summary: An Oregon-based group poured nearly $475,000 into D.C.'s foie gras ban as part of a strategy to "storm the nation" with local ballot campaigns.
story: Pro-Animal Future’s 10-year plan calls for statewide factory-farming bans, while Butterworth’s chef Bart Hutchins warns the campaign could eventually target other types of meat.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — CodePink D.C. Coordinator Olivia DiNucci last month posted a TikTok video of herself in a home supporting an issue far afield from her usual battles supporting the Communist Party of Cuba and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

This time, she was backing a local ballot measure, Initiative 86, introduced in early February in the D.C. City Council to ban foie gras, a fine-dining delicacy made from duck liver, and other products made from birds. D.C. residents will vote on the measure on Election Day with early voting already started.

The campaign presents itself as a grassroots effort to advance animal welfare, but public financial filings reveal a far more heavily funded operation. A national animal-rights network has supplied hundreds of thousands of dollars in financial support, underwriting paid petition circulators, political consultants, staff salaries and advertising in a campaign that could reshape Washington’s restaurant industry.

Far from a shoestring local initiative, the effort has reported nearly half a million dollars in contributions and expenditures, much of it backed by an organization that openly describes local ballot measures as stepping stones toward a broader "pro-animal future."
WHO’S FUNDING AMERICA’S PROTEST UNREST? FOX NATION'S NEW 'RIOT INC.' FOLLOWS THE MONEY TO FIND OUT
Olivia DiNucci, D.C. coordinator at CodePink, marches at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

A Fox News Digital investigation of campaign finance records, nonprofit filings and the groups’ own organizing documents traces the people, money and long-term strategy behind Initiative 86 and raises questions about how a fight over one luxury menu item became part of a much larger political campaign over what Americans eat.
A political sign directs D.C. voters to select "yes" to banning foie gras in the district. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

Pro-Animal Future, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit based in Portland, Oregon, launched the campaign, nicknamed I-86, in D.C. and says its local ballot efforts are part of a broader push to change public attitudes toward common animal agricultural practices. Its IRS filing also lists its name as Pro-Animal DC.
In seven financial reports filed with the D.C. Office of Campaign Finance, Pro-Animal DC provides a window into a local political campaign’s operational, financial and logistical infrastructure.

According to its latest filings, Pro-Animal DC collected a whopping $474,190.62 between Sept. 23, 2025, and Oct. 26, 2026, for the local campaign, with Pro-Animal Future as its major backer, providing it $386,435.77.

Its largest expense is stipends totaling $126,780.36, or about one-quarter of the campaign’s expenses, to a paid professional protest organizer, Cady Witt, whose LinkedIn profile lists her as "community impact coordinator" at "DC Voters for Animals." Witt is also listed as the treasurer of Pro-Animal DC in its campaign reports.

Pro-Animal DC reported another $89,224, or about 20% of its expenses, for 293 payments to 64 people described as "consultant-circulator" from September 2025 through Oct. 26, 2026. They got an average payment of $1,394.13 per person.
‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

Also a professional organizer, CodePink’s DiNucci is typically a fixture at anti-Israel demonstrations and foreign affairs hearings. CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans is married to an American-born, China-based tech tycoon, Neville Roy Singham, whose funding of activist groups has drawn scrutiny from congressional lawmakers and is the subject of a federal investigation.
Pro Animal Future said CodePink doesn’t have a role in its campaign beyond DiNucci’s appearance in her TikTok video.

Pro-Animal Future alleges that birds are "force-fed" to gain the weight needed to produce foie gras, and it says its campaigns seek to end "force-feeding" birds and shift public views on animal agriculture. According to its latest available IRS 990 tax filing, Pax Fauna, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Denver, says it’s related to Pro-Animal Future, which it described as doing "lobbying" work.
In 2024, Pax Fauna outlined a 10-year roadmap to build local ballot campaigns and eventually pursue statewide "factory farming" bans and establish "animal freedom."

A graphic from Pax Fauna’s 10-year plan to "storm the nation" outlines a strategy that moves from research and pilot campaigns to city-level initiatives and statewide bans on factory farming.  (Obtained by Fox News Digital)

The roadmap called such measures a way to "provoke a sort of identity crisis for the voting public" and "storm the nation." The group sought to launch as many as 10 local chapters during the 2025-2026 election cycle.

An anonymous purchaser bought the web domain ProAnimalDC.org in April 2025, according to online records. Today, Pro-Animal Future lists its current campaigns as running in D.C. and Denver and says it worked with Portland’s City Council to ban foie gras sales in June.
Pax Fauna’s founders said they have spent years organizing with Direct Action Everywhere, an animal-rights 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Berkeley, California.

Last year, according to its filings, Pro-Animal Future spent $7,703.70 for Airbnb accommodations. This year, on July 31, it spent $22,418.69 for Airbnb accommodations. Pro-Animal DC has stated that the lodging was for about 60 out-of-town "volunteers" who came to Washington, D.C., in July for a signature-gathering effort called "Goosapalooza." On its website, it promoted the "free housing."

The measure’s language has raised questions about how far the ban could reach. Its definition of a "fattened bird liver product" covers food or byproducts made from birds’ livers when the birds were fattened "through any method or practice," and specifically lists pâtés, spreads and processed meat products as products to be banned. The initiative separately defines "force-feeding" as causing a bird to eat more than it would voluntarily consume.
MAMDANI ACCUSED OF BETRAYING NYC WORKERS AS UNION BOSS BLASTS 'ANTI-LABOR' HORSE CARRIAGE BAN
Former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine told City Cast DC, a local media outlet, that the text "includes le poulet," which means chicken in French.
Jon Mandel, an attorney and former D.C. Council legislative staffer, told the same outlet the sales provision could reach poultry liver products made without force-feeding.

A graphic shows the D.C. ballot measure’s definition of a "fattened bird liver product," which includes foie gras, pâtés, spreads and processed meat products made from the livers of birds fattened "through any method or practice." (Getty Images, Pro Animal DC)

Pro-Animal Future spokeswoman Natalie Fulton told City Cast DC the campaign isn’t trying to ban chicken and "is about foie gras." She added that the D.C. Council could clarify the language if voters approve the measure.

However, restaurants in the district who serve the delicacy aren't buying what activists are selling. Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s, a Capitol Hill restaurant popular with Trump administration members, raised a similar concern in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"Realistically, that could ban at least 20 products that I can think of right off the top of my head that aren’t foie gras," he said. Hutchins said his restaurant would consider legal challenges if the measure passes.
Hutchins sees the initiative as part of a broader effort to restrict what Americans can eat.
"If they ban foie gras here, they’ll eventually ban meat here, and they’ll bring that to the rest of the country," he said.
Pro-Animal Future’s 10-year roadmap calls for statewide factory farming bans but doesn’t define "factory farming." Hutchins said he worries the term could be interpreted broadly.

Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s, a Capitol Hill restaurant popular with Trump administration figures, opposes a ballot measure that would ban foie gras and possibly other products made from force-fed birds. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

This week, the dispute followed Hutchins to the 17th Street NW High Heel Race, a Halloween drag event in the District. Witt, D.C. campaign director for Pro-Animal Future, appeared dressed as Hutchins, wearing a chef’s hat, glasses, a drawn-on mustache and a white corseted outfit.
Nearby, a person in a duck costume crouched with a feeding tube in its mouth. Washingtonian food editor Jessica Sidman shared photos on X, describing Witt simply as "Pro-Animal campaign coordinator."

By late Thursday, the photos had 42,200 views, amplifying the campaign even further. Hutchins didn't appear phased by the mimicking. He took to X and said, "Bart derangement syndrome enters the lexicon."

The measure has also drawn opposition from celebrity chef José Andrés, whose D.C. restaurant serves foie gras. He questioned the ban’s broader implications on X, asking, "If duck goes, all goes next?"

The D.C. chief financial officer, Glen Lee, estimates implementing the measure would cost $314,000 from fiscal 2026 through 2029, including $274,000 for an additional inspector and $40,000 for public education. The fiscal impact statement says the District’s Department of Energy and Environment doesn’t inspect restaurant kitchens or other back-of-house operations and isn’t likely to do so.

It says the inspector would investigate complaints, inspect establishments and coordinate with other agencies, but doesn’t detail how regulators would verify a product’s origin during routine inspections.

Hutchins said he would continue serving foie gras until the city resolves how to enforce the measure. He disputes the animal welfare case for a ban, saying he doesn’t believe the feeding process that farms use to create foie gras hurts ducks. Pro-Animal DC’s findings say the practice causes pain and illness. Hutchins also said losing D.C. as a major market could threaten the country’s two commercial foie gras producers, Hudson Valley Foie Gras and La Belle Farm in New York state’s Catskills region.

The measure would regulate sales in D.C. The D.C. chief financial officer’s fiscal impact statement says, "The Office of Revenue Analysis is not aware of any bird farms or bird feeding operations in the District."

The Catskill Foie Gras Collective, a producer group, says its member farms raise ducks cage-free and use small, flexible plastic tubes to deliver feed to a pouch in their throats. It argues the process causes no pain, citing ducks’ anatomy, and says feeding is skipped if a bird hasn't finished digesting its previous meal. The collective also says Catskills foie gras farms employ about 400 people.
GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS

Fox News Digital reached out to Pro-Animal DC, which disputed critics’ claim that Initiative 86’s wording could extend to poultry-liver products beyond foie gras. The campaign said the measure is intended only to prohibit force-feeding and foie gras sales. It said "fattened" refers to the extreme enlargement of birds’ livers associated with foie gras production, not ordinary poultry farming. The campaign pointed to the measure’s findings, which describe covered products as luxury foods made from diseased, enlarged livers, and said the broad definition of "bird" is meant to prevent producers from switching species.
SEND US A TIP

Pro-Animal DC said D.C. agencies and courts look to a law’s stated purpose when its wording allows more than one interpretation, and said it would welcome Council clarification if voters approve the measure. Asked what language could clarify the measure, spokeswoman Natalie Fulton didn’t elaborate.

The dispute leaves D.C. voters weighing a ballot measure presented as a foie gras ban while others raise broader questions about its wording, enforcement and the campaign’s long-term goals. For Hutchins, the stakes extend beyond one item on a restaurant menu; for Pro-Animal Future, Initiative 86 is one step in a larger effort to change farming practices at a national scale.

Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani and Ava Palschakov contributed to this report.
Brooke Curto is a breaking news editor at Fox News Digital in Washington, D.C.

title: Trump admin threatens Iran with 'consequences' as allies convene amid threats of post-election escalation
summary: The Trump administration warned Iran of consequences as Marco Rubio raised energy security and Strait of Hormuz concerns at the G20 meeting.
story: State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott discusses Iran, threats to U.S. personnel and the Trump administration’s priorities at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting.

The Trump administration warned Iran that there "will be consequences" if Tehran continues its malign activities amid growing concern over a potential new round of U.S.-Iran hostilities after the midterm elections.

With just days until the 2026 elections and with war raging on in the Middle East, foreign ministers from the world's largest economies gathered in Atlanta, Georgia, ahead of the G20 leaders meeting in December.

"The Iranian regime has had a choice ... to either pursue the path towards normalcy, towards prosperity for their people, the path towards diplomacy. Or they can continue their malign activities, but there will be consequences for that. And we've seen the president taking concrete action," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital Friday.

Pigott was responding to reports that U.S. officials have warned regional partners to prepare for the possibility of heightened U.S. military action against Iran after Tuesday's elections, as well as potential Iranian retaliation.
State Department Deputy Spokesperson Tommy Pigott told reporters nuclear talks between the U.S. and Iran have been "constructive" and that President Trump wants to see diplomacy. (State Department)
IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES

President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on renewed strikes, but U.S. diplomats and defense officials have privately urged several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for the possibility of new military action and Iranian retaliation, according to an Associated Press report citing two diplomats briefed on the warnings.
The warnings come amid heightened concerns about Iranian threats against Americans overseas.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton wrote in an unclassified memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the U.S. had received intelligence that Iran had "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" and that lethal Iranian plots had reached "advanced stages" in the Middle East and elsewhere, according to Scripps News.

Johann Wadephul (center front, CDU), Minister of Foreign Affairs, attends the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting chaired by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio (center back). (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Asked whether those threats were being discussed with G20 counterparts and whether the U.S. was sharing intelligence with allies to disrupt potential plots, Pigott declined to discuss intelligence matters.
"We're going to work with our partners to make sure that any transnational threat has the appropriate transnational response to protect our citizens," Pigott insisted.

The prospect of renewed fighting with Iran loomed over the G20 foreign ministers' meeting, where Rubio has put energy security, secure supply chains and freedom of navigation among the U.S. priorities.

Rubio opened the two-day gathering Friday by warning that the world's largest economies face "interconnected economic and geopolitical crises" threatening energy and food supplies, trade, global supply chains and freedom of navigation.
Pigott said the administration's position remains that "there cannot be a situation where a country decides that they can control an international waterway and charge tolls over that waterway."
TRUMP THREATENS 'UNPRECEDENTED' ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR ANY NATION AIDING IRAN
Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, Aug. 31, 2026.  (Reuters/Stringer/File Photo)
During the war, Iran began asserting greater authority over the Strait of Hormuz and insisting on the right to collect fees from ships for services including navigation and environmental protection.
Asked what the U.S. wants G20 countries to do to keep the strait open, Pigott pointed to a broader principle that international waterways must remain free from coercion.

"Fundamentally, the principle here is so important, making sure that we are having secure international waterways in the sense we're not having these tolls or coercion, making sure we have secure supply chains," Pigott said. "That is so important."

title: Trump's push to oust Omar faces historic Supreme Court test, but legal experts see ‘uncharted’ twist
summary: President Donald Trump's push to oust Ilhan Omar faces a key legal test, but experts say Powell v. McCormack may actually support her expulsion.
story: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., faces scrutiny as federal investigators probe her immigration paperwork for potential fraud and age discrepancies. Fox News contributor Paul Mauro joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze the legal implications after a warrant listed potential immigration crimes.

President Donald Trump's push to oust Rep. Ilhan Omar amid allegations of immigration fraud could trigger a constitutional fight, with legal experts telling Fox News Digital a landmark Supreme Court case involving another entrenched Democrat may not stand in Republicans’ way.
Federal investigators are examining whether the Minneapolis Democrat improperly obtained U.S. citizenship through allegedly fraudulent immigration paperwork involving her late father.
Omar has denied wrongdoing, and there has been no finding that she lacks U.S. citizenship.
ILHAN OMAR SHOULD BE JAILED, DEPORTED IF CITIZENSHIP FRAUD PROVEN, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN SAYS

Experts said Omar may not have the protections established in the landmark case involving former House Chairman Adam Clayton Powell Jr., D-N.Y., in which the Supreme Court blocked an effort to exclude him from Congress.

Powell faced allegations of misusing congressional funds and improperly paying his wife from the congressional payroll. Despite his re-election, the House voted to exclude him in 1967, but the Supreme Court later ruled that Congress could not refuse to seat a duly elected member who satisfied the Constitution's qualifications.
Rep. Adam Clayton Powell Jr., D-N.Y., in 1969 (Bettmann/Getty Images)

The first potential route for Republicans would be to challenge whether Omar meets the Constitution's citizenship requirement. Former Deputy Assistant Attorney General John Yoo and constitutional scholar Cully Stimson told Fox News Digital the Powell ruling does not prevent Congress from enforcing constitutional qualifications.

"Powell essentially means that Congress cannot add on to the minimum qualifications set out in the Constitution," Yoo said. "[S]ince citizenship is set out in the text of the Constitution as a qualification, it clearly can be enforced by Congress. Powell, in fact, would support a congressional decision to oust Congresswoman Omar if she was, in fact, not a citizen."
Stimson argued that citizenship itself is not a legal gray area.
"The Powell v. McCormack decision did not involve expulsion. It actually was to judge qualifications. That's a subtle but important difference," he said.

Stimson envisioned a January showdown if federal authorities presented evidence challenging Omar's citizenship before the new Congress convenes and House Republicans attempted to prevent her from being seated. Such a move would likely face a legal challenge from Omar, he said, raising questions about whether Congress could act before her citizenship status was resolved.

The Constitution requires House members to be at least 25 years old, have been U.S. citizens for seven years and inhabit the states they represent when elected. Stimson argued that even if alleged immigration irregularities originated with Omar's father, Nur Omar Mohamed, the central question would be whether she legally acquired citizenship, regardless of whether she knowingly participated in wrongdoing.
"It's like you're either pregnant or you're not," he said. "You’re either wet or dry. You're a citizen, or you are not a citizen."

In multiple public comments, Trump has called for Omar’s resignation or expulsion, specifically citing reports that she used a pseudonym when she was sworn into office and that she "married her brother."
"Let’s get her the hell out of there," he said Monday in Alcorn County, Mississippi.
Fox News Digital reached out to Omar for comment.
COULD TRUMP REVOKE ILHAN OMAR'S CITIZENSHIP FOR ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE? EX FEDERAL PROSECUTOR BREAKS IT DOWN
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)

A second route would involve seating Omar and then pursuing expulsion for misconduct, a separate constitutional power requiring a two-thirds House vote. Unlike exclusion for failing to meet constitutional qualifications, expulsion is a disciplinary action that was not at issue in the Supreme Court's Powell ruling.
At least one House Republican has already threatened to pursue that option.
Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., said Friday that if Omar is found not to be a citizen, "I absolutely will demand expulsion immediately."

Omar faces a separate investigation into her financial disclosures, which U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro previously confirmed to Fox News. The inquiry follows scrutiny of businesses tied to her current husband, Timothy Mynett, whose reported valuations reached as high as $30 million before Omar amended the filings, citing accounting errors. No financial wrongdoing has yet been established.
Stimson pointed to the 2023 expulsion of former Rep. George Santos, R-N.Y., as an example of the House exercising its disciplinary authority over misconduct that began before a member took office.

Former House counsel Michael Stern wrote in an examination of the Constitution’s expulsion clause that while Santos’ alleged misconduct largely preceded his term, House investigators found that his misrepresentations continued while he was in office.

"Thus, acts committed before a member’s first election may constitute disorderly behavior subject to congressional discipline, at least if the misconduct relates to the election and particularly if it involves deceiving the electorate," Stern wrote.
Stimson said Omar’s case is largely "uncharted waters," but the Santos case could still be instructive.
"I think the argument would be, ‘Well, her misrepresentations continued during the time in Congress.’ They would pull a Santos and use the same logic that they used," he said.

Any federal determination challenging Omar's citizenship could trigger a legal battle over whether she meets the constitutional requirements for office and what recourse she would have to contest such a finding, Stimson said.

"The hard part for her is ‘how do you prove a negative’," Stimson said, adding that placing blame on her father wouldn’t stand up in court because people cannot legally benefit from others’ criminal acts.

"It’s a harsh world, but it’s a binary situation."

title: Troubling discovery on state voter rolls sparks action days before midterms: ‘Should have been fixed’
summary: A conservative legal group's complaint alleges 3,181 potentially dead voters and 693 duplicate registrations remain on Maine's voter rolls.
story: J. Christian Adams, president of the Public Interest Legal Foundation, spoke to Fox News Digital about the group’s complaint alleging potentially dead voters and duplicate registrations on Maine’s voter rolls.

A conservative legal group filed an election complaint in Maine Tuesday, alleging that more than 3,000 potentially dead people and hundreds of duplicate registrations were discovered on the state’s voter rolls just days before the pivotal midterm elections.

The Public Interest Legal Foundation (PILF) said it identified 3,181 potentially dead voters and 693 duplicate registrations and urged the state to take action as Maine voters prepare to cast their ballots Tuesday.

"Now we know why they were hiding them because there were problems on them," J. Christian Adams told Fox News Digital. "They have dead people, they have lots of duplicates and they have general problems. It's something that should have been fixed a long time ago."
The complaint, filed with Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, argues election officials have not made a "reasonable effort" to remove ineligible voters from the official list.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL
A Maine resident casts a ballot at a polling station inside the Augusta Civic Center oJune 9, 2026, in Augusta, Maine.  (CJ Gunther/Getty Images)
Adams said the state, not his group, should have discovered the information.
"Why does it take a third-party group like the Public Interest Legal Foundation to find these duplicates?" Adams said.

The group is asking the state to take "additional corrective action," warning it "may have no other recourse" but to appeal through the complaint process under the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), a 2002 election reform law, if nothing is done.

The group compared those findings with its previous investigation in 2025, which found 18,453 potentially dead voters and 1,498 duplicate or triplicate registration records in Maine. The state addressed many of the records identified that year, but PILF said some errors remain while "new problems have arisen."

Several searches were used in the analysis to identify records that shared the same address, first and last names and birth year, as well as typos, punctuation errors, common nicknames and birth-year discrepancies.
DOJ GIVES CALIFORNIA 48 HOURS TO REVIEW LIST OF POSSIBLE NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS

Shenna Bellows, Maine's Secretary of State and a candidate for governor, speaks during a May Day rally organized by local unions May 1, 2026, outside City Hall in Portland, Maine. (Graeme Sloan/Getty Images)
The complaint requests that Maine review the group’s analysis, immediately remove ineligible voters and implement a plan to ensure the state complies with HAVA "now and in the future."
"I hope she gets the job done and removes all these duplicates," Adams said.

Adams said his group has been embroiled in an ongoing legal battle, and Bellows has a history of trying to "criminalize" the PILF for revealing what they found. The PILF sued Maine roughly six years ago over access to the state’s voter rolls and won a federal appeals court case in 2024 that required the state to make the records public.
"There's a history here of Secretary Bellows not wanting the public to know what kind of job she's doing," Adams said.
Adams accused Bellows of focusing on "defending sort of blue theories" rather than keeping Maine's voter lists accurate and up to date.
"Unfortunately, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows is not getting the job done," he said.
MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY
Campaign signs for Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson along a road in Bangor, Maine, Oct. 14, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

One of Adams' biggest concerns is that someone could use a dead person's registration to illegally vote. He said progressive state officials are reluctant to immediately remove dead voters out of fear they could mistakenly remove eligible voters, potentially leaving the door open for fraud.
"The problem is that sometimes people vote for the dead people," he said.
But Adams said he believes Maine has been trying to keep its problems out of the public eye for a long time.
"Maine has a longstanding problem trying to hide public information about whether or not they're doing a good job," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Bellows’ office for comment.

The legal filing comes just days before Mainers vote in a critical and tight U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. The winner could determine the balance of power in the Senate.
