title: Federal judge dismisses Trump attempt to interfere in Alaska Senate race
summary: A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the Trump’s civil lawsuit against the state, which sought to separate and preserve certain ballots in the state’s upcoming Senate election
story: A federal judge in Alaska on Sunday dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit seeking to separate and preserve certain ballots in the state’s upcoming Senate election, where GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola.

In the last week, Peltola’s campaign has faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported the campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent senator.

Citing potential voter confusion, the Trump administration sought to separate and preserve ballots with votes for Dan J. Sullivan, arguing that if the incumbent loses, it may be because people voted for the other Sullivan by mistake.
In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason voiced concerns about voters’ right to a secret ballot.

“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” Gleason wrote.

Later, she added: “Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.”

The lawsuit also sought to block the certification of the Senate election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. On Saturday, the Republican-led state government in Alaska implored a federal judge to prevent that effort in a court filing.

In response to the ruling, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign told NBC News, “No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska’s working families. Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator — not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies.”
Shortly after the judge’s ruling, the Justice Department appealed.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters. DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said.

Republicans have criticized Dan J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot for months, after he won a primary bid to be the fourth candidate on the general election ballot in August. The senator and his GOP allies long accused Democrats of recruiting the second Sullivan, a charge Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied.
In a post on Truth Social Sunday, President Donald Trump accused Dan. J Sullivan of committing a “criminal act.”
“The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement. He knows that he committed a Criminal Act,” the president wrote.

Last week, the Times report cited on-the-record comments from Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August, about the campaign’s efforts to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run for office. The campaign manager and several unnamed sources said operatives from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee joined the effort. Elisa Rios, the campaign manager who was fired, later sought to retract her comments.
On Sunday, the senator called Democrats’ effort “rigged and corrupt” in a CNN interview. He added that no matter the outcome, “I’m going to accept the election results.”

title: Democrats in key battlegrounds throw Joe Biden under the bus on the border
summary: Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability.
story: WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue.
Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country.

“I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan.
He’s not alone.
In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

“I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.”

Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year.

Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024.

Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings.

Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38%, polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term.
“The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night.

Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.”
In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.”
For Subscribers
Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border.
For Subscribers

In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.”
She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.”
Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement.

“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad. “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.”
Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.”
Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz.

Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum, he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people.

“We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.”
“So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.”

title: Sen. Tim Scott dodges on whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race
summary: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the battleground seat
story: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins following a bombshell report from The New York Times about Democrats’ alleged efforts to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
Asked on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether he would accept the election results if Peltola is certified to have won the Senate seat, Scott did not directly answer the question.
“Dan Sullivan is going to win, Kristen,” he told moderator Kristen Welker. “You know that, and that’s the only thing I’m going to tell you because it’s the truth.”

Scott went on to criticize Democrats for allegedly working to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a controversy that exploded last week following a report from The New York Times.

“What I can tell you about the truth is you can’t trust Mary Peltola’s campaign and the collusion between her campaign and the DSCC,” said Scott, who also serves as the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP counterpart to the DSCC.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democrats allegedly sought to recruit a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan. The report said the efforts allegedly involved members of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats to the Senate.

Following the report, the DSCC said in a statement that it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” Peltola, too, said she “knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”
Asked a second time whether he would accept the election results, Scott dodged the question.
“Number one, Dan Sullivan, the real Dan Sullivan, will win,” said Scott. “And number two, it actually is a federal offense to confuse voters.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit the challenger Dan J. Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law.

Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, participated in interviews with The New York Times, but later said she retracted “all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate race.”

Before The New York Times report was published, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block the certification of the results of the Senate election if Dan S. Sullivan loses. The DOJ cited potential voter confusion over having another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
In the aftermath of the Times’ report, President Donald Trump has said that both Peltola and the challenger Sullivan should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.

On Thursday, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering a state investigation to determine whether the alleged “scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.”

title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke
summary: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized Saturday after a stroke, a spokesperson for the senator said Sunday.
story: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized Saturday after a stroke, a spokesperson for the senator said Sunday.
The senator “started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game,” Allison Herwitt, Murphy’s chief of staff, said in a statement.

“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she added. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
For Subscribers
Murphy, 53, is not up for re-election this year but has traversed the country on behalf of Democratic candidates running for elected office.
The senator was slated to be in New Hampshire today, campaigning alongside Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee for Senate there.
For Subscribers

Murphy is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and on Thursday spoke at an event in Washington for the Middle East Institute, where he called the president’s plan to potentially resume the war with Iran after the midterms “insane.”
Earlier this fall, Murphy was one of over a dozen lawmakers whose offices received letters containing suspicious substances.

title: Martha Stewart responds to backlash over ‘hungry’ homeless Halloween costume
summary: Martha Stewart on Sunday responded to backlash about her Halloween costume, saying she was “distressed” to learn that her outfit, which depicted a “hungry” homeless person, had caused offense.
story: Martha Stewart on Sunday responded to backlash about her Halloween costume, saying she was “distressed” to learn that her outfit, which depicted a “hungry” homeless person, had caused offense.

Stewart, who built a lifestyle empire around cooking and home entertainment, shared a photo of herself in tattered clothing, holding a clipboard that read, “I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!” She posed with a tired expression and makeup meant to look like dirt on her face.
The photo was the third slide in an Instagram carousel promoting her candle collection on QVC.
“My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!” she wrote in the caption. The post was removed shortly afterward, but the costume and backlash continued to circulate elsewhere online.
Many interpreted the costume as mocking the poor, and some called it “out of touch” and “dystopian.”

“I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” Stewart said Sunday in a statement to NBC News.

She added that homelessness “continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic.”
“I am committed to continuing to make a difference,” she said.
Stewart wasn’t the only public figure to draw criticism over a Halloween costume.
Content creator McCall DaPron, who is slated to star in the upcoming Orange County spinoff of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” faced similar backlash over the weekend for her family’s costumes.

In a since-deleted Instagram post, DaPron wore an all-pink blazer and skirt with a matching pillbox hat, the outfit that Jackie Kennedy wore the day her husband, President John F. Kennedy, was assassinated. DaPron held a bouquet of red roses as she posed beside her husband, Kirk DaPron, who dressed as John F. Kennedy. Two of their children were dressed as Caroline Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr., and two others as Secret Service agents.
“Happy Halloween 🩷The Kennedy’s,” DaPron wrote in the caption before removing the post.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Commenters on one Reddit discussion thread called the costume “gross” and “disrespectful.”

“I’ve seen this costume a few times. Jackie O was a fashion icon and this is her most recognizable outfit,” one user wrote in the thread. “It’s pretty macabre. Including the children is really f-----g weird.”
Representatives for DaPron did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The reaction recalls the outrage that actor and model Julia Fox sparked last year when she dressed as Jackie Kennedy in the bloodstained suit.

Fox defended her decision, writing in an Instagram post that she wore the outfit “not as a costume, but as a statement. When her husband was assassinated, she refused to change out of her bloodstained clothes.”

title: Golden State Valkyries defeat Atlanta Dream for franchise’s first WNBA title
summary: In only their second season in existence, the Golden State Valkyries are WNBA champions.
story: In only their second season in existence, the Golden State Valkyries are WNBA champions.
The Valkyries won their first-ever title on Saturday, defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history. Forward Gabby Williams led with 30 points.
Confetti rained down onto the court as the crowd erupted in cheers, and the Valkyries celebrated the historic victory.
Valkyries win their first WNBA title

“I love moments like this,” Williams said after the final buzzer. “Nat told me to be patient in the first half. It was hard, but I listened to her. She’s right as always and she got us here,” she said, referring to head coach Natalie Nakase.

Williams was named the Finals MVP following her stunning performance, scoring more points than anybody in a half in WNBA postseason history. Though she scored just two points in the first half, she rallied with 15 points in the third quarter and 13 in the fourth.
Accepting her award, she said, “I wasn’t gonna lose on Halloween.”

title: Stores looted in German riots as Gen Z activists protest living costs, military service
summary: Rioters looted stores and set fires to barricades in Frankfurt on Saturday as protests across Germany demanded lower living costs and better education.
story: Rioters looted stores and set fires to barricades in Frankfurt on Saturday as protests across Germany demanded lower living costs and better education.

Tens of thousands of people across more than 30 cities took to the streets, including in the capital Berlin and financial hub Frankfurt, in protests organized by the campaign group Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge).
The activists demand spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service.
But the largely peaceful protests, which coincided with Halloween and came weeks after some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in neighboring France, turned violent in some areas.

“In ⁠the city center, windows have been smashed at several shops,” Frankfurt police said on X. “Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the ​city center or to leave the area.”

title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
summary: Wildfires in Indonesia are blanketing the country and other southeast Asian nations in toxic smog, prompting widespread protests.
story: Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.
Wildfire smoke covers Indonesia skies in orange haze

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.
“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”
The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.
“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.
Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.

title: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
summary: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.
story: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.

Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.

The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.

Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”

“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.
The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.

“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”

The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”

title: ‘Heat’ director Michael Mann injured in accidental weapon discharge at LA gun range
summary: “Heat” director Michael Mann was hospitalized this weekend after an accidental gun discharge at a gun range in Los Angeles.
story: “Heat” director Michael Mann was hospitalized this weekend after an accidental gun discharge at a gun range in Los Angeles.

The incident resulted in a minor, subcutaneous injury to Mann, according to a representative for the Emmy Award-winning filmmaker. Mann, 83, has been a target shooter for decades and was practicing at the range when the accident occurred.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann,” his representative said in a statement. “He was treated and is being released.”
The Los Angeles Police Department also confirmed that officers who responded to a radio call of shots fired at the location on Saturday determined that the shooting was accidental.
The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition, a spokesperson said, and LAPD cleared the scene after completing an injury report.
Mann is best known for his crime dramas, including his 1981 feature debut “Thief,” the 1986 thriller “Manhunter,” and the 1995 crime epic “Heat.”
For Subscribers
He told Vulture in 2017 that the cast of “Heat” shot full-load blanks to recreate the sound of real gunfire rather than relying on edited sound effects.
For Subscribers

“That’s the sound the weapons actually made and you couldn’t imitate or improve upon them,” Mann said. “It was terrifying as hell because we were in these glass and steel canyons and the gunfire reverberated in a certain real way, so they had an authenticity to the place that really was unique.”
Mann is reportedly developing “Heat 2,” as an adaptation of his 2022 novel of the same name, which he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner.

title: Federal judge dismisses Trump attempt to interfere in Alaska Senate race
summary: A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the Trump’s civil lawsuit against the state, which sought to separate and preserve certain ballots in the state’s upcoming Senate election
story: A federal judge in Alaska on Sunday dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit seeking to separate and preserve certain ballots in the state’s upcoming Senate election, where GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola.

In the last week, Peltola’s campaign has faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported the campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent senator.

Citing potential voter confusion, the Trump administration sought to separate and preserve ballots with votes for Dan J. Sullivan, arguing that if the incumbent loses, it may be because people voted for the other Sullivan by mistake.
In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason voiced concerns about voters’ right to a secret ballot.

“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” Gleason wrote.

Later, she added: “Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.”

The lawsuit also sought to block the certification of the Senate election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. On Saturday, the Republican-led state government in Alaska implored a federal judge to prevent that effort in a court filing.

In response to the ruling, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign told NBC News, “No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska’s working families. Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator — not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies.”
Shortly after the judge’s ruling, the Justice Department appealed.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters. DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said.

Republicans have criticized Dan J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot for months, after he won a primary bid to be the fourth candidate on the general election ballot in August. The senator and his GOP allies long accused Democrats of recruiting the second Sullivan, a charge Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied.
In a post on Truth Social Sunday, President Donald Trump accused Dan. J Sullivan of committing a “criminal act.”
“The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement. He knows that he committed a Criminal Act,” the president wrote.

Last week, the Times report cited on-the-record comments from Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August, about the campaign’s efforts to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run for office. The campaign manager and several unnamed sources said operatives from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee joined the effort. Elisa Rios, the campaign manager who was fired, later sought to retract her comments.
On Sunday, the senator called Democrats’ effort “rigged and corrupt” in a CNN interview. He added that no matter the outcome, “I’m going to accept the election results.”

title: Martha Stewart responds to backlash over ‘hungry’ homeless Halloween costume
summary: Martha Stewart on Sunday responded to backlash about her Halloween costume, saying she was “distressed” to learn that her outfit, which depicted a “hungry” homeless person, had caused offense.
story: Martha Stewart on Sunday responded to backlash about her Halloween costume, saying she was “distressed” to learn that her outfit, which depicted a “hungry” homeless person, had caused offense.

Stewart, who built a lifestyle empire around cooking and home entertainment, shared a photo of herself in tattered clothing, holding a clipboard that read, “I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!” She posed with a tired expression and makeup meant to look like dirt on her face.
The photo was the third slide in an Instagram carousel promoting her candle collection on QVC.
“My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!” she wrote in the caption. The post was removed shortly afterward, but the costume and backlash continued to circulate elsewhere online.
Many interpreted the costume as mocking the poor, and some called it “out of touch” and “dystopian.”

“I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” Stewart said Sunday in a statement to NBC News.

She added that homelessness “continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic.”
“I am committed to continuing to make a difference,” she said.
Stewart wasn’t the only public figure to draw criticism over a Halloween costume.
Content creator McCall DaPron, who is slated to star in the upcoming Orange County spinoff of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” faced similar backlash over the weekend for her family’s costumes.

In a since-deleted Instagram post, DaPron wore an all-pink blazer and skirt with a matching pillbox hat, the outfit that Jackie Kennedy wore the day her husband, President John F. Kennedy, was assassinated. DaPron held a bouquet of red roses as she posed beside her husband, Kirk DaPron, who dressed as John F. Kennedy. Two of their children were dressed as Caroline Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr., and two others as Secret Service agents.
“Happy Halloween 🩷The Kennedy’s,” DaPron wrote in the caption before removing the post.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Commenters on one Reddit discussion thread called the costume “gross” and “disrespectful.”

“I’ve seen this costume a few times. Jackie O was a fashion icon and this is her most recognizable outfit,” one user wrote in the thread. “It’s pretty macabre. Including the children is really f-----g weird.”
Representatives for DaPron did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The reaction recalls the outrage that actor and model Julia Fox sparked last year when she dressed as Jackie Kennedy in the bloodstained suit.

Fox defended her decision, writing in an Instagram post that she wore the outfit “not as a costume, but as a statement. When her husband was assassinated, she refused to change out of her bloodstained clothes.”

title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke
summary: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized Saturday after a stroke, a spokesperson for the senator said Sunday.
story: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized Saturday after a stroke, a spokesperson for the senator said Sunday.
The senator “started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game,” Allison Herwitt, Murphy’s chief of staff, said in a statement.

“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she added. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
For Subscribers
Murphy, 53, is not up for re-election this year but has traversed the country on behalf of Democratic candidates running for elected office.
The senator was slated to be in New Hampshire today, campaigning alongside Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee for Senate there.
For Subscribers

Murphy is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and on Thursday spoke at an event in Washington for the Middle East Institute, where he called the president’s plan to potentially resume the war with Iran after the midterms “insane.”
Earlier this fall, Murphy was one of over a dozen lawmakers whose offices received letters containing suspicious substances.

title: Rep. Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race that could determine which party controls the Senate.
story: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race that could determine which party controls the Senate.
“Hey, Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video.
“And he’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” she said. “I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign.”

The congresswoman’s announcement marks a whirlwind turnaround from just days ago, when she said she would support her party’s ticket and planned to attend a campaign event on Sunday to support Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

But leading up to the rally, Stevens and El-Sayed released dueling critical public statements, prompting concerns from Democrats that the spat was a distraction from what is widely seen as one of the most competitive Senate races.

Stevens had said that she expected El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside group that she said was antisemitic. El-Sayed responded, accusing Stevens of being “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The winner of Tuesday’s election will succeed Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, who is not seeking another term.
NBC News reported Saturday that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to no longer attend campaign events following the dueling statements.
In her endorsement video, which was less than two minutes, Stevens referenced El-Sayed’s ties to Hasan Piker, who has appeared with El-Sayed at campaign events.

“I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” she said. “A dear friend of mine earlier today was saying that education is the ballot, and she’s absolutely right. And what our students see, what our children see, and who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.”
Stevens said she was “still a very proud Democrat.”
By Sunday afternoon, Curtis Hertel, chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, wrote on X that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Speaking with reporters shortly after she posted her endorsement, Stevens reiterated that El-Sayed “made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign.”
“At some point, you got to look at who’s standing for country,” she added later.
NBC News has reached out to El-Sayed’s and Rogers’ campaigns for comment on Stevens’ endorsement.

Speaking to reporters after Stevens, Rogers said he was “honored” to have the congresswoman’s support. He said that sometimes “the hate grows so loud that it jeopardizes some of our citizens in this state.”
He referenced Jews hiding symbols of their faith and being “harassed for being Jewish.”

“This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else,” Rogers said. “And I just want you to know: She reminded me at the end of the call, ‘Remember, I’m still a Democrat.’”

Later on Sunday, El-Sayed addressed reporters ahead of a unity event alongside other Democrats. El-Sayed noted that Michigan is “a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government” and that he was “a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about.”
When asked later about Stevens, El-Sayed said that “at the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” going on to contrast his campaign with Rogers’.

President Donald Trump praised Stevens for her endorsement of Rogers, saying in a Truth Social post that she “showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did.”
“It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!” he said.
Stevens’ announcement came after she appeared alongside Rogers at church in Detroit, Rogers spokesperson Abby Ronson confirmed.
“Mike welcomes her,” Ronson told NBC News ahead of Stevens’ endorsement.

Stevens’ criticism of El-Sayed, her onetime primary opponent, and appearance alongside Rogers on Sunday have infuriated Democratic allies of El-Sayed, who have spent the weekend responding to Stevens’ criticisms of the party’s candidate in the crucial window before Election Day.
Even within her own congressional office, Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers appeared to have quick ripple effects.

A person familiar with the matter confirmed that Stevens’ longtime chief of staff Justin German, as well as several other staff members in her congressional office, are resigning over Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers.
In a statement, German said his team was “shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”

“As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself,” he said later in the statement. “We encourage everyone to exercise their civic duty, vote for Abdul and Democrats up and down the ballot, and stand up for the America we all believe in.”

Beyond her office, the Democratic National Committee’s Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins excoriated Stevens, saying in a statement that the congresswoman “revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.”
“Congresswoman Stevens has lost her way, and Michiganders know that Mike Rogers is a shill for Trump and has failed Michigan,” Rollins said.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary but endorsed El-Sayed after his primary victory, said in a statement that “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed.” He said that El-Sayed “will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.”
Michigan’s other Democratic senator, Elissa Slotkin, chastised Stevens in an X post Sunday afternoon.

“I was knocking doors in Sterling Heights yesterday and to a house, those folks were hyper-focused on how expensive everything in their life seems to be, and they’re desperately worried — often in tears — about the future for their kids,” Slotkin wrote “And it is for that reason that I have avoided commenting on the actions of Congresswoman Haley Stevens until now.”

Slotkin then added, referring to Stevens: “So anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good.”
A Democratic operative who has worked in Michigan questioned why more state Democratic leaders were not immediately coming out hard against Stevens’ move.
“Ask yourself where is Gretchen Whitmer right now?” this person said. “What is she doing?”
Whitmer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“No one’s quite sure what’s going on here, but the party has basically said, if you’re a surrogate, go on the attack against her [Stevens] right now,” this person added.
Earlier on Sunday, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said ahead of Stevens’ endorsement that he spoke with the congresswoman last night.

“My wonderful friend Haley Stevens wants me to represent to you and everybody else I talk to that she is voting straight down the line on the Democratic ticket, and she’s going to be celebrating with Democrats across the country when we win on Tuesday night,” Raskin said Sunday morning.
Still, it’s unclear how much Stevens’ endorsement could affect the race’s outcome. More than 2 million votes have already been cast in the state, according to NBC News data.

title: Israel’s president says parties need to engage with ‘open heart’ to avoid fresh election
summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result.
story: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result.
Last week’s elections saw Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc denied a majority, with the parties in his ruling coalition claiming 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.
Parties in the bloc aligned with Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, leaving neither man with an obvious path to forming a government.

The balance of power is held by parties representing Israel’s minority Arab community, which nearly doubled its representation in Israel’s parliament with 19 seats. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot had ruled out working with them prior to the vote.

Netanyahu has since continued to attack the Arab parties, accusing them of holding stances on Gaza and the West Bank he considers unacceptable. Eisenkot, however, has indicated he is open to working with anyone who agrees to four conditions on Israeli sovereignty and opposition to Hamas, potentially opening a path to a deal that could propel him to power and avoid fresh elections.

While Netanyahu is the leader of the single largest party, it is up to Herzog — largely a ceremonial figure — to decide who has the first shot at forming a government. He will hold initial consultations with party officials on Wednesday, beginning a delicate process that could last weeks.

“I hope the representatives will come with an open mind, and today I add: with an open heart,” Herzog said in a statement Sunday. “Come to listen and to be heard, to share ideas, and to find creative solutions to prevent another round of elections.”
Israel launches strikes on Gaza

Netanyahu, who is set to remain in his post as a caretaker until a new government can be formed, has claimed Arab parties used foreign backing to “steal” the elections, without providing evidence. Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has said it is investigating possible foreign interference in the election but that the probe was not intended to “cast aspersions” on any specific group.
Arab party leaders have strongly denied any wrongdoing, while Herzog pushed party leaders to accept the election result.

“During an election campaign, candidates naturally and predictably climb to lofty positions,” Herzog said in his statement. “But the elections are over. The election results are a fact. They are a reality. And now is the time to call on all our leaders to stop climbing and face this reality.”

The four conditions Eisenkot set out for prospective partners include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state, committing to the values of its independence, accepting mandatory military service for all Israeli citizens and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization.

“Every Knesset member who is willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner on the path to establishing a new and better government for Israel,” he said in a statement on Saturday. “The door to the government we will form will be open to every public representative who accepts these principles and is ready to rise to the occasion.”
Netanyahu, meanwhile, said Sunday that it was “forbidden” to form a government with Mansour Abbas, head of Arab-led party Ra’am.

He said on X that Abbas wants to establish a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, and evacuate Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, citing an old Ra’am policy platform.
During the campaign, Netanyahu’s Likud party repeatedly alleged that Eisenkot would usher the Arab parties into power.
In one of several AI-generated videos posted by Netanyahu, Eisenkot was portrayed astride a wooden Trojan horse, with Abbas and left-wing politician Yair Golan inside.
Abbas said Friday that he was coordinating with other Arab leaders on “the prospects for forming a government to replace the one led by Netanyahu.”

Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc contains a broad array of ideologies and views on the issue, ranging from Golan, who has publicly advocated for a deal with the Arab parties, to Avigdor Lieberman of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, who continues to oppose working with them.
With that much friction, a stalemate and more elections remain a real possibility.

Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News that Israel still appears stuck, adding that Eisenkot’s conditions for the Arab parties are effectively asking them to “forsake their identity.”
“I don’t think we will see the opposition led by Eisenkot forming a government in Israel,” he said. “So what we have now is a deadlock.”
For the major Israeli parties, it is a choice “between Israel as a democratic state or Israel as a Zionist exclusive society,” he said.
But Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at U.K. think tank Chatham House, sees flexibility that could yield a breakthrough.
Parties “make all these promises before the election, and it is obvious that you break at least some of them after the election,” he said.

title: ‘Please help us’: Savannah Guthrie issues new plea for help in mother’s kidnapping
summary: Heartbroken “TODAY” co-host Savannah Guthrie on Sunday renewed her plea for information about the kidnapping of her 84-year-old mother, Nancy Guthrie, from her Tucson, Arizona, home nine months ago.
story: Heartbroken “TODAY” co-host Savannah Guthrie on Sunday renewed her plea for information about the kidnapping of her 84-year-old mother, Nancy Guthrie, from her Tucson, Arizona, home nine months ago.

Guthrie posted an image on Instagram of a drawing by her young daughter that evoked her feelings about her elderly mother’s disappearance. The drawing shows a blue umbrella surrounded by raindrops, with a caption that reads: “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
Her child’s artwork “says so much about how I feel,” Guthrie wrote.

“For Annie and Tommy, for Cam and Kristine, for Mike and me and for all of mom’s beloved grandchildren: we ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” Guthrie said in the post, naming members of her immediate family. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know.”
Nancy Guthrie was reported missing from her Tucson home on Feb. 1.
Authorities have said the crime involved a ransom demand. The investigation by the Pima County Sheriff’s Department, with assistance from the FBI, has not produced any significant breaks in the case.
A hair found in Nancy Guthrie’s home did not lead to a suspect after testing, investigators said in July.
For Subscribers

A task force created to solve the crime is still chasing leads in an effort to find Nancy Guthrie and any suspect involved. The team “traveled to Florida to meet with lab scientists to see what more could be done to advance the case,” the sheriff’s office recently said on X.
For Subscribers

Guthrie said her family has been changed forever by the tragedy. She called her mother “a light in this world” and begged for answers so her family can “celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves.”
The morning show host noted that the reward for information is still available.
“We are begging you,” Guthrie wrote. “Please help us.”

title: Sen. Tim Scott dodges on whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race
summary: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the battleground seat
story: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins following a bombshell report from The New York Times about Democrats’ alleged efforts to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
Asked on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether he would accept the election results if Peltola is certified to have won the Senate seat, Scott did not directly answer the question.
“Dan Sullivan is going to win, Kristen,” he told moderator Kristen Welker. “You know that, and that’s the only thing I’m going to tell you because it’s the truth.”

Scott went on to criticize Democrats for allegedly working to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a controversy that exploded last week following a report from The New York Times.

“What I can tell you about the truth is you can’t trust Mary Peltola’s campaign and the collusion between her campaign and the DSCC,” said Scott, who also serves as the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP counterpart to the DSCC.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democrats allegedly sought to recruit a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan. The report said the efforts allegedly involved members of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats to the Senate.

Following the report, the DSCC said in a statement that it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” Peltola, too, said she “knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”
Asked a second time whether he would accept the election results, Scott dodged the question.
“Number one, Dan Sullivan, the real Dan Sullivan, will win,” said Scott. “And number two, it actually is a federal offense to confuse voters.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit the challenger Dan J. Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law.

Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, participated in interviews with The New York Times, but later said she retracted “all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate race.”

Before The New York Times report was published, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block the certification of the results of the Senate election if Dan S. Sullivan loses. The DOJ cited potential voter confusion over having another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
In the aftermath of the Times’ report, President Donald Trump has said that both Peltola and the challenger Sullivan should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.

On Thursday, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering a state investigation to determine whether the alleged “scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.”

title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
summary: Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.
story: Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.

Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents.

Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture.

When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain.

But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%.

After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data.
And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%).

“The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.

Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war.

Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year.
Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security.
“Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now.

Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years.

Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election.

Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections.

That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks.

It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular.
Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties.
Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year.

“Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response.
“I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added.
Republican disappointment
Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year.
Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%.
Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises.

Trump still maintains an important hold on his base, with near-unanimous job approval (93%) among Republicans who say they support the MAGA movement. But he’s slipped significantly with Republicans who don’t consider themselves part of the MAGA movement: 54% of them approve and 46% disapprove of his performance. Meanwhile, 20% of those non-MAGA Republicans say they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after this election.
The president has seen other important voting blocs drift away, too.

His net approval rating has dropped 18 points among white voters without college degrees compared to the first NBC News poll of his second term, in 2025. He’s also seen significant declines among young voters and Latino voters, groups that he overperformed with on his way back to the White House in 2024.

One of Republicans’ big advantages in 2026 is a favorable political map: Democrats have to win back districts and states Trump won in 2024 to take back Congress. In the Senate, they need to win at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins.

But the president’s approval rating is underwater in states he won in 2024: 53% of registered voters there disapprove of his job performance, while 47% approve. In March 2025, his approval rating in those states was 10 points higher.
Democratic warning signs
There are some warning signs for Democrats, on top of the fact that a lower share of voters have positive views of the Democratic Party compared to the Republican Party.
For Subscribers

The fight for control of the House and especially the Senate will take place in Trump-won areas, and Republicans are leading on the congressional ballot in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024. The big question is whether that’s enough to withstand shifts in some key places.
For Subscribers

Government corruption has been a central theme of Democrats’ message this year, but voters narrowly trust Republicans to better handle the issue by 5 points. Even so, Democrats are leading on the congressional ballot among the 28% of voters who do not trust either party on the issue.
Republican leaders in Congress are also slightly better off than their Democratic counterparts, but that’s mostly because voters don’t know how to feel about them.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has the highest positive rating of congressional leaders: 24% have positive views of him and 34% have negative views. Just 10% of voters have positive views of Johnson’s counterpart across the Capitol, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, while 22% view him negatively.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is viewed positively by 18% of voters and negatively by 35%. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who’s led Democrats in the body for almost a decade, is far better defined — to his detriment. Just 13% of voters view him positively, and 53% view him negatively.

“It’s not great for the Democrats … for 2028,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, when asked about the low marks for Democrats. “But I don’t see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers.”
Half of voters have negative views of tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has emerged as one of the most prolific Republican donors in the country over the last two years, while 34% view him positively.

Voters are more split about a pair of prominent progressives, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Sanders is more popular: 41% view him positively and 42% view him negatively, while Ocasio-Cortez’s numbers stand at 31%-42%.

Democrats hold a significant lead in the battle for Congress despite those factors. But there are indications throughout the poll that the party’s lead is propped up strongly by anti-Republican sentiment, not warm feelings for Democrats.
Voters who want Democratic control of Congress are divided between whether their vote is more in favor of Democrats or driven more by opposition to Republicans.
“Get your s--- together, Democrats,” an Ohio Democratic woman said when asked what message she wanted to send with her vote this year. “I’m voting for you, but work it out.”
The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Oct. 28-30 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

title: Minor detained after U.S. warned Russia of possible Moscow terror attack, FSB says
summary: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) ​said it had received information from ‌the United States through established partner channels about preparations for a terrorist attack ​in Moscow.
story: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) ​said it had received information from ‌the United States through established partner channels about preparations for a terrorist attack ​in Moscow.

The FSB said Sunday that it had “verified” the information received from U.S. law enforcement, and “as a result of these operations, a Russian minor was detained,” Russia’s TASS state news agency reported.

It said that an individual “had posted photos on the short-video platform TikTok showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, a cap, protective eyewear, and headphones—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon.”
For Subscribers

A subsequent search of his devices revealed a “subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the messaging app Telegram, and a significant number of search queries concerning past terrorist attacks, mass shootings, and other acts of violence,” TASS reported, citing the FSB.

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow ⁠said separately it was “aware of ​a credible threat of a mass casualty ​event” on Saturday at Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve and that the U.S. government was ​coordinating with Russian authorities.
For Subscribers

The Tsaritsyno ​Museum Reserve, a palace museum and park complex ‌south ⁠of Moscow, was temporarily closed on Saturday and access to the park was restricted, the RIA news agency ​reported, ​citing Russian ⁠law enforcement agencies.

Russian tabloid Baza reported that the venue was evacuated toward the end of an organ concert, which was cut short with about ten minutes left in the program. A separate concert dedicated to the folk traditions of the North Caucasus region was subsequently canceled, the outlet reported.

In March 2024, the U.S. Embassy warned ​that extremists had imminent plans ​for ⁠an attack in Moscow. Days later, gunmen attacked the Crocus City Hall ⁠concert ​venue outside Moscow, killing ​more than 140 people.
